div.head: POULTRY PEN.
div.p: POULTRY PEN.
HINTS AND INTERESTING FACTS AND CHATS FOR AMATEURS.

SOLDIERS AS EGG FARMERS. We import millions of eggs every year from the Continent. They are of a second-grade quality, which cannot be sold in the neighbour- hood in small or retail quantities, and so arrive here at wholesale rates. Is it possible for us to capture this foreign trade? The cruel, har- vest of the war will yield thousands of disabled soldiers. It is the moral duty of the Govern- ment to look after the nation's heroes, and if possible to accomplish this by finding them suitable employment. This could be done by taking over land and erecting the necessary buildings for poultry farming, the " farmers " being the soldiers.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

THE IMPORTANCE OF HEALTHY STOCK. Under no circumstances whatever should an unhealthy bird be aliowv..l a place in the breed- ing pen, since such cannot fail to have an ex- tremely injurious effect upon the progeny. Hens that are selected either for laying or breeding purposes should possess sound and vigorous constitutions, any that show the least evidence of disease being rigidly excluded. I do not mean that should a hen have a cold Or a purely exterior complaint, such as bumble foot or scaly leg, that she should be rejected, for these are not infectious, and cannot be trans- mitted to the offspring. They are really only temporary matters, and as such cannot affect either the eggs or the chickens. It is when a fowl is suffering or has suffered from an in- fectious and organic disease that the danger arises. The only really satisfactory way of eradicating disease from the poultry yard, Or preventing it from making an appearance, is to rely entirely upon stock birds that are thoroughly healthy and vigorous. There are several signs that indicate good health—a bright red comb, activity, readiness for food, and a glossy and smooth appearance of the feathers. Fowls that are unhealthy, on the other hand, are rarely active; their combs, as a rule, are either dull or of a whitish tinge, their feathers are usually rough and draggled, while they seldom possess good appetites. There are, of course, other indications peculiar to the com- plaint from which they are suffering, but these can only be learnt by experience. Even when eggs are intended for edible and not for breed- ing purposes unhealthy fowls should be allowed no place in the pen, since they are rarely profit- able, besides which the idea of eating eggs from unhealthy birds is exceedingly unpleasant. Then, too, fowls that are in a hard condition should be selected in preference to those that are flat and flabby, since those in the latter state never prove reliable or satisfactory for stock purposes.—lefiddlesex, in "Farm and Home."

div.head: ABOUT FOODS.
div.p: ABOUT FOODS.

Foods should be correctly balanced so that they contain 1 part albumen to La parts car- bohydrates and fat. To find the correct ratio, multiply the fats by a, add to the carbohydrates, and divide by the albumen. A food handy for balancing a ratio is clover, 'hay, meal, it is rich in albuminoids. Oyster shell helps form the egg-shells and sharp flint grit helps grind the food. Meatmeal, bonemeal, and fishmeal are good egg producing foods, but they must be usecl sparingly. Fresh, clean water must be before the birds at all times Feed early and regularly, never keep your fowls waiting beyond their usual time. Maize is a good grain for the cold weather, ii should be seldom used in summer or early autumn _ _ _
A gocd scratching feed is composed of buck- wheat. oats, millet and wheat.—" Poultry World."

div.head: USEFUL HINTS.
div.p: USEFUL HINTS.

Dry and well ventilated houses are impera- live, and it must always be seen to that the grit. box is well supplied with grit and shell. The dust bath is very useful in keeping vermin down, so by all means see that the birds can indulge in this most necessary exercise. Tht effects of the dust bath can be greatly improved if sulphur Er a little black hellebore powder h

mixed with it. Very few insects can resist these powders. The plumage of many a good bird is spoiled by want of attention during the time the feathers are growing. If the quill be- comes hard and does not break off, the feathers, if allowed to remain so, will become spoiled. How common it is to find when a bird has moulted into its new plumage that there are bars or notches write hollow in the webbing, a: if the same had been cut. They are caused by the quill or sheath becoming hard and refusinv to leave the feathers until the spoliation of it has taken place. This shows that the sheath must be kept rather juicy, and not allowed to dry up to such an extent that it will not peel off. Birds should be handled at least once a
week, and if the sheath is not peeling off tis-

should do it should be taken off. Great care must be used, or the feathers may be easily pulled out. In order to remove it soak well in warm water, when by the manipulation of the finger and thumb it will easily come away. The drying of the sheath to such- an extent that it will not peel off is usually due to the bird being below par, hence steps should be taken to get it in a better condition.—" Feathered World."
Eggs, Poultry, &c.

div.head: KAVARIS
div.p: KAVARIS

Thenew Food for Poultry and Young Animals. (Hargreaves Pattnt). Makes Birds strong and healthy; eggs plentiful abd fertile; lightens trouble and risk in rearing young stock; ensures good constitution; remarkable results.Tß Y IT.

The prolonged spell of dry weather has affected both the hay and root crops, and in view of the reduction in yield and the in- creased demand for hay and fodder next winter the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries wish to draw the attention of farmers to ensilage. This system of storing fodder in the green state is well known, and silage has an. established reputation as a food for stock; but under present circumstances it has two special advantages. Ensilage affords a safeguard against waste should the autumn prove too wet for harvesting late hay crops, and it provides, in silage, a form of green food which makes a very good substitute for roots. In many cases hay aftermath might be con- verted into silage. When the atermath is grassy a top dressing of icwt. sulphate of ammonia or other quick-acting nitrogenous manure would be useful. It is not too late to sow crops for silage purposes in July and August, A mixture such as vetches, oats, and a little rape would make good silage, and prove an effective " smother " crop if sown early in July on land where roots may have falled be- cause of drought. If the stubbles are broken up as soon as the corn is in stock, and sown with white mustard or rape, useful crops for filling the silo may be expected. The main essential in making silage is com- pression, to exclude air, and this subject is usually best attained when the silage crops are cut while still in the immature condition, ano carted soon afterwards. Silage is now generally made in stave silos or in stacks. The stave silo, which is widely used in the United States, has been successfully tried in some parts of Eng- land. It entails less waste than the stack, and needs no artificial weighting; the fodder is chaffed before being stored, and the greater depth of the silo as compared with its diameter ensures sufficient compression. On the other hand, a stack saves the initial cost of a silo, and may be erected in any convenient position. For particulars on the making of silage will be found in Leaflet No. 9, and on catch crops in Special Leaflet No. 28. Copies of either may be obtained free of charge, and post free, on appli- cation to the Secretary, Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, Whitehall-place, London, S.W. Letters or postcards of applications so addressed need not be stamped.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
A PROGRESSIVE COUNTRYSIDE.

The farmer finds himself to-day in a remark- able position, and it is doubtful if he has yet realised the full significance of the • change. which has come about in his relationship to the community. For years past he has been told by windy carpetbaggers that his methods are archaic. The particular political party which he has made his own has calmly thrown him over, lie has not received a particle of sym- pathy when he has demonstrated his inability to grow wheat at a profit. The children of his villages have been educated out of them into the towns. Now a dramatic change has come. The nation is faced with that world shortage of wheat which formed the subject of many prophetic letters in the "Agricultural Econo- mist and Horticultural Review" before the war was thought of and at last it discovers the im- portance of the farmer.—" Agricultural Econo- mist and Horticultural Review."

div.head: WATERING STOCK.
div.p: WATERING STOCK.

The majority of the ailments—acute indiges- tion, colic, enteritis, &c.—affecting the,- diges- tive system of 'ffirm animal S arise from im-- proper feeding and watering. The water supply for stock, says "Farm. and Home," is an especially important matter, but (M 3 which often receives too little attention -from stock- owners. So long as an animal will drink it, no water is on some farms considered too foal for horses and cows. There has been much im- provement in this matter of late years, but greater attention to the supply is still needed. Not only is this neglect on the part of stock- owners responsible for many cases of colic in horses, but many other diseases also are trace- able to impure water. An unlimited supply of pure water is essential to the health of all animals used for farm purposes. Pools formed from surface drainage where large quantities of organic matter are carried into them, and wells or pools contiguous to farmyards or manure heaps, are especially to be avoided. Water from good tanks or wells, running streams, and properly-constructed pools is usually good, but too much care cannot be taken in reference to
this matter. The quantity of water is also o importance. No animal will drink too much i watered sufficiently often.

div.head: ENSILAGE A SAFEGUARD AGAINST
div.p: ENSILAGE A SAFEGUARD AGAINST
WASTE IF RAIN THREATENS LATE CROPS
IN THE GARDEN.
CONTINUED FLOWERING OF SWEET PEAS.

The condition of the plants and their promise of profuse and long-continued bloom may be expected to turn on the treatment to which the soil and seedling plants have been subjected. Growers will compare their own plants with those of their friemis. Where there is superi- ority the reasons for it Will be elicited, in order that the lessons learned may be applied in future years. But a good deal of help may be given to plants now. It may be given in the form of liquid manure, water, and mulching, a thorough soak- ing with plain water, followed by the spreading 11 of a coat of manure along the rows, ought to ' help the plants enormously. As to liquid manure, that from natural sources, where available, may be applied twice a week. Then, much good may be done with prepared fer- tilisers. Even where natural liquid manure is at command, special fertilisers should be used alternately, as they provide valuable in- gredients in a concentrated form and in care- fully balanced proportions.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

div.head: LETTUCES IN THE SUMMER.
div.p: LETTUCES IN THE SUMMER.

To be tender, lettuces need to be grown quickly, and sowing at least every fortnight should be made up to the end- of July. Rich soil should in all cases be the rule, and as the season advances a somewhat shaded position should be selected. If the weather is very dry frequent applications of water are necessary, and those who may have a light, gravelly soil to deal with may with advantage mulch be- tween the plants with some rotten manure

div.head: PARSLEY.
div.p: PARSLEY.

The present is a good time to make a sowing of parsley, and as ooe clunot have *,03 ;arch of this in winter a:.d early gpring, it is well to sow in various aspects. it the soil is in good heart and the seeds are watered freely, should the weather be dry, germination soon takes place. The seedlings when strong enough may be _freely thinned, the thinnings being used to form another bed. These transplanted batches come in well for lifting, say, in October for placing in frames, as the plants have abund- ance of fibrous roots and a ball of soil can be usually lifted with the roots. It is also a good plan to sow in some sheltered corner, where in the autumn a frame can be placed over the plants.

div.head: WALLFLOWERS.
div.p: WALLFLOWERS.

Those who sowed wallflowers, as advised in a previous issue, will now have nice strong seed- lings, which should be pricked out into lines one foot apart, allowing a distance of nine inches between The plants in the row. Before planting it is well to take the point of the tap root off, as this causes fibrous roots to be pro- duced, which, when lifted for putting into their permanent position, have a nice ball of soil at- tached. It is well, too, to bear in mind that rich soil is not necessary, as this engenders a gross sappy growth, which in the event of a severe winter invariably suffers. Until the seedlings become established watering if the weather is dry should be attended to.

div.head: EVERLASTING PEAS.
div.p: EVERLASTING PEAS.

The common pink everlasting pea and its white variety will, when established and nourished by timely mulchings of manure and frequent soakings of wEiter, continue in bloom for a long time. What causes a cessation of blooming is allowing the seed pods to form. As soon as the flowers set the shoots; cease to ex- tend, but if the seed pods are removed flower- ing will continue. One need not hesitate about gathering freely, as the more bloom taken from the plants the more will come. The same thing holds good in the case of the sweet pea.—Wick, In "Farm and Home."

Before Councillor Roberts (in the chair) and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes, Jane Patten was sum- moned at Tuesday's Borough Police Court for neglecting her children, Annie, May and John, in such a way as to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health. Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C. Mr. Browne said that defendant lived in a house in Eaton-square, off Orford-lane, fof which she paid half-a-crown a week. A Good Mother Up To The Beginning Of The
been done to reform the woman, but without

avail. Mrs. Rogerson, the keeper of the lodging- house at which prisoner stayed, said that pri- soner was drunk the previous Saturday night and the children were badly 'neglected. - Mrs. Dickenson corroborated Mr. Browne's statement as to the gift of twopence and what the prisoner did with it Tried to Get Rid of the Children. Mrs. Dickenson's cousin, Mrs. Moran, of 36, Kerfoot-street, said that on Tuesday morning she saw prisoner, her two children, and a man who afterwards left her. Prisoner asked five or six men whether they knew of anyone who would "have the children." They referred her to a lodging-house, but she replied that she did not want a lodging-house, but someone to take the children.

Inspector Wainwright, of the N.S.P.C.C., said he saw the woman begging in Froghall-lane and followed her. When he spoke to her she denied that she had been begging. She was the worse 'for. drink. He examined the children and,,,fciund ,thera, though, fairly well nourished;' in very- dirty -condition. The boy's boots were worn out, and it must hare been painful for him to walk. Prisoner said that her hus- band had.. dvetejte,cl. her. Witness took the woman—who vTas,cakite destitute--and the chil- dren 'to :the' Workhouse. - - • Prisoner said she went to the Workhouse at Wrexham a week the previous Monday, be- cause her husband ill-treated her. Her boy was aiterwards brought to the Workhouse by a policeman. She came to Warrington by train to look for work. Her husband gave her no money for clothes for the children, and they had "got dirty with knocking about."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1915.
IN THE COURTS.
A STOLEN SHIRT,
Lodelpg-liouse Theft Leads To Two
Months' Hard Labour.

At Saturday's sitting of the Borough Police Court, before Mr. R. T. Fairclough (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion and Mr. A. J. Jolley, Andrew Feeney Thompson, a general labourer, giving a lodging-house at 10, Town-hill, War- rington, as his address, was charged with steal- ing a shirt, valued at 25., the property of Frederick Elliott, another lodger at the lodging- house. He told the Court that he took the shirt in mistake. The Chief Constable said prisoner came to Warrington on June Bth, and went to the lodg- ing-house. In accordance with the Aliens Restriction Order, he filled up the required form, but did so incorrectly, and although he was not charged under the Act, he had, by making the false statement, committed an offence. On Friday of the previous week prisoner appeared to have gone to a pile of shirts and to ilave taken therefrom one which did not'belong-to him, subsequently pawning it. The pawnticket had not been found.

div.head: Gave a False Name and Address.
div.p: Gave a False Name and Address.

He told the pawnbroker that the shirt was his own property, but tendered a false name and address. Acting-Sergeant Armstrong made in-' quiries, and they went to show that there was a concerted larceny on the part of prisoner and another man, who had absconded after pawning the stolen property—in this instance, also, a shirt. Prisoner said that another man who was lodging in the house sent him to get his shirt. Being drunk at the time he took Elliott's shirt by mistake; in fact he supposed he took the first one• he came to and pawned it for his friend: He was sent to gaol for 21 days' hard labour.

div.head: DRINK, AGAIN.
div.p: DRINK, AGAIN.
Given Another Chance To Put Things

- - Right. Clara Sharp, a married woman, of 54, Turner- street, was summoned at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday for neglecting her four chil- dren in such a manner as to cause them un- necessary suffering and injury to health. Mr. A. Browne, for the N.S.P.C.C., said that the case was an adjourned one. Defendant had been brought up before, and had been given a chance. Her husband was employed at the Gas Works, and was a respectable man. An improvement had been noted by Inspector Wainwright, but retrogression followed, and now things were again in a bad condition. " Not Much Excuse for Defendant."

There was not much excuse for defendant, ap there had been as much as 375. 6d. coming into the house, for in addition to the husband, two daughters were working. The Chairman (Councillor Roberts) said that he thought the Bench ought to give defendant one more chance, and addressing the lefendmit, he asked: "Are you prepared, if we give you another opportunity, to put things right? .
Defendant: Yes, -sir. Promised to Give Up the Drink!

The Chairman: Why do you take drink? With food at present prices you can't afford drink. It's the cause of all your trouble. Why do you take it? You promised us before that you would not take it. Are you prepared to give it up altogether? Defendant (in tears): Yes. The 'case was adjourned.

div.head: WHILST HER HUSBAND FOUGHT
div.p: WHILST HER HUSBAND FOUGHT
Soldier's Wife Went On The " Drink " And Neglected Children.

div.head: Year.
div.p: Year.
Up to the beginning of the present year she had looked after her children well. Her hus- band was in the Liverpool Scottish, and was at _

the present time abroad. Inspector Wain- wright called at the house on February Bth, and found things in a bad state. He learned that defendant was in the habit of going out and leaving the children alone in the house. When she received her allowance she "went and drank the money." The Inspector made a number of calls at the house and found the home in a filthy state, and learned on one occasion that the woman was drunk and at another house in Pocket-street. The Husband Wounded.
When taxed with neglecting the children, defendant said she had been worried on account of a rumour that her husband had been killed.

Mr. Browne added that it was quite true that defendant's husband had been said to be killed, but, as a matter of fact, he had only been wounded. The woman asked for another chance, but subsequent calls at the house revealing little improvement, the Inspect°, decided to take proceedings. The eldest child, Annie, was found, on the occasion of the last visit, to be suffering from glandular enlarge meat. The other children had sore heads, and all were in a dirty State, like the rooms of the house.

div.head: Children in a Bad State.
div.p: Children in a Bad State.

Dr. Peacock gave a certificate to the effect that the children were in a bad state and suffering unnecessarily, also that the girl Annie (aged eight), was suffering, from glandular enlargement. Defendant was a good mother when she was sober. The Rev. Father Wilson, of St. Mary's Church, and the Mother Superior had been very good to her. A sentence of one month's imprisonment was passed.

div.head: "A THOROUGH BAD LOT."
div.p: "A THOROUGH BAD LOT."
Police Character _Of A Neglect!
Mother.

A sad story of a woman's depravity was un- folded at the Borough Police Court, when Kate Edwards, a young married woman, of no fixed abode, but belonging to Wrexham, was committed to gaol for three months on a charge of neglecting her two children during the past six months, a charge to which she pleaded not guilty. Husband Not At All To Blame.

Prosecuting on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., Mr.' Arthur Browne described the case as a most extraordinary one, and said that the prisoner was the wife of a miner, who lived near Wrex- ham. The husband was in regular work and received good wages, and he was not at all to blame for his wife's conduct towards the chil- dren. Prisoner would persist in leaving Wrex- ham and in wandering about the country, tak- ing her children with her anti then neglecting them., On Tuesday of last week she arrived in Warrington and went to stay at Rogerson's lodging-house, in Ship-yard, along with a man who was not her husband. They registered themselves as "Mr. and Mrs. Edward Lister." The than stayed one night and then left the woman and had not been seen since. That sort of thing, said Mr. Browne, was, he under- stood, a regular thing, and it went without saying • that with the mother living• such a life the children must be neglected. Begged Coppers and Spent Them on Beer.

On the Friday Mrs. Mary Dickenson, of 11, Appleton-street, was talking to her cousin, when prisoner and her two children came up. Prisoner said, "Will you give my baby a butty'? I have nowhere to go and the chil- dren are hungry and have nothing to eat." Mrs. Dickenson's\ cousin gave the woman two- pence, and told her to buy some cakes. One of the children remarked, "Yes, come on, mother, and buy one," but the woman went into a public-house and had a pint of beer. The children were dirty, their boots were worn out, and they were sadly neglected. Inspector Evans (of the N.S.P.C.C., stationed at Wrexham), said prisoner's -"husband was a respectable, hard-working man. Everything had

The Bench imposed a fine of 20s. Rounding a Corner at Twenty Miles an Hour. A similar charge, in relation to the driving of a motor-car, was preferred against Herbert Ferarrio. of "Richmond," Barton-lane, Eccles, near Manchester. He was summoned for driving a motor-car along Mersey-street at a rate of twenty miles an hour, on June 20th. P.C. Taylor gave evidence as to seeing defend- ant approach Warrington Bridge from Mersey- street at a sneed of twenty miles an hour and turn round the corner, the wheels skidding six inches in the process. For the defendant, who said he didn't think he was going at the speed stated, evidence was given by an occupant of the car, named Mr. Steinart. who stated that the car stopped in about five yards. A fine of 20s. was imposed.

div.head: Had Been Given Many Chances.
div.p: Had Been Given Many Chances.

The Chief Constable told the Court that the Deputy Chief Constable of Denbighshire had furnished him with a report on the woman, one sentence of which said that she was "a thorough bad lot" and deserved no sympathy. Her husband and the authorities had given her many chances to reform, but they were all thrown away. She had been in prison several times for various offences, and in 1914 was con- victed no fewer than. six times for being drunk
whilst .in charge ofa child. Prisoner was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

div.head: DANGEROUS DRIVING.
div.p: DANGEROUS DRIVING.

Two Motorists Fined For Travelling At Excessive Speeds. A joiner named Giggs, living in Willis-street, Warrington. was summoned at the Borough Police Court on Thursday, for driving a motor- cycle at a dangerous speed, in the Knutsford- road, Warrington, on 28th June. P.S. Hewitt and P.C. Taylor told how on the day in ques- tion, defendant came along the Knutsford-road. towards Warrington Bridge, at a speed of about twenty-five miles an hour. He did not sound his horn, and passed another motor-cyclist quite easily. When stopped, defendant said he didn't know he was going as fast as that. Defendant said that he was travelling at the rate of twelve miles an hour. and when the Sergeant put his hand up he stopped at once. He couldn't have stopped so promptly if he had been travelling at twenty-five miles an hour. ' A clean record was revealed by defendant's licence.

div.head: BELL-RINGERS FINED.
div.p: BELL-RINGERS FINED.
Boys Who Have _Made Themselves
A Nuisance.

Four lads, John Burns, (15), of 21, Frederick- street; Percy Worthington (15), of 36, Thelwall- lane ; John Tickle (16), of 312, Knutsford-road, and William Wareham (16), of 44, Wash- lane, were summoned at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday for wantonly ring- ing a door-bell in Museum-street, to the annoyance of the resident of the house, on Monday evening, June 21st. Detective Green proved the case. The magistrates, after hearing the evidence, told Burns he could go, whereat The Chief Constable said that the police were constantly receiving complaints about bells being rung by boys who ran away. Doctors were amongst the worst sufferers, for the door had to be opened, for fear of an urgent case needing attention. He (Mr. Nicholls) thought an example might be made of the boys. A fine of ss. each was imposed on the other three defendants, who were warned that they would be severely treated if they came up again.

div.head: MILK!
div.p: MILK!
The Question Of Fat Dejicieney.
At the Knutsford Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, J. Herbert Barker, of White House Farm, Bexton, was summoned for selling milk which was deficient in milk fat to the extent of 6.6,per cent.

A police inspector stated that on the 31st May he took a sample of the defendant's milk from his cart, which was in charge of the de- fendant's brother. On analysis it was found to contain 2.8 per cent. of milk fat. The standard laid down by the Board of Agriculture was 2 per cent. On taking a sample from the cows a week afterwards the sample proved on analysis to contain 3.3 per cent. of milk fat.

Mr. T. S. Sto;el, of Warrington, who defended, said that he should, prove that the milk was sold as it came from the cow, and if the justices were satisfied with that evidence, then the de- fendant was entitled to an acquittal. Evidence was given that the milk had not been tampered with, after which the Chairman said they were satisfied the milk was sold as it came from the cow, and the case would be dismissed.

div.head: PRESERVING EGGS.
div.p: PRESERVING EGGS.

As regards the eggs to be preserved care should be taken to examine them carefully, to see that the shells are sound, as a cracked egg will not only go wrong itself, but most injuri- ously affect the eggs in its immediate neigh- bourhood. The eggs must be new-laid and they should be packed with the narrow end down- wards in layers from the bottom to the top of the vessel. The latter should be either an earthenware crock or jar, or a tub or barrel, and in either case the vessel should be per- fectly clean, and it should be purified • and sweetened by being scalded with boiling water. Put three layers of eggs at the bottom of the vessel, then add the solution keeping it well stirred; when the three layers are covered three additional layers .can be put down and simi- larly covered with the solution, and so on un- til the vessel is filled within an inch of the top. Let this inch be filled with Ohf! solution and then cover the vessel with a tight fitting cloth outside so as to exclude the air as far as possible. In case of preserving with water-glass the prescription is: 1 quart of water-glass to each, 10 quarts of water, the latter should be pure and thoroughly boiled, and then cooled. A cool, dark place, such as a dry, cold cellar is the most suitable storage for the eggs. On no account should the eggs be washed before packing, to do so would be to remove the natural greasy coating on the outside of the shells already mentioned. :Water-glass is scientifically known as sodium and potassium silicate, and it is a very cheap product, solium silicate being usually the cheaper.— Poultry World."

The scholars of Orford Sunday School met at the school at 1.30 p.m. and marched in pro- cession to the Church, where a short service was held, conducted by the Vicar (the Rev. G. Vale Owen). After prayers of intercession and the singing of the hymn "For thee, 0, dear, dear country," the procession was reformed and proceeded to the field very kindly lent by Mr. T. H. Pretty. During the rain the chil- dren gathered in the school and whiled away the time singing patriotic songs. Tea was served at 4 o'clock, and the evening was spent in games in the field. The sports were not held. The money usually spent on prizes will be used to buy comforts for the woundeed soldiers and divided amongst the various hospitals.

div.head: HAPPENINGS AND ARRANGEMENTS.
div.p: HAPPENINGS AND ARRANGEMENTS.

Walking Day" is living a long time, con- sidering the number of folk who have been sitting on it. The weather stepped in last week- end, with the result that the festival will be spread over nine days from t vinning to tnd. Happenings of last Saturday and Sun:lay, and arrangements for this week-end will be found below.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: THE PARISH CHURCH.

The Parish Church gave ilp the idea of held- ing a procession last Sunday or a( count of the I rain. It will take place to-morraw, if find, from 2to 4. The procession will start from Fairfield, the clergy, choir and ,church officers leading. The route is •Ma fiebesi6r;-r:lad, Church-street, •Greenall-street, Ellesmere-street, Napier-street, Mersey-street, Church-street, Fennel-street, School Brow, Dalton Bank, Claud-street, Hume-street, Marsh House-lane, Padgate-lane, Alexandra-street, Manchester, road, Church-street, to the• 'Church. The Church-street boys will meet the procession at the top of Greenall-street and follow the girls. The St. Clement's scholars will join in at the junction of Napier-street and Mersey-street, and the St. George's scholars at the junction of Hopwood-street and School Brow. Singing will take place at four points, viz., the junction of Napier and Mersey-streets, the junction of Hopwood-street. and School Brow, the junction of Marsh House-lane and Padgate-lane, at the Church. The scholars ;had their -games, &c., and ea on Saturday, the former in the Training College field in Salisbury-street, and the latter in the various schools. The Blue Coat School Band played in the field from 6 to 8.

div.head: ST. JAMES', LATCHFORit.
div.p: ST. JAMES', LATCHFORit.
The members of St. James' Sunday School

had their annual field day on Saturday. The large field at Wilderspool had ben :kindly lent by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and"CO.,'Ltd., and in this spacious enclosure the children and their friends passed a very enjoyable afternoon. Tea was served in St. James' School for the elder scholars, while the infants were enter- tained in a large shed on the field at Wilders- pool. A large parochial procession had been arranged for Sunday afternoon, but had to be abandoned on account of the rain. If it is fine to-morrow the procession will start from St. James' School at 2.30 p.m. and wend its way to St. Hilda's Mission Church in Slater-street, where .a halt will be made and hymns sung, and will then return by way of the Knutsford- road, .halting at the old burial ground, where again hymns will be sung and intercession prayers offered.

div.head: ST. ANN'S.
div.p: ST. ANN'S.

The scholars of St. Ann's had tea on Satur- day in the schools. Afterwards thay wended their way to a field, kindly loaned by Mr. R. C. Shaw, near Orford Hall. Here, as the weather picked up, a very happy low hours wc.re spent in a variety of games—ericket, roundrys, Sze. Before leaving the field the st%holars were the recipients of the usual edible present. The rain prevented the intended procession being held, but there was a special service in the Church. The collection was devoted to the purchasing of comforts for the wounded soldiers.

div.head: ORFORD PARISH CHURCII.
div.p: ORFORD PARISH CHURCII.
ELM WOOD-AVENUE CONGREGA-
TIONAL.

Owing to the unsettled state of the weather the children were entertained on Saturday in the school, where tea was provided for over 300 scholars. Later in the day an adjournment was made to the recreation field in Padgate-lane, but the stay was only .of short duration, as the rain again commenced to fall. • It was decided to postpone the children's sports until August Bank Holiday. On that day a garden party will be held in connection' with the forthcoming sale of work, on the school's recreation field. All scholars will be 'admitted free. This will, no doubt, make up for the disappointment that was felt last Saturday.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN.

In lieu of the usual Sunday school treat to Frodsham, the teachers and scholars of St. John's are joining their Presbyterian friends at Risley to-114. The children leave the Church by motor lorry at one o'clock, friends and others cycling out or taking the train to Padgate and walking the rest of the way to the field, which is close to the •Risley Presbyterian Day School.

div.head: GOLBORNE-STREET BAPTISTS.
div.p: GOLBORNE-STREET BAPTISTS.

The scholars of Golborne-street Baptist Church, together with a number of friends, were conveyed in trams to• Stockton Heath, by special arrangement with the Corporation. From the terminus they walked to Hill Cliffe, where tea was served at the school. After tea, the children adjourned to a field kindly lent by one of the friends of the Church at Stockton Heath. Competitions and races were arranged, and the prizes were distributed, just before returning, by the Pastor (Rev. H. Ogden). Despite the unpropitious weather, those who took part in the proceedings agreed that a very delightful day had been spent.

div.head: 011IER SCHOOLS.
div.p: 011IER SCHOOLS.

Tea was served to the Holy Trinity scholars in the Patten Hall on Saturday afternoon, and the remainder of the day was spent on Messrs. Peter ,Walker t and Son's Recreation Ground. A special service was held in the church on Sunday afternoon. The scholars of St. Luke's spent several happy hours on the Recreation Ground near the school, in which they had tea. The Factory-yard Mission . celebrated , with a tea in the Patten Hall on Friday. The children of St. Peter's Church had tea in the school and subsequently passed the time merrily in a field off Padgate-lane. As usual, the Unitarians went to Lymm for the half-day, visiting the grounds of Mr. John Houghton. Wycliffe Congregational scholars had tea at their school, and later went to a field at Apple- ton.

Bank Quay Working Men's Mission sent their junior scholars to a field at Bewsey, kindly lent by Mr. Warburton. The children of Bewsey-road Wesleyan School proceeded, after tea, to a field in Longshaw- street.
Owing to the doubtful weather, Legh-street Primitive Methodists put oil their field day, but tea was served in the school.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: THE SALVATION ARMY.

The Salvation Army Sunday School did not observe Walking Day last week, but it is arranged that the children shall take part in the processions to-morrow (Anniversary Sun- day) if fine. The youngsters will have theft: treat the first week in August.

When once a beginner has mastered the art of riding, his next thought is how to secure the greatest amount of speed and the maximum amount of comfort with the smallest expendi- ture of energy. This is not a lesson that can be learnt at once. In the first place, the rider Inuit be sufficiently practised to make riding mechanical, as regards position and action. These must become second nature before one can really enjoy the pastime. The position of the rider is also important. This must depend to a certain extent on the length of leg, but most riders agree that the best position is with the centre of a roadster saddle from 81 to 12in. behind the crank centre. The reach should not be too long, a shorter reach is less tiring on long journey. Such a position allows for ankle , action—the art of real cycling, both in additional comfort and reduced effort. Until you have learnt how to use your ankles you are not a real cyclist.

SOUTH AFRICAN RELIABILITY TRIAL. The annual trial for the Vacuum Cup under the auspices of the Cape Peninsular Motor Cycling Club, took place on the 13th May. The distance was comparatively short—some eighty odd miles—and the route fairly easy, but the trial included a hill climb on formula. The hill selected was the steep Sir Lowry Pass, three miles long and rising 1,200 feet. At the time of the run there was a strong south-east wind blowing down the pass, which made the descent more trying. Many of the riders had trouble with their tyres, one entrant having four punctures in the first sixteen miles. A water splash had to be negotiated, but the majority of the riders pushed their mounts through this, though one or two took the water at full speed. The winners were: 1, J. F. Smuts; 2, A. Moralee; 3, P. C. Flint, a newcomer to the route.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY CHURCH
div.p: GREAT SANKEY CHURCH

CHILDREN HOLD HIGH REVELS. On Saturday the annual Walking Day cele- brations in connection with St. Mary's Church and Sunday Sohols took place, though in a modified form. Owing to an outbreak of measles and scarlet fever in and around the dis- trict, the usual public procession was dispensed with, much to the regret and disappoi-ntment

the ignior section, who were. unable to display their treasured finery to advantage. The after- noon unfortunately developed into a wet even- ing, but even the climatic conditions could not damp the ardour of the holiday-makers, who held high revels in the Rectory field.

There is a proposal on foot to construct arterial roads in London. If carried out it will do much to alleviate the congestion of many of our overcrowded thoroughfares. A meeting was held a few weeks ago at the offices of the Local Government Board of the 'Northern Sectional Conference to consider the recommendations of the Special Investigation Committee. The report recommended the construction of the pro- posed new Cambridge-road, North Circular- , road, the road from City-road to Hackney-road, the road from Essex-road to Lea Bridge, and the widening of High-street instead of the pro" posed by-pass at Chipping Barnet.' All of these recommendations were agreed to. The report has still to be considered by the main con- ference, and although nothing will be done ip starting the work until the war is over, it is good news that the matter has not been put Oil one side.

div.head: With The Car.
div.p: With The Car.
RULES FOR COMFORT.
(Queries and correspondence should be addressed to "The Hub," c/o The Editor. Replies can- not be sent by post and all queries will be answered in our columns.)

To ensure ease of running a bicycle should be oiled at least every hundred miles. The neces- sity is more apparent when running over dusty or dirty roads. Only a few drops of oil should be run into each bearing; a larger amount is quite unnecessary and only liable to clog the parts. The hub of the wheels, crank brackets, head bearings and the pedals shouldill come in for their share of attention. ft is not un- common with bicycles in use to find one side of the bearing well oiled, while the other is dry. This is due to the uneven position in which the machine is often left standing, or to the cycle being oiled when it is reclining against a wall. The best way to overcome this difficulty is to put in one or two drops of oil when in a reclining position, then to turn the machine round, giving one or two more drops. In this way the bearings are thoroughly well oiled and the. easy and smooth running of the machine is assured.

div.head: HOW TO RIDE.
div.p: HOW TO RIDE.
A LEFT HAND CORNER.

One of the most perplexing points in connec- tion with driving a sidecar outfit is the action qf the sidecar when taking a left hand corner. Many novices come to grief, until they realisc that such a corner requires a great amount of skill and care in the undertaking. The ten- dency of the sidecar to rise in the air is due to centrifugal force. There are two ways of over- coming the danger. The centre of the road should be kept. and then the corner cut as finely as possible. If it were not against the law it would be better to keep to the right of the road before the corner is taken. Under most conditions it is better to change down before taking the left hand corner. It is a great advantage to do this, and it assists in enablinfr one to keep the sidecar wheel on the road. If the road is known and there is a rise

div.head: PENKETH WESLEYANS' TREAT POSTPONED.
div.p: PENKETH WESLEYANS' TREAT POSTPONED.

The officials of the Penketh Wesleyan Church, after deliberate consideration, decided to put off their Walking Day, which should have been held on Saturday last, until the recent outbreak of scarlet fever and measles had abated. Naturally a great deal of disappoint- ment was felt, especially by the children, but after the soaking which their confreres in the adjoining parish experienced, they felt that, after all, they had not much to feel dis- appointed about, realising that there was a pos- sibility of a brighter outlook for them in the near future.

div.head: Tammas' Lack of Sense.
div.p: Tammas' Lack of Sense.

A young Scotchman living in London mar.led a beautiful and talented Englishwoman, of whom he was justly proud. Not long aster his marriage he went to Scotland on a flying trip to see an old bachelor uncle.
"Well, Tammas, ye have gotten a wife," said the old gentleman, "now what can she do, lad?"
" Do!" echoed Tammas.

"Yes, do," repeated his uncle, firmly. "Can she sew on your buttons an' make your porritch an' your scones?" "Oh, no, she doesn't know how to do those things," said Tammas. "But she has the loveliest voice that ever you heard. She's a grand singer." "Hoot, mon'!" cried his uncle, indignantly, " could you nae get a canary. in Lunnon?"

div.head: MOTOR KITCHEN.
div.p: A MOTOR KITCHEN.

Owing to the generosity of the Alpine climbers of Great Britain and Ireland, through the instrumentality of Mrs. Aubrey le Blond, the President of the Ladies' Alpine Club, a motor kitchen has been presented to the Chasseurs Alpins. It will be remembered that this section of the French Army did great work in the Vosges in turning hack the onslaughts of the enemy. Something like 300 subscriptiaite have been received, amounting to £756. Tfie British Ambulance Committee are finding the small necessary balance to pay for the equipment The internal fittings of the kitchen are remark- ably complete, nothing seems to have been for- gotten- The arrangements for cooking, for water, for storing and for lighting are quite uP to date, and it is surprising how much has been- got into a little space. Such an outfit should be. of great use to our Allies.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 10, 1915.
the Paving and Sewerage committee on the whole subject, but the time was hardly oppor- tune for discussing the matter.
FIGHTING THE WHITE PLAGUE.
The systematic efforts of the Health Committee

towards the prevention of tuberculosis were continued during the year. As in the preceding years an attempt had been made to secure a non- tuberculous milk supply for the borough. All cases of tuberculosis occurring within the bor- ough were now compulsorily notifiable to the Medical Officer of Health. During the year a total number of 375 notifications were received as against 367 in the previous year. This in- crease might be accounted for partly by the fact that compulsory notification was only in force for eleven months of the year 1913. The num- ber of persons suffering from pulmonary tuber- culosis living in Warrington on the 31st Decem- ber 1914, was 339; from other forms of the disease 222. With regard to the prevention of this disease, attention must here be drawn to the question of indiscriminate spitting in the streets and public places. The beds at Sankey Sanatorium have been kept in full use during the year, both insured and uninsured patients receiving treatment there. Cured Consumpthies in The Army.

Leaving out of account any personal benefit to the individual, only 3 out of 224 (1.3 per cent.) were able to work before admission, whereas 71 (31.6 per cent.) had been able to follow their employment regularly ever since. Eight of them are at present serving in the Army. The full scheme for dealing with tuberculosis in the borough involved the enlargement of the Sana- torium so as to accommodate 50 patients (these patients comprising both early and advanced cases) and the opening of a tuberculosis dispen- sary on land behind Garven. House, where the examination and treatment of cases who were residing at home could be carried out. An Assistant Medical Officer of Health was to be appointed who shall reside at Sankey Sana- torium and carry out the routine work at the sanatorium and at the dispensary under the supervision of the Medical Officer of Health. The borough had to provide a Smallpox Hos- pital in lieu of Sankey Sanatorium. according to the requirements of the Loral Government Board. The completion of this scheme had been greatly hampered by the war, but it was to be hoped that the work would be at once proceeded with. The country was likely to be flooded With cases of tuberculosis after the war, as it was after the South African campaign, but, of course, to a much greater extent, and it behoves them to be prepared for dealing with them. Housing and Social Conditions to Blame.
The visiting of cases of tuberculosis at their

homes with a:view to controlling the spread of infection had been continued as in previous years. It is abundantly dear, however, that much must be done to improve the housing and social conditions of the people if this disease was to be stamped out. No multiplication of sanatoria alone was going to rid the country of tuberculous disease.

The local sanitary authority was each year performing much valuabre work in getting rid of slum property and in improving the 'dwellings of the working classes. Still a great deal re- quires to be done, not only in this, but also in raising the morals of the people in order to en- able them to take advantage of better and healthier surroundings, and when they took into consideration that something like 50,000 persons died in England and Wales every year from tuberculosis alone, it was seen that ultim- ate success would be worth any effort, financial or otherwise, that could be made to attain it.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S HEALTH BILL.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S HEALTH BILL.
Conditions Under Which Our People Live, And Why
Some Of Them Die.

div.head: POINTS FROM THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: POINTS FROM THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
Ignorance Which Leads To "The Slaughter Of The
Innocents."

The annual report of the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. G. W. N. Joseph) on the sanitary conditions of Warrington and the other numer- ous matters that come within his province is a highly interesting and comprehensive docu- ment of just upon a hundred pages, to say noth- ing of. the numerous and elaborate tables of facts and figures with which it is freely insetted. In this report, the compilation of which must have evolved much time and pains, every phase of the work of the public health authority is dwelt upon, diseases are traced to their causes, and practical means of remedy and prevention— which is better than cure, so we are told—are suggested. Just as there is a wealth of sug- gestion that is valuable in the report, so also is there a plenitude of material that is extremely interesting and suggestive to the student of sociology; the report containing much informa- tion and material that is of intense value to the person who is interested in learning an import- ant something about how the other half live— and die; and why! .
This valuable, Interesting and comprehensive document was presented to the Town Council for their consideration at their monthly meet- ing, held on Tuesday evening.

FACTS AT A GLANCE. The report included the following vital statistics : Population Population at census, 1911 Acreage of Borough Number of persons per acre Number of hOuses in occupation Number of houses not in occupation lB3 Number of houses built during the year 58 Estimated average number of persons per house Number of births (males, 1,119; females, 2,225 29.7
1,106) Birth-rate per 1,000 living Number of deaths (652 males, 567

females) Death-rate per 1,000 living Death-rate per 1.000 living corrected for age and sex distribution Excess of registered births over deaths.. 1,008 Number of marriages Marriage-rate per 1,000 living Phthisis death-rate per 1,000 living Death-rate per 1.000 population from other forms of tuberculosis Death-rate from all forms of tuberculosis, 2.16
including phthisis Death-rate from diseases of respiratory organs other than tuberculosis 2.72 Infantile mortality-rate (per 1,000 births) 111

throat or illness ,suspected to be infectious occurring among the school children within the borough and coming to the knowledge of the teachers. No case of this kind can be re-ad- mitted to school until certified free from infec- tion, either by the medical man in charge of the case or the Medical Officer of Health. Although the death-rate from enteric fever is still high, the actual number of cases of the disease occurring in the town has diminished each year since 1909.

During the year 18 cases of ophthalmia neonatorum (occurring among the 2,225 living births) were notified in this borough, and were visited and re-visited by the health visitors in order to see that the parents obtained adequate medical treatment. The majority of the cases were mild, and cleared up without any severe after-effects.

In preventing the spread of infectious disease special visits have been paid during the year to the ‘different places of entertainment in the borough. In consequence of the attention of the proprietors having been called by the Health Department to certain conditions, considerable improvement in sanitary details has been effected.

div.head: HIGH BIRTH-RATE.
div.p: A HIGH BIRTH-RATE.

In the course of his repprt the doctor elabor- ates the statements summarised above, and sets forth that-the birth-rate for Warrington (29.7) was the same as in the previous year, and was considerably higher than that for England and Wales as a whole, or than the average for the ninety-seven great towns. At the same time there was a considerable reduction in the infan- tile death-rate from 131 per 1,000 births last year to 111 for 1914. This was lower than the average for the ninety-seven great towns, and was the second lowest on record for the borough. The general death-rate for the year was 17.5, a figure slightly greater than the corresponding rate for the previous year. The actual death- rate for the borough was 16.2 for the same period, but this had fo be multiplied by a cer- tain factor in order to arrive at the corrected death-rate. The following table gave the general and infantile death-rates for the borough and the ninety-seven great towns of England and Wales during the years 1913 and -1914 :7
General Infantile Death-rate. Death-rate, Warrington 1913 17.2 131 1914 17.5 111 97 Great Towne 1913 14.7 117 1914 15.0 114

The slight rise in the death-rate was not to be attributed to any one cause, but was spread fairly generally over all. A table comparing some of the principal vital statistics for Warrington, with the average for the year in different parts of the country, showed that although the borough compared somewhat unfavourably with the rest of the country in some rates, especially infantile mor- tality rate, there was an improvement over last year. However, comparing the borough rates with the other Lancashire county boroughs, they found that out of 17 towns only one having so high a birth-rate had lower general and infan- tile death-rates.

---`;Aienii-o-n-,;;- the doctor continued, was drawn in my report last year to the question of sunc?rtified deaths in this borough. There was some improvement in the figures for 1914, but they were still very unfavourable when com- pared with the rest of the country."

div.head: SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC.

The chief feature with regard to infectious diseases to be noted in the past year is the epi- demic of scarlet fever, which has been in evi- dence continuously throughout the year. Dur- ing the year 1913 the incidence of this disease was high throughout the country, and Warring- ton escaped comparatively lightly compared with other Lancashire towns at that time. The number of cases of scarlet fever increased dur- ing the autumn of 1913, and never really dimin- ished all through the winter, so we were quite prepared for a fairly large epidemic during the spring and summer. In my opinion the exces- sively mild winter of 1913 had something to do with the continuance of this epidemic up to the spring time. There has been no large epidemic in this town since 1904, and so a large susceptible population has grown up, who readily became victims when exposed to the infection. The epi- demic was extremely mild, and this had an im- portant bearing on the spread of the disease. In many instances owing to the mildness of the attack parents haye not known the child was ill, and have never sought medical advice, whilst in other cases, having suspected the cause, they have thought it of no consequence, as the child did not seem, in their opinion, ill enough to be isolated. It was quite a common thing to hear mothers say they thought "the child just had a touch of the fever." In addition, showing the extreme mildness in certain instances, a series of cases have even been missed by general practi- tioners in the town and allowed to run about or "attend school until noticed to be "peeling" by our inspectors or the teachers. There have only been 24 deaths out of 1,133 cases, a case mor- tality of 2.1, which is lower than we have had for more than ten years. It is also interesting to observe that the attack-rate per 1,000 persons living was lower than in the epidemic of 1904. How Diseases are. Spread.

The epidemic started in Whitecross Ward in August, 1913, and spread throughout the town. No special cause could be assigned, although careful inquiries were made into every case. Bew.sey. Ward, which has practically no slums, and where there is plenty of work at good wages, probably had a larger number of cases than any ward. Here it was essentially due to the care- lessness of parents. Undoubtedly one great cause of the amount of infectious disease seems to be the utter indifference of a certain class of mother. This applies not only to scarlet fever, but also to diphtheria, measles and whooping cough. Even after they have been told by the .medical man in attendance that the case is in- fectious,. they taken no precautions whatever to prevent 'other -children from coming in contact with the case, ev6n in those homes in which they have enough accommodation to enable them to do so. As a rule the child is kept in the kitchen, and neighbours allowed to come in to look at the case, often carrying babies in their arms. I cannot help thinking that prosecution of the offending parent in every instance where a child suffering from infectious disease was exposed to the public danger would have very materially reduced the number of sufferers from scarlet fever during the year. Attention may here be called to one of the difficulties in deal- ing with infectious disease in this borough, and one which increases in importance each year. We have a system of close co-operation between the Health and Education Departments where- by our inspectors Inquire into every ease or sore'

div.head: LESS INFANTILE MORTALITY.
div.p: LESS INFANTILE MORTALITY.

The infantile mortality rate (i.e., number of deaths of children under one year of age per, 1,000 births) shows a reduction over last year. The Mothers' and Babies' Welcomes in the town were an important adjunct of the public health
service.

In a special report issued by the Local Govern- ment Board in July, 1914, a ciimparison is made between the average rates of infantile mortality for each county borough in Lancashire in 1902-4 and in 1911-13. It was there shown that South- port was the only one out of the 17 county bor- oughs that had a greater reduction in the death- rate during that period than Warrington. Again, during 1914 the death-rate in this town among infants compared very favourably with that in the other county boroughs of Lanca- shire, which county holds the unenviable record of having the highest rate in the country. The provision of a maternity centre and a centre for infant consultations was essential. The con- sideration of this matter was postponed owing to the war, as it was bound up with the question of extension of the school clinic. To Save the Babies. On studying the list of causes of death in infants one was struck by the large number attributed to congenital malformations, prema- ture birth, atrophy, debility and marasmus—in fact, 86 out of 249, or 34 per cent. Further, the number of stillbirths in the borough of War- rington which were notified for the three years, 1911-12-13, averages 79, and for 1914 is 94. On looking through the list of causes as far as can be ascertained, it is evident how very many are preventable if only the mother could have advice early enough. It should be possible to, every woman, however poor, to be able to obtain advice and treatment when needed. By this means not only would the health of the mother be improved, but a large number of the still- births and premature births might be avoided, whilst the health of those children who were born alive would be greatly benefited. One of the greatest causes of the large numbers of premature and stillbirths was ignorance on the part of the mothers—ignorance of thelact that they needed medical treatment. Good Work That Might Be Done. The health visitors were doing a lot of good work in the homes of those people, but a great advance would be made if they had a centre where the women could attend and receive in- struction from a medical officer. They had in addition to recognise the fact that at present there was nowhere for an emergency case of midwifery to go in the borough but to the Workhouse. This had been even more evident since the beginning of the war. He would sug- gest the provision of a few beds, probably three at first would be quite enough, looked after by a trained midwife, into which any urgent case could be sent by the doctor in charge. A mater- nity centre, such as lie suggested, would (1) co- ordinate the whole of the work of our health visitors; (2) be a centre for giving advice and instruction to expectant mothers; (3) make pro- vision for any urgent emergency cases brought to the notice of doctors in the town; and (4) be a centre of instruction for the midwives of the borough. Certain of the defects found in the children at the routine medical inspection during school life were found to have had their origin during the pre-school age. A great many of those might have been remedied if the attention of the par- ents had been called to them at the outset. The health visitors in the oast hail done valuable work by following up infants from birth until 12 months of age, and giving advice to the parents on the best methods of rearing their little ones. During the past year a further advance had been made by tackling the cases of children between the ages of twelve months and the date of their beginning to attend school, and thus coming under the supervision of the School Medical Officer. Still more could be done, how- ever. The Baby Welcomes, of which there are two at present in the town, carried on by volun- tary lady helpers assisted by members of the Medical Officer of Health's staff, had done really excellent work. The beneficial results to the infantile mortality rate of the town would be still further enhanced if some system of medical inspection were inaugurated. All de- fects in these children requiring treatment would then be pointed out to the parents and records kept, which would be attached to the school schedule when the child reached school age. In this scheme the old Baby Welcomes would not be superseded, but included. New quarters would be provided, and the ladies who at present were giving so much valuable time and service to this work would be asked to help, as before. The annual expense would be small.

OUR ANTIQUATED SANITATION. As to the sewage question, the report stated that however carefully closets on tile coAserv- ancy system were emptied • and cleansed, the conditions associated with them in urban com- munities were a menace to the public health, and .especially the health of children; and the Local Government Board would urge that wher- ever a sufficient sewer and water supply were available fresh water closets supplied with flush- ing cisterns should be substituted for existing closets on the conservancy, system and provided in all new buildings. In the best administered districts conservancy closets and ashpito had given place to fresh water closets and movable ashbins with covers. There cpuld be no doubt , that statistics throughout the country went to show the beneficial effects on the health of the community of the conversion from conservancy. methods to the water carriage system. Before conversion on anything like a large scale could take place in Warrington, the question of re- sewering the borough must receive attention. That would be an expensive matter, but sooner or later it had to be faced, and every year only added to the initial cost that would be neces- sary. And it must not be forgotten that a con-. siderable expense in connection with the collec- tion and treatment of pail contents would be saved. Once satisfactory arrangements were provided then all new buildings could have water closets installed where needed, instead of 1 the present objL•ctionable pail closets, which would only have to be converted in the near future.

div.head: Great Difficulty.
div.p: A Great Difficulty.

One great difficulty in the case pf Warrington was that parts of the town were so low-lying that sufficient " fall" could not be obtained for the sewage without pumping. Moreover, no scheme should be adopted that permitted the pouring of crude sewage into the Mersey, as at present obtained. All sewage must first be ade- quately treated. The best method for the treat- ment of sewage is a controversial subject, and which •method was most suitable for this bor- ough to adopt would need careful consideration. I sub-committee of the Health Committee had been formed to confer with a oub-conamittee of

div.head: SOLDIERS AND INFECTION.
div.p: SOLDIERS AND INFECTION.

In any case where infectious disease occurred in the home of a man engaged in military or naval service whilst on leave, the man was quar- antined with the consent of his commanding officer in a non-infected dwelling 'until consid- ered free from infection before being allowed to re-join. That these arrangements worked satis- factorily was shown by the fact that although 89 cases were thus dealt with, in no instance had a case of infection been reported as having been carried by a man on his return to his regiment. On the other hand, they had cases on record where infection had been brought into the town by men on furlough.
PUBLIC HEALTH THE MOST IMPORTANT CONSIDERATION.
Alderman JAMES EVANS, in submitting to the Council the report of the Health Committee, which included the Medical Officer's report, called attention to many of the points men:.

tioned by Dr. G. W. N. Joseph, and opined that there was, perhaps, nothing more impor- tant for the consideration of the Council from year to year than the health report, for after all the health of the borough was its greatest asset. If they were a healthy people they could be a thrifty people, whilst if they were not healthy and their sanitary surroundings were not good it scarcely mattered what else they had got. Councillor DICKENSON seconded the proposal that the report be adopted.

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT AND THE SMOKE
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT AND THE SMOKE
NUISANCE.

Alderman BENNETT congratulated the Medical Officer on the .manner in which he had pre- pared his report and noted with satisfaction that the birth-rate compared so -satisfactorily with that of other large towns. That fact, coupled with the fact • that the infantile mor- tality was oq the decrease, was, indeed, a matter -for congratulation, It was a -healthy sign when the birth-rate increased, and specially healthy at this time when the nation was being bereft of so many of its young and virile men owing to the war. As to the smoke nuisance, the Inspector said that he was pleased to be able to report a marked im- pMvement, but he (the Alderman) thought that, whilst the town might be better off than it was in that respect, the improvement was not quite so marked as all that as yet. Still, he was glad to think that owing to the •reason- able businesslike stand that was now being made by the Health Committee, an improve- ment was being obtained. In hie opinion the number of observations had not been quite as big as it might be, or ought to be; indeed, he could not help thinking that the number of observations was not large enough, having regard to the many chimneys in the town.

DEPUTY-MAYOR AND SELFISH PARENTS The DEPUTY-MAYOR referred to the fact that the bulk of the cases of scarlet fever which went to make up the present epidemic were very mild ones, and said that anybody who remembered scarlet fever as he remembered it, in Warrington, some thirty years ago, would think that it was quite a different thing alto- gether. There was one thing he would like to go to the public, and that was that if they had lad consideration for others as well as thprodelves the epidemic would not .have been so widespread. The first thing with so many people, when there was a child in the house ill, was to think of the inconvenience and the expense, and not to think that other people's 'children might be endangered. That savoured -of selfishness and thoughtlessness combined. This led him to his own particular bete noir— diphtheria. The number of cases of diph- theria was steadily increasing. It might, of course, be said that they were increasing all over the country, or, at any rate, all over the county. But that was not satisfactory at all. With regard to enteric fever, the number of cases was small, but the rate of mortality was exceedingly high—between 29 and 30 per cent. of the total number of cases. With regard to the question of sewage, he still said that until they could get a proper system of stvilisation they were far, safer with the old pail system "Better Bear the Ills We Have Than —." In retaining the present system they were running a definite danger, of which they could see the limits, but in going in for any other system which did not provide for perfect steril- isation they would be embarking on a danger that was vague and uncertain, not only for themselves, but also for others. He considered the advice from the Local Government Board on the subject most thoughtless, until they were ready for conversion from the present system to something that was demonstrably better, and he must enter his protest against it. Replying to the discussion, Alderman JAhms EVANS asked Alderman Bennett to remember that, if the smoke inspection had not been on quite so big a scale as he could have wished, they had been passing through a period of war, when economy was necessary. However, he was pleased to learn, for once, from Alder- man Bennett. that, in this respect, they were better than they used to be. (Laughter.) The report was then adopted.
There is no lack of opportunities to do the things we shouldn't.

div.head: WARRINGTON DOCK.
div.p: WARRINGTON DOCK.
Canal Co. Will Re-open Question When Council Is Ready.

When the minutes of the General Purposes Committee were before the Warrington Town Council at their monthly meeting on Tues- day evening, Alderman BvsNETT referred to a private report which had been issued to the members on the result of the deputation which was recently appointed by the Council to wait upon the Manchester Ship- Canal Co_ with reference to the provision of a dock at Warrington. He said the report was satisfactory on the whole, The Cortepr.ny met tne deritation in a ran- able spirit, and the Council would be glad to know that they were prepared to reopen the question when the corporation felt ready for a step forward. They promised not to tip any of the dredgings on the Available site until the last possible moment, so that it would always be open to the Council to get the facilities which he personally had always considered. necessary for the full development of the town. (Hear, hear.) The ItAtoit seetended the adoption of the minutes, and the proposition was carried.

div.head: MARKET-GATE SCHEME.
div.p: MARKET-GATE SCHEME.
Alderman Bennett A Victim 01. His
Own Improvement.

When the minutes of the Street Improvement Committee were submitted for approval at Tuesday night's meeting of the Warrington Town Council,. Alderman BENNBrr made reference to the Market Gate improvements now in progress, and said he thought the matter was one upon which the Council might congratulate them- selves, adding that during the last few days he had worked as hard as he had ever done in his life in connection with the demolition of property. (Laughter.) He had been in premises at Market Gate for 28 years, and the irony was that he was the victim of his own improvement. (More laughter.) He was, however, proud to say that he was the humble instrument of in augurating the circus scheme. He now felt sorry in some respects—(renewed laughter)—be- cause one became attached to a place with which he had been long connected. However, hc would be able in his new premises still to linger on_the circus. (Hear, hear.)

Councillor ROBERTS said that many-tongued Rumour had been busy and some extraordinary stories had gained currency during the last few days, and he could not help referring to what he considered to be the most remarkable of the lot. Was it a fact that the Town Clerk con- sulted the Chairman of the Street ImProvement Committee as to the desirability of obtaining an ejectment order to persuade Alderman Ben- net to get out of his office? (Loud laughter.) Alderman BENNETT : They nearly had to pu! the slates off over my head. (More laughter.)

div.head: WARRINGTON WATER-
div.p: WARRINGTON WATER-
WORKS.
Borough Treasurer Reports On The Undertaking's Finances.

To the Town Council on Tuesday evening the Borough Treasurer (Mr. John Fairhurst) sub- mitted the revenue and capital accounts of the waterworks undertaking for the year ended March 31st. They showed that the gross income during the year was £31,987 (as against £33,029 in 1913-14), and the expenditure £11,735 (against £11,178), leaving the gross profit at £20,252 (against £21,851). The amount charged against the net revenue account for loan charges, less interest received was £20,012 (against £19,839), leaving a net profit of £240 (against £2,012). The water rents and charges showed a decrease of £4, and the income generally had been normal, as last year's figures included £1,137 for work done in connection with Warrington Bridge.

div.head: OUTSTANDING DEBT OF NEARLY £400,000.
div.p: OUTSTANDING DEBT OF NEARLY £400,000.

The expenditure on rents, rates and taxes had increased by £1,300, chiefly owing to the revised assessment of the undertaking, and pumping expenses had increased by £244, The percentage of expenditure to income was 36.69, as compared with 30.4 for the preceding year. The increase in the net revenue charges, after deducting interest received, was £173. The net profit had been carried forward, making the balance £7,100, while the reserve fund, with the aid of £176 for interest on investments, had been brought up to its maximum of £lO,OOO. During the year the capital expenditure had been £2,679, and it should be noted that the amount of £6,000 sanctioned in 1910 for the provision of new mains had now been ex- pended. The loans repaid during the year amounted to £6,547, leaving a debt outstanding of £392,209.

div.head: BIG INCREASE IN RATES REDUCES PROFITS.
div.p: BIG INCREASE IN RATES REDUCES PROFITS.

In moving the adoption of the report, Alder- man JoHN EVANS, the Chairman of the Water Committee, said that it would be seen that the profits of the waterworks undertaking during the past year had been seriously reduced from £2,012 to £240. It was due to the Council to give the reasons. The decrease in revenue was £27 Bs. 3d., the increase in rates £1,500 ss. 7d., and the increase in capital charges £202 9s. 2d., making a total of £1,530 as. The increase in working expenses (comprising the management, Appleton pumping and distribution) was £268 3s. 6d. In the increased item of £268 3s. 6d. was included the cost of the war bonus and allow- ance to enlisted men £55 12s. 6d., the wages of station guards amounting to £137 15s. 9d., and the cost of guns and ammunition for same totalling £l4 15s. 11d. Taking the total revenue for water rates and charges, the town- ship rates absorbed 16 per cent. of the total and capital charges 67 per cent., or a total of 83 per cent. Councillor FIRTH LINDLEY formally seconded, and the committee's report was adopted.

div.head: RELIEF FOR ALLIED FARMERS.
div.p: RELIEF FOR ALLIED FARMERS.

The Duke of Portland (president) made an earnest appeal at last week's meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society, at the Nottingham Show, for contributions to the Agricul- tural Relief of Allies Fund, which has been initiated by the Royal Society. The object is to supply seeds, live stock, and implements to ruined farmers when the time comes for re- patriation in the territories now occupied by enemy forces. There is urgent need for imme- diate help in Serbia, where the holdings of the peasant farmers have been devastated. Contri- butions in kind as well as in money are being made, and county societies all over the country are co-operating with the Royal Society in this benevolent work. .
We live and learn. Until I became an inmate of a boarding-house I never knew there were so many stewed prunes in the world.
Not going away this year.?

Not going away this year? Times too bad! War work too pressing! You will sigh for the balm of seaside breezes: the bracing moor- land air. Make the best of the situation. div.head: Control.
div.p: Control.
TEN COAST DISTRICTS.

A supplement to the "London Gaiette " was issued this week. eilor.iining an Order in Coun- cil under the Defence of the Realm Act applying the Defence of the Realm (Liquor Control Regulations) 1915, to a number of speci- fied areas. The Order sets forth that " it appears to his Majesty that it is expedient for the purpose of the successful prosecution of the present war that the sale and supply of intoxi- cating liquor in the respective areas defined and specified in the schedule hereto should be con- trolled by the State on the ground that war material is being niade, loaded, unloaded, and dealt with therein." The regulations issued on June 12th gave to the Central Control Board (Liquor Traffic) various and extensive powers to regulate, pro- hibit, and conduct the sale and supply of in- toxicating liquor in a scheduled area. The areas defined and specified in the schedule are as follows 1. BRISTOL.—The City of Bristol, several neighbouring parishes, and the area within a circle having a radius of five miles measured from the South Pier Lighthouse, Avonmouth. 2. NEWHAVEN (Sussex).—Within a radius of miles from the Town Railway Station. 3. SOUTHAMPTON.—Within a radius f six miles from Bargate. 4. NEWPORT (Mon.).—Within a radius of seven miles from Vie Town Will. 5. CARDIFF.—Within a radius of eight miles from the City Hall. 6. BARRY (Glamorgan).—Within a radius of five miles from the Town Railway Station. 7.—BARROW-IN-FURNESS.—WIthin a radius cf ten miles from the Town Hall. 8. FRITH DISTRICT (Thames).—The Urban Districts of Bexley, Dartford and Erith, and the parishes of Crayford, Darenth, Stone, Sutton-at-Home, Swanscombe, and Wilming- ,ton, in the County of Kent. 9. LIVERPOOL, SOUTHPORT & DISTRICT. —The City of Liverpool, the County Boroughs of Birkenhead, Bootle and Wallasey, the Urban District of Ellesmere Port and Whitby, and the Petty Sessional Division of Wirral in the County of Chester, and the Petty Sessional Divisions of Southport, Kirk- dale, Ormskirk, and Presc,ot, in the County of Lancaster. 10.. NORTHUMBERLAND AND DURHAM.— The City of Newcastle-on-Tyne; the County Boroughs of Tynemouth, 'Gateshead, South Shields, Sunderland, West Hartlepool, Middlesbrough, and Darlington; the Boroughs of Stockton-on-Tees, Hartlepool, and Jarrow, and 'the Petty Sessional Divisions of Gates- head, Chester-le-Street, South Shields, Sun- derland, Houghton-le-Springs, Seaham Har- bour, Castle Eden, West Hartlepool, Stockton and Darlington, in the County of Durham; the Borough of Wallsend and the Petty Sessional Divisions of Bedlingtonshire, East Castle " Ward and West Castle Ward, in the County of Northumberland; and the Petty Sessional Divisions of Thornaby and Yarm, North Langbaurgh, East Langbaurgh, and West Langbaurgh, in the North Riding of Yorkshire.

div.head: DRINK IN DOCKYARDS.
div.p: DRINK IN DOCKYARDS.
New Regulation Provides For
-Prohibition.

A supplement to the "London Gazette," con- tains a new Order in Council under the Defence of the Realm Act Regulations to the following effect 2 " Where the competent naval or military authority has control of any dock premises he may, by order, prohibit any person from bring- ing into or having in his possession within those premises or•on board any vessel therein, any intoxicating liquor except for such pur- poses and subject to such conditions and restric- tons as may be specified in the order, and if any person contravenes any provision of the order he shall be guilty of an offence under these regu- lations, and any person authorised by the com- petent naval or military authority or any police constable may search any person entering or within the dock premises, and may seize any intoxicating liquor found on him in contrtiven- tion of the order."
