div.head: WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
div.p: WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOLS.
Alarminfi Decrease In The Number
Of Scholars.

Referring in the current issue of the Wes- leyan Methodist (Warrington Circuit) Church Record to the recent circuit quarterly meeting, the editor says :—" The Sunday school report was disappointing, we should almost say alarmingly so. A decrease of 15 teachers and 348 scholars is a very serious matter, although it may be partly explained by errors in register- ing. After all allowances it is a matter requir- ing very serious consideration. The temperance returns also show a decrease, which is most un- satisfactory. At this time of trouble, trial and difficulty, we would at least have expected an increased temperance return, if not an in- creased membership, and an increase in the Sunday school roll." The next quarterly meeting of the circuit will be held at Lymra on Thursday, September 9th.

div.head: WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THE COUNTRY'S CALL.
div.p: WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THE COUNTRY'S CALL.
80;000 Serving With The Forces.

The Wesleyan Methodist Church is always well organised for work among soldiers and sailors, writes a Wesleyan correspondent in the "Manchester Guardian." It has a complete staff engaged in this work, with a ministerial secretary at its head, and chaplains are set apart for the work. In all the great garrison towns and naval ports it fulfils a manifold min- istry. It has 38 homes for soldiers and sailors, valued at £153,550, and containing 1,084 beds, which have been used by no fewer than 172,295 men during the past year. There are few churches, even in the smallest villages, which have not made some contribution to the forces, and it is computed that the total number of Wesleyans now serving with the colours is 80,000. More than 100 are serving as non-com- missioned chaplains to the troops. About twenty of these are in large military centres in this country, managing soldiers' homes and min- istering to the needs of the men. Eighty are actually with the troops, the greater portion of them being either in Flanders or at the Dar- danelles. Twenty-five ministers have volun- tarily enlisted as soldiers in the ranks, and 44 students from the training colleges have also enlisted. Six hundred and eighty-five Wesleyan ministers are now officially recognised by the military authorities. They give part of their time to their ordinary church work, and the other part to the needs of soldiers who are billeted in their towns or neighbourhoods. One hundred and sixty-five ministers are similarly recognised in the various hospitals throughout the country where wounded soldiers are being cared for. In addition, the Wesleyan Church is providing a great many huts for soldiers in camp. It has placed schoolrooms in town and country at the disposal of troops during week evenings and made other provision for recreation. From the Manchester and Salford Mission alone about 1,200 men have enlisted, and recruits are still coming in. Every effort is made—as in all the churches in the country—to keep in touch with these soldiers and sailors after en- listment. The roll of honour includes 100 casualties.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH IN DANGER!
div.p: PARISH CHURCH IN DANGER!

The German Emperor and his murdering understudies will assuredly rub their hands in glee if they ever hear of the success that has attended their efforts locally to shatter our nerves by their policy of frightfulness. German frightfulness may mean anything or nothing. If we allow ourselves to be hustled into a panic-stricken state it will have achieved its object and left us naked to tho assaults of our enemy.. If we refuse to be stampeded, and tell the Germans, in effect, to do their worst, but expect a day of reckoning, German frightfulness will have been so much waste energy and resource, of which they ma,y be in sore need before long. We have received a letter from Mr. W. W. YATES, of Dewsbury,, which shows that some people in Warrington are not, at all events, prepared to take any. risks. In the course of this letter the writer says :

Some relatives of mine residing in a suburb of Manchester decided to make me a present of a framed photograph of Warrington Parish Church, in which I was both baptised and mar- ried; but they were not able to obtain one any- where in the neighbourhood. They therefore wrote to , Warrington, and asked if he would kindly furnish them with the name and address of a local tradesman to whom they could give an order for a photo of the church. No reply was received, but in a few days they were surprised at being informed that a policeman had been making inquiries about them. What his object was they were at a loss to divine. However, some light—a bright light—was thrown on the proceeding, for next day a ser- geant of police called and mad* strict inquiries from the lady of the house, who was astonished and amused at finding that the police authorities had been informed by of the applicat4on for the address of a local tradesman able to supply a suitable photo of your parish church. The sergeant preserved his dignitT, though a quiet smile played about his menth,.when the lady had given him the facts..

Evidently , when he opened the letter sent by ray relatives, said to himself, "Ile! here is a plot which I must earn the gratitude of all Warriagtoniana by revealing- I wilt save the sacred edifice from German Zeppelins. The police shall be put ea the qui vise—and they were.

We should have thought that a German spy who knew his business would have spent 2s. 3d. on a tourney. to Warrington to make his purchase, rather than risk the dangers attaching to the post and to approaching un- known personages for favours of this kind.
We should not have thought a photograph of the Parish Church would have been much good to any prospective raider.. A plan of the town would have been a serious matter, but a photo of the church—.

div.head: WAR LOAN.
div.p: THE WAR LOAN.
How Societies And Firms Are Helping To Raise The Money.
SUBSTANTIAL REQUIREMENTS.

In an article, "Banish Waste," on page 8, we urge the claims of the War Loan upon the notice of those who have •large or small sums which they can place at the disposal of the Government for the purpose of prosecuting the War.

div.head: WORKMEN'S FACILITIES.
div.p: WORKMEN'S FACILITIES.

Locally there has been a keen desire to place money for such an object on such favourable terms. For instance, most of the firms of the town have at the request of the Government, offered facilities to employes fsr subscribing under the Post Office scheme.

• War Loan Scrip Vouchers of ss. are obtain- able on application at the time weekly wages are paid. Twenty of these vouchers will be exchanged at any Money Order Post Office between Ist and 15th December, for a £5 Government Bond, which will carry interest amounting to 4s. 6d. per annum. _ _ .

Subscribers pay weekly or at other regular intervals, and they should have in contempla- tion a total of 20- vouchers or some multiple of 20 vouchers. On the exchange of. vouchers for a Bond, interest at the rate of id. for each voucher for each month, including month of purchase, will be paid, and in addition a bonus of is. with each £5 Bond.

Information will be given freely at the offices of the firms or at the Post Office. We under- stand that workmen have taken advantage on a considerable scale of this opportunity for saving and investing. -

div.head: PATRIOTIC lAIREDRAWERS.
div.p: PATRIOTIC lAIREDRAWERS.
Lend £21,000 to The Government
From Their Surplus.

How patriotic have been the wiredrawers of the country the recruiting officers could tell and the casualty lists, unfortunately, show. The Amalgamated vv iredrawers' Society of Great Britain has a membership of 3,000 .and of these, roughly speaking, 1,000 belong to the Warrington district. About ten per cent. of the members are setting with the Colours, while the balance, or the great proportion of the balance, are engaged upon most important war work. It is unnecessary to specify the kind of work or the location of the workers.

Now they are coming forward to assist the Government financially. At a meeting of the Executive Council .on Saturday, held at Sheffield, it was Unanimously decidoNd to invest .221,000, part of the surplus funds of the Society, in the national war loan.
Mr. A. Siddall, 19, Liverpool-road, is the War- rington district corresponding secretary.

div.head: IRON AND STEEL WORKERS.
div.p: IRON AND STEEL WORKERS.

They also elected representatives to attend a conference of the Societies composing the Iron and Steel Trades Federation to consider the question of amalgamation, details of which will be placed before the members of the various Unions for their consideration. Mr. James Cx, secretary to the -Union and Federation, is again able to resume his duties after a serious illness..
ODDFELLOtVS' BIG INVESTMENT.

The local Lodges of the. Mancthester -Unity of Oddfellows have decided to invest £1,500 of their surplus capital in the loan. The Board of Directors of the Unity are in- vesting £200,000, and have issued a circular to 4.D(10 branches belonging to the Order advie.ing investment in the loan as a sound security. The local Druids have resolved to take ..k.600 in the loan; and the Order, as a whole, al- though the amount has not been stated, will invest as much of their funds us can be applied to that purpose.

div.head: CHILDREN IN FIRE.
div.p: CHILDREN IN FIRE.
Exciting_ Skylight Rescues In
Scotland Road.

An exciting incident took place on Wednes- day afternoon, when an outbreak of fire occrtrred on the premises of Mr. A. Rutter, stationer, Scotland-road. Here a room on the top floor is used for the storing of stock, and at the time it was well filled with fireworks, Christ- mas cards and stationery. Towards tea-time Mrs. Rutter was in the kitchen, when she heard some "rip-raps going off." A.t once she rushed upstairs and into the storeroom. It was filled with fumes and flames that almost overcame her. She ran downstairs again, her head and arms very badly, burned, and called to the men who were engaged iz building the new hotel next door.

The fire was caused by the little boy, who, witk his baby sister, was playing in the room, and who struck it" Bengal light." The two then went into a smaller room which opens into the storeroom, shutting the door behind them. This door Mrs. Rutter had been unable to open. The workmen clambered on to the roof and succeeded in raising the skylights of both .rooms. Dense volumes of smoke poured out, and a large crowd quickly collected. The fire. engine was summoned. In the meantime two men had attempted to rescue the children from the inside room—into which fumes were now penetrating—but were overcome and gave up the effort. However, a third succeeded in dropping into the room and handed the children through the root' to his mates, who conveyed them, frightened but otherwise unharmed, to safety. With buckets of water they .all then set about extinguishing the flames, and after some few minutes succeeded. Thus the out- break was completely quelled by the time the brigade arrived.
The damage (estimated at between £2O anti 230) is, we understaild, covered by im,ttrauce.

div.head: PRESENTED TO THE
div.p: PRESENTED TO THE
QUEEN.
Signal Honour for Warrington's Mayoress.
BOROUGH AMBULANCE MOTOR.

The Queen inspected at Buckingham Palace on Monday afternoon twenty-six of the fleet of about sixty motor-ambulances which have been provided as a result of appeals by lady mayoresses and mayoresses throughout the country. The cars have been built to War Office specification. Each car will accommodate eight patients. About 50 lady mayoresses (including the Lady Mayoress of London) and mayoresses (including the Mayoress of Warrington, Mrs. Peter Peacock), were presented .to her Majesty in the gardens of the 'Palace, after which the ambu- lances were driven slowly past and were in- spected by the Queen. After the inspection some of the cars were taken to Folkestone, on their way to the Front. The lady mayoresses and mayoresses were afterwards entertained to luncheon at the Mansion House by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress.
HER MAJESTY RECALLS HER VISIT TO WARRINGTON.

Along with the lady mayoresses and other mayoresses; the Mayoress of Warrington was presented to her Majesty by the Lord Chamber- lain. The Queen graciously shook hands with her and mentioned that she remembered War- rington quite well, having visited the town about two years ago, on the occasion Of their Majesties' memorable tour through industrial Lancashire, during which his Majesty, King George found time to open the then completed portion of Warrington's fine new bridge, sub- sequently visiting Messrs. Crosfield's works, &c. It is worthy of note that this is the first time that a mayoress of Warrington has had the honour of presentation to Royalty at Buckingham Palace. The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), along with the lord mayors and mayors of the other towns which have provided cars was present at the reception of the lady mayoresses and mayoresses.
THE MAYORESS'S PRESENTATION GOWN

The Mayoress of Warrington was charminglF attired in a gown of foulard vert, embossed with gold and black, the bodice being softly drapeo with ninon to match, and having a high-stand- ing lace ruffle at the throat, over the bodice being worn a quaint black taffetas coatee. A black Tagel hat completed an exceedingly dainty toilette, the work of Messy Hodgkin- son's, of Bridge-street. A brass plate in the Warrington ear bears the inscription: "Presented by the Mayoress of Warrington to the British Peri Cross 804.4ety." THE COUNCIL GRATIFIED.

At Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council, the Mayor made allusion to' the interesting event of the previous day, and said that he thanked the members on behalf of the Mayoress for assisting her to obtain the car. It was gratifying to know that the car was on view at Buckingham Palace on Monday, and he was very pleased to add that the Mayoress of War- rington was presented to her Majesty.. (Hear, hear, and applause.)

div.head: LICENCES.
div.p: LICENCES.
Justices Offer £5,000 Compensa.
tion In Two Cases.
A POINT AT ISSUE.

A supplementary meeting of the Licensing Authority for the County Borough of War- rington, was held at the Borough Police Court yesterday morning, when the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst, Pierpoint and Jas. Evans, and Messrs. G. Pilling, S. Wright, C. Jackson Holmes and A. J. Jolley. The meeting was called for the purpose of fixing the amount of compensation to be paid to the parties interested in the two licensed houses—the White Hart (in the Market-place) and the Smiths' Arms <in Legh-street), which were referred for compensation at the annual Licensing Sessions. ALL PARTIES SATISFIED.

Mr. H. J. Westbrook, who appeared for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., in the case of the White Hart, said that the total amount agreed upon between the parties interested was £1,305 6s. 9d., and it was suggested that of the amount awarded, one-tenth should go to the licensee, plus the amount allowed for tenant's 'fixtures.
Mr. C. H. 17nsworth, for the licensee, Mrs. Minnie Turnbull, announced that his client was quite satisfied with the terms. CASE OF AN ANTE '69 BEERHOUSE.

Mr. Hatton, for the parties interested in the Smiths' Arms—the Trustees of the late Mr. Chas. Lonsdale (owners), Messrs. Greenell, Whitley and Co. (lessees) and Mr. Jack Cheadle (licensee)—said that the total amount of com- pensation agreed upon was £3,6.18 12s. 4d. It had been further agreed upon that the appor- tionment to the owners should be £2,918 17s. 10d., and that to the tenants ,£729 14,5. 6d., whilst the licensee had agreed to accept one-tVird of the aggregate amount awarded to the brewers. The Mayor announced that the justices had agreed to the figures submitted with regard to the White Hart, but, in reference to the Smiths' Arms, they would like to know if Mr. Hatton could make a claim, there and then, on the basis of the rental, which was at the moment being paid for the house, as against the rental which was likely to be received when the premises were converted into ordinary business premises. If such a claim were made the justices were prepared to consider it again; otherwise they would have to make another suggestion. Mr. Hatton said there had been considerable difficulty in arriving at an agreement between the parties interested in the house, and unless he could persuade the justices to deal with the claim in the form in which it had been sub- mitted that day, he was afraid that that agree- ment fell to the ground. He had no instructions to put forward any claim cave that which was based on the sales at the house.

Should Rent or Trade be the Basis of Claim? The Mayor: If you do not feel inclined to base your claim on the rental we have another alternative. Do you think that if. we adjourned the case for a week you would be able to base your claim on the rental?

Mr. Hatton replied by pointing out that this was the first case of an ante-1869 beerhouse that had come before that Court, though in other Courts there had been many. The practice in Laneashire, in cases of this kind, had been to take the actual trade of tho house as the basis for compensation. He regretted that he could not comply with the suggestion to alter the basis of his claim, and pointed out that the selling price of a licensed house entirely depended upon the trade done in that house. Brewers made purchases of property not on fictitious rentals, but on the basis of the volume of trade.

The magistrates having considered the matter further in private, the Mayor, addressing Mr. Hatton, Bald: "As you are not prepared to make an amended claim the justices have no alterna- tive but to refer the ca.se of the house to the Inland Revenue authorities."

div.head: WARRINGTON D.C.M.
div.p: WARRINGTON D.C.M.
The Mayor_ Extends Congratulations
To The Parent;.

I feel sure that his parents will be extremely proud of the manner in which he has upheld the splendid traditions of Warring- ton and the South Lancashire Territorials."

div.head: SIR ARTHUR CROSFIELD.
div.p: SIR ARTHUR CROSFIELD.
Council Congratulation On Elevation.
HONOUR TO THE TOWN.

The minutes of the General Purposes Com- mittee presented for approval at the monthly meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday even- ing, contained the following item " It was resolved that the hearty congratu- lations of this Council be tendered to Sir Arthur Henry Crosfield, Baronet, on the mark of dis- tinction conferred by his Majesty by. elevating him to the Baronetage of the United Kingdom." Alderman Bennett drew attention to the minute, and said he desired to offer his per- sonal congratulations to Sir Arthur, and also to Lady Crosfieltl. He had known Sir Arthur practically all his life, and it was gratifying to know that the worthy baronet's services to his country had been recognised in so eminently honourable a way. (Hear, hear.) The Mayor said he particularly desired to associate himself with the remarks of Alderman Bennett. Warrington had been highly honoured by the baronetcy which had been conferred upon their friend and fellow townsman. War- rington had not many honours conferred upon it, and he could not help thinking that this one was really overdue. (Hear, hear.) They were all immensely pleased and intensely proud that Sir Arthur had been honoured by his King. (Hear, hear.) The proposition was carried with applause.

Additional congratulations have been received by Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield from:— Messrs. Isdale and McCallum. Messrs. Ogston and Tennant, of Renfrew, Aberdeen and London, soap and candle manu- facturers. Mr. A. C. Thomas, of J. L. Thomas and Co., Ltd., Exeter, soap and candle manufacturers. The resolution passdd by Messrs. Isdale and McCallum, of Paisley, stated : " It was unaniniously resolved to congratu- late Sir Arthur H. Crosfield, Bart., on the well deserved honour he has received from His Majesty, which we look upon also as a compliment to the trade, and hope that he may be long spared to uphold with grace and dignity the honour he has now received." Messrs. Ogston and Tennant wrote that a resolution was passed by the Board unani- mously congratulating Sir Arthur on the honour conferred on him by the King, and adding that "The Directors feel that this honour is reflected on the soap trade generally." THE SOAP TRADE AND THE HONOUR. It will be seen that the directors of soap firms in all parts of the kingdom continue to refer to Sir Arthur and his services to the trade in the most handsome manner. As was to be imagined, the recipient deeply appreciates all such resolutions, and especially one passed by the great firm with which Sir Wm. Lever is so closely and permanently identified. There were special reasons for gratification at the congratulations of Messrs. A. and F. Pears and many others who figure in the list. As to the compliment that emanated from the directors of Messrs. Edward Cook and Co., who recalled the very great ser- vices rendered for many years to the soap trade by , Sir Arthur Crosfield, it may be interesting to mention that in 1884, the chief authority in the management at Bank Quay devolved upon Mr. Arthur Crosfield, and so rapidly did he warrant his selection for so much responsibility that in the early months of 1877, when he was still but 21 years of age, he was proposed and elected, in spite of his protestation that he was fully occupied at War- rington, as secretary of the Northern Soap Association. He continued to occupy this

responsible, and at times onerous position till 1896. From 1898 to 1902, when Sir Arthur was more concerned with politics, and less in- cessantly absorbed in business at Bank Quay, he held the secretaryship, jointly with colleagues there.' It had always been the object of his ambition to devote himself as soon as circumstances allowed of it, to political work, and after the General Election of 1900, in which he first contested the constituency, IkrY eased off at business. It is- well known that for the last fifteen years and more the chief responsibility and the control of affairs at Bank Quay have devolved in the main upon Mr. J. J. Crosfield, who recently retired from the chairmanship of the firm.

During many of the years when he acted as secretary for the Northern Soap Makers' Association, Mr. 'l'. A. Cook was secretary for the Southern Makers' Association. During those years the two were constantly and con- fidently in touch with each other, each of them haying to undertake a large share of the com- mercial diplomacy which such a situation involves.

div.p: AMBULANCE MEN!
Have You Got The Certificate? If So

We have received the following letter from Superintendent Baldry, 125, Church-street, chief officer and acting secretary (Officer Spann being on active service) of the headquarters division of the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade:—
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—Will you permit me, through the columns of your paper, to ask for volunteers for military hospitals at home and abroad? I have had an intimation from the Deputy - Commissioner of this district, Colonel C. J. Trimble, C.M.G.V.D., that very large demands are about to be made on the Ambulance Bri- gade, and askinc, for men between 18 and 40, holding the St.°Jolin certificate, to votaateet for this service. It is now a national neces- sity that the wants of the ioNlhal sr.icefi should be supplied, and officers in charge of divisions are commanded to use every eadea your to obtaip. men. Any furtnsr information may be obtained from yours faithf-ully, S. BALDRY. 125, Church-street, Warrington.

The Order of St. John has hitherto played a most patriotic part in discharging its duty towards its King and country. The divisions in Warrington—headquarters and Crosfield's— have sent all their men and are training new classes. What is wanted are:— (1) Recruits for new classes to qualify for the first-aid certificate; and (2) Holders of first-aid certificates to volun- teer for service.

Wonderful Colour-Photographs. On Tuesday evening the members of the War- rington Photographic Society had the pleasure of listening to a very interesting and instructive lecture on colour photography by Mr. Beava.n, of Chester. The lecturer described the process from the beginning to the finished lantern slide, and said he hoped to show when he came again in the winter, prints done according to the cor- rect colour process, but just at present photo- graphers were waiting for an English paper that would take the colours. The lecturer showed between 60 and 70 slides, mostly made by him- self. Among the slides were those of animals, birds, flowers, and persons, as well as iewe taken on the West Coast of Scotland, .3/c., and in all the colouring was perfect.—At the close Messrs. Bishop and Rowlands expressed the thanks of the meeting to Mr. Beavau for an en- joyable and instructive evening. No Quorum !

On the agenda for "Tuesday evening's meeting of the Town Council, Councillor Gough was again down to propose that the resolution passed by the Council in February last with reference to water charges to manufacturers be rescinded, and " that the old scale of charges for water by meter for manufacturers that were working before March 26th last become operative on June 26th." The requisite num- ber of members to constitute a quorum were present when he commenced a somewhat lengthy speech, but a few of them stole away, and eventually the Councillor's carefully pre- pared exordium was cut short by the declara- tion by the Mayor that as there was no quorum the meeting must be considered at an end. This was the third time that the motion had made its appearance in the agenda without being decided ups*,

div.head: Free Church Intercession Service.
div.p: Free Church Intercession Service.

The monthly war-intercession service, arranged by the Warrington and District Free Church Connell, took plaoe in the vestry of Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Thursday evening, when there was a gratifying attend- ance. The chair was taken by Mr. Geo. Dale, of the Bank Quay Working Men's Mission, who, In the course of a short address, \emphasised the necessity of prayer in these times, and said that he believed that God, in his own good time would bring the present horrible conflict to a close. The speaker was the Rev. A. J. Morton (of Pac!gate Wesleyan Church), who laid Fitress upon the importance of personal holiness. More now than at any other time there existed the necessity that Christians should be sure of their fellowship and communion with the Divine. He believed that the British Army was never so lofty in tone as it was to-day, and said that the other day he was in conversation with an officer, who expressed himself as very anxious not that England should be given wealth, or territory or power, but that, after the war, she might be a very godly and righteous Empire..

The National Free Church Counoil readily are responding to the social and religious oppor- tunities created by the war. In view of larger possibilities in future, a most important Con- ference has just been held at Bournemouth, when at the invitation of the President (the Rt. Hon. Sir Joseph Compton-Rickett), the District Federation Secretaries for all purts-of England and Wales spent nearly a week in con- ference- The altered conditions facing the Churches, the improvement of methods Of organisation, and the extension of the work, especially for the preparation for dealing with problems at the close of the war were con- sidered. The conference was private, and con- clusions affecting the whole organisation were arrived at. The Rev. Alexander Harvey (Wid- nes) the secretary of the South-West Lancashire Federation, was present, and is preparing f' report, which will be presented at a special meeting of the Federation, and afterwards 19 each of the Free Church Councils in it

Mr. Clare had enjoyed his usual health until a week ago, but succumbed to an attack of pneumonia. He was in his seyeaty- second year. During the past 30 years he If" in the employ of Messrs. div.head: NEW CATHOLIC CHURCH.
div.p: NEW CATHOLIC CHURCH.

Cardinal And Distinguished Assembly At St. Benedict's. To-morrow and the following day will go down to posterity as famous days in local religious history; for his Eminence Cardinal Bourne, of Westminster, is paying a visit to Warrinon for the purpose of opening the new St. Bene- dict's Church, in company with his Grace the Archbishop of Liverpool and the Bishops of Shrewsbury and Menevia. The Rev. Father Herbert Vaughan will preach at the opening Pontifical High Mass—to be sung by the Right itev. the Lord Albot of Ampleforth on the KW of the ceremony. In the evening the Cardinal will preach. Cardinal Bourne will be the first Cardinal to officiate at any religious service in Warrington since the Reformation, as well as the only Car- dinal to visit the t,own since Cardinal Manning delivered his lecture here on temperance manY years ago.

- The Abbot of Ampleforth, it will be remem- bered, visited the church last July and laid flay . foundation stone. Since then many vicissitudes have marked the erection of the church—owing to the war. However, it is now completed, and, may he included amongst those structures or which this well-favoured town may be justli proud. Erected in the Byzantine style, it will accommodate some six hundred people, and has oast between six and eight thousand pounds. Many beautiful stained-glass windows are bfing installed.

Cardinal Bourne will arrive this afternoon at Bank Quay Station, where he will be met Privately by Father Swarbreck. Afterwards a eivic reception at the hands of the Mayor tind Mayoress will take place at the Town Hall. On Monday morning His Grace The Arob- bishop of Liverpool will sing Pontifical Hlla Mass in the presence of the Cardinal; and * sertnon will be delivered by the Lord Bishop Of Itenevia.
To all these ceremonies tickets of admis4:l-01 may be purchased at places enumerated in aur d ert ilment columns.

SERGEANT H. J. CItEAMER.
Crosfield's Employe In Hospital With Damaged Arm And Ribs.

The wound which Sergeant-Hugh J. Creamer received on June 22nd happily turns out to be less serious than the bald announcement pub- lished in the casualty list issued to the Press last week-end might have led one to suppose. It appears that a piece of shrapnel caught him in the left arm, whilst other fragments slightly damaged his ribs. He is now in hospital at Rouen.
SERGT. HUGH CREAItEII. Wounded.

they were conveyed in a letter written on June 23rd by Surgeon-Lieutenant Charles D. Law, the popular house surgeon at the Warrington In- firmary, who is now serving at the Front with the R.A.M.C., and who has been called upon to tend the hurts of. many a Warrington lad who has suffered in the fighting. "Your husband," writes the Lieutenant-Surgeon; "received his slight wound in the arm during a shelling which we experienced at the hands of the enemy. His ribs were also contused. He has been sent to hospital, and I promised him that I would write to you. There is no reason for you to be anxious . . . as I can assure you that he is not in any danger. I hope that he will soon be seeing you and your children again. We are sorry to lose your husband's services, but are very glad that his injuries are not severe." Won Three Stripes Since Mobilising.

Sergeant Creamer has worked in Warrington for about ten years, and enjoys the respect and esteem of a large circle of acquaintances. A keen oivilian soldier, he was a member of the old Volunteers, and joined in with the Terri- torials when the old force was metamorphosed into the new and more effective one. He was among the first of his company to volunteer for active service and he was made a lance-corporal at Christmas, whilst undergoing his war train- ing with "the boys" down South. A month later he received his second stripe and became a full corporal, and shortly after landing in France he was awarded the coveted third stripe, and thus was promoted to his present rank.

div.head: "No Reason to be Anxious."
div.p: "No Reason to be Anxious."
Tidings of his injury were first learned by his wife, who resides at 180, Wellfield-street, and

div.head: Musical Enthusiast.
div.p: A Musical Enthusiast.

At the time of offering his services in the field Sergeant Creamer was working for Messrs. Crosfield, with whose employes he enjoyed great popularity and from whom he has received many welcome, little gifts during the time he has been fighting at the Front. He was formerly con- nected with the Cro,sfield Fire Brigade, and he took an active interest in National Service League propaganda, rendering valuable assist- ance to Major George Crosfield in this connec- tion. He is a member of the Crosfield Operatic Society, and also of the Borough Band, being an enthusiastic and competent instrumentalist. Thirty-one years of age, Sergeant Creamer, before coming to Warrington, was engaged in the Merchant Service; and had visited many parts of the globe, lie has a brother serving ix the Royal Navy.

div.head: PRIVATE CIIARLES E. LITTLER.
div.p: PRIVATE CIIARLES E. LITTLER.
Recovering From Shrapnel Wound In
The Head.

Private Charles Edward Littler, who was wounded by a fragment of a shell—which struck him in the head—during the battle in which the " Terriers" were engaged on Sunday, June 27th, writes to hie wife, who resides at 4,5, Birchall- street, Warrington, under date July 3rd, to say that he is going on well and that he was sailing for England. "My head aches a. bit," he says: and adds, philosophically, "but it is a bit of luck that I have got a head at all. It was a near

thing for me when that shell burst. It tore the back out of my overcoat, and I was fortunate that it did not blow both of my legs off. I believe the •three mates who were by my side were blown to pieces. . . . After the piece of shell hit me in the head I knew no more for a time; indeed I must km lain unconscious in

The photographs, when suitable, will be published in "The Examiner," which has an established reputation as a picture paper. All letters and photographs are returned after utes widaMagede to tho owners.

We hope to all meet on equal terms; no distinctions of class or rank separat- ing us."

div.head: One of a Fighting Farnili.
div.p: One of a Fighting Farnili.

The dead hero was only 21 years of age, and he received his schooling at St: Alban's' R.C. School. He attended St. Alban's Church. He enlisted about three years ago, prior to which he worked for Messrs. Pearson and Knowles in the Bewsey Forge. He has four uncles and six cousins fighting with the colours, three of the latter being in the neighbourhood of the Dar- danelles, one in Fiance, one in India and one in training. The laWPrivate•was unmarried.

div.head: REPORTED KILLED.
div.p: REPORTED KILLED.
PRIVATE W. HODGSON.
Said To Have Been Killed By Shell %INlst Trench-Digging.

Private W. Hodgson, who was serving in the 2nd South Lancs. Regiment, Kitchener's Army, is reported to have been killed in action. The news was first received by a neighbour, who got a letter from her husband, in which he said that the Battalion had orders to entrench them- selves, and volunteers were asked for to go and dig a trench. Along with fifty others, Private Hodgson volunteered and commenced the task. It was dark, and suddenly a shell burst just against the men who were busily digging, kill- ing many of them.
A Keen Footballer.

Private Hodgson was a married man, 21 years of age, and resided at 9, liesk-itli,street. He was emplJr2d before the wlr in the shipping department of Messrs. J. Crosfield and Son's. He was educated at the People's College, and worshipped at the Legh-street Primitive Metho- dist Church. As a boy he also attended the Sunday school attached to that Church. He was a keen f),Aballer, and he played several times for Crosiiebl's in the Works' Competition.

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
A Very Narrow _Escape From German
Bullets.

CAP SHOT THROUGH. Many stories E:re being told in town as the men come home on brief holidays of the grout gallantry shown by Major Crosfield in the ii. 441. He has shown himself absolutely fearless, and his men have been willing to' follow his lead implicitly. Major Crosfield has himself been in Ebglafla for three days' leave of absence, and Sir Arthur Crosfield, writing from London to the Works' Bowling Association to apologise for his absence from their gathering- last Saturday, as reported on our sports page, gave some indica- tion of the danger through which his brother had passed. - "The narrowness of the escape he has had," said Sir Arthur, "you may judge from the fact that when he appeared here, in khaki, we noticed two ominous holes in his khaki-coloured cap, both of them calmed by bullets. A narrower shave no man could have. It is only the briefest possible visit that Major Crosfield is able to pay this time, as he is obliged to start back for the Front on Saturday evening, or Sunday at the latest."

div.head: LIEUTENANT LEONARD HENSHALL.
div.p: LIEUTENANT LEONARD HENSHALL.
Wonderfully Cheerful And Glad To Have Done His Bit.

Mr.. Louis Henshall, Stockton Heath, re- cently paid a visit to the Fishmongers' Hall Hospital, London Bridge, where his son, Second-Lieutenant Leonard Henshall, is being treated for his various wounds received in the Territorial charge upon German trenches last month. He found that the patient's right arm had been amputated at the shoulder and that he had wounds in the head. The patient had then to face another operation for the removal of shell splinters from the shoulder. The gallant Lieutenant has made good progress, he is wonderfully cheerful, glad to have done his bit, but would have been better satisfied if he had been given a chance to return. Wounded While Rescuing Buried Men.

In the general action, Lieutenant Henshall told his father, the Germans shelled the posi- tion occupied by the Territorials. He, with many others, was buried, and several unfortu- nately were not recovered. It was while assist- ing to get these men out that he-sustained his wounds.

Ile would have had to lie by all day for re- moval; but, obtaining permission, chose to try to reach, afoot, the dressing hospital. He performed the journey#under continuous shel- ling—the Germans simply raining shells when they get going. It is fine, he says; to note the courage and elan of their men, not only in action, but in the manner of accepting their casualties.

Mr. Henshall found Captain Layton and Lieutenant Quint in the same hospital. It was amazing to note how cheerfully -all in hospital accept their troubles. • . Yesterday we learnt that Lieut.. Henshall was making good progress and that the operation had not yet taken place.

div.head: PRISONERS OF WAR.
div.p: PRISONERS OF WAR.
"Pleasure Given By Real Bread From Homo" Indescribable.

. . The work of pending parcels to the prisoners of war belonging to the South Lancashire Regiment continues week by week at the Parr Hall. Despatches of groceries are now for- warded to about 120 prisoners weekly. Acknowledgments of the parcels which were despatched six weeks ago are now coming in, and one extract from them will be sufficient to show why this good work should be, supported in order to assure its continuance. The writer says

"Senilelager, 21st June, 1915. "Accept my sincerest thanks for your parcel, which I received on the 9th inst., quite safely. Words can't describe what a pleasure it is to receive real bread from home. If it is not asking too much, I should dearly like another consignment of comforts, especially cigarettes.—Hoping to hear from you again, I remain, yours sincerely, EDWARD JONES."

The above post-card is an example of other similar acknowledgments. Our readers are asked to send contributions of money to the Mayor or the Borough Treasurer at Bank House, and gifts of food-stuffs will be gladly received at the Parr Hall. Each parcel is about 3s. value, and is varied each week. Usually a parcel contains :—Two-pound loaf well-baked bread, sugar (loaf), cocoa or tea, lib. tin golden syrup, crushed oats, condensed milk, Oxo tablets, tobacco (plug) and cigar- ettes, &c.
PRIVATE GILBERT SAVORY. Killed in Action.
Allen—who said: "I am exceedingly sorry to have to inform you that your husband passed away in action on June 16th, whilst doing his

dut; Our company were moving under a heavy shell-fire in order to take up a new position, and men were being struck down on all sides, without any warning. Your hus- band was hit in the back of the head by a piece of shell and was rendered unconscious.

div.head: Passed Away Without Suffering.
div.p: Passed Away Without Suffering.

He never regained his senses and passed away, without suffering any pain, at about six p.m. the same day. Ile was buried by men of his own company the following day, his resting-place being in a secluded spot. We are erecting over his grave a small wooden cross bearing the inscription :

div.head: Gilbert Savory (D Company), 9th Rifle Brigade. R.I.P.
div.p: Gilbert Savory (D Company), 9th Rifle Brigade. R.I.P.

We, the comrades who have served with him for ten months, desire to express our deepest sympathy with you in your sad bereavement." Rifleman J. Allen's home is at 118, School Brow, Warrington, and he was the dead man's "closest chum and best friend." As a pathetic souvenir of her dead husband, he for- warded to Mrs. Savory her late husband's cap- badge.

div.head: His Captain's Tribute.
div.p: His Captain's Tribute.

Mrs. Savory has also received a letter of con- dolence from Captain Willoughby, of the Rifle Brigade, in which he says that the dead soldier always did his duty well, and that his loss will be keenly felt by his late company. Rifleman P. Harper has also written to Mrs. Savory. "I was close to your husband," be says, "when he received the fatal shot. He was one of the jolliest in our company—always cracking a joke with everybody and having a smile for every one. In consequence he was well-liked by all with whom he came into con- tact. His bed chum misses him very much. . .
The battle we were in was a very severe one, but we were successful." A Kitchener's Man.

The dead warrior was 28 years of age last November, and although married, he had no children. He was employed as a labourer at Messrs. Crosfield and Son's soapery, and joined Kitchener's Army on August 30th last, being drafted into the Rifle Brigade. It was in the big charge on the 16th of June that he met his fate.

div.head: PRIVATE THOS. GAFFNEY.
div.p: PRIVATE THOS. GAFFNEY.
Fetched The Ammunition Which Saved A Position.

The following letter, written to Mr. and Mrs. Denis Gaffney, of 24, Kerfoot-street, by Private T. McNicholas, of D Company of the Ist Border Regiment, serving with the British Mediter- ranean Expeditionary Force, acquainted them with the news of the death of their eldest son, Private Thomas Gaffney: "it is with deepest regret that I write to inform you that your son was killed in action at about 8 o'clock on the morning of Friday. June 18th. It may lighten your sorrow to know that his death was painless and instant, the fatal bullet entering his fore- head and penetrating his brain. lie was a great
PRIVATE T. GAFFNEY..
Killed.
PRIVATE GEORGE WARBURTON. Died of Wounds.
week—there came from Mrs. Carter, wit* Major Carter, a very sympathetic letter, con- veying the news that Private Warburton ka d died in hospital at Armentieres.

div.head: Major's Wife's Tribrite to the Dead Man.
div.p: Major's Wife's Tribrite to the Dead Man.

" He died at his post doing his duty," the writer added. " You may es I.rond- that you were the wife of a brave, good tear)." Private Warburton was voll•kv/wn in War- rington, notwithstanding the fact that he bed, for the past two years, lived in Birmingham. Ile was the son of Mr. Daniel Werburtai, ef Priestley-street, and for ten years was f reployei as a fitter in the gas department of the War- rington Corporation. Later, he held a similor position under the Birmingham Corporati3n.

div.head: Successful Bowler,:
div.p: A Successful Bowler,:

When living in Warrington the late Private Warburton was a member of the Conservative Club, and took a successful part in several bowling mains en the Sankey-street green. He was also a member of a local lodge of the Order of Oddfellows. It is only two years since h. was married at the Warrington Parish Chun) to Miss Witton, daughter of Mrs. Wilton, ef 17, Marsh llouse-lana. He leaves one child

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
PRIVATE M. MEL' lA.
Reservist Who Was Called Up When The War Broke Out.

Private If. Melia, who in peaoe time resided with his wife and family at 37, Napier-street, has been wounded in action. He is a Reservist. and is attached to the Bth King's Liverpool Regiment, and he was called up at the out- break of war. He went to the Front in Sep- tember. Private Melia is 34 years of age, and formerly worked at Messrs. Porshaw's in Mersey-street fL9 an iron-dresser. He received his education at St. Mary's School, in Buttermarket-strest.

div.head: Wanted for the Wounded.
div.p: Wanted for the Wounded.

The Ladies' Committee of the Lord Derby War Hospital, Warrington, solicit gifts of all kinds (luxuries and necessities) for the wounded soldiers. A list of the articles specially required will be foun4l in our advertisement columns.

div.head: STORIES FROM THE TRENCHES.
div.p: STORIES FROM THE TRENCHES.
MUST HAVE MORE RECRUITS.
Fighting "Tommy's" Call To The Young Men Banging Back.
The following letter as received by Mtrs. Poole, of 21, Gee-street, from her brother, Private Lemon, who is serving at the Front with the 2nd South Lancs. Regiment : __ _ _ _ _

"We have been knocked about a bit !Ate'''. but still we keep going on, first pace.' lam getting on all right, and doing my share of the task allotted us, along with the younger ones who are out here. I read in the paper that they are asking for recruits. It would be bet- ter if those at home would come forward with- out waiting to be dragged, and then come and help to wipe the brutal and inhuman Gettaans off the face of the earth.

Heartrending Plight of Women and Children. "It is heartrending out here to see the poor women and children who have had their rtbnies broken up, and have had to flee for safety. People at home cannot realise what it is like— it is impossible to do so without you see with your own eyes. Thank God, however, I do not think it will happen in our homes, as I think we have got the upper hand of the enemy ;low, but still it will take a little time yet, and we must have more recruits.

div.head: Now Then, Single Young Men!
div.p: Now Then, Single Young Men!

"I am not asking men to leave their wives and families—far from it—but I think there are plenty of single men at home who could be spared. It would mean a lot if they would deP •forward and come out here and give us a chance to get a rest before the winter comes on, for I am afraid we are likely to spend it out here."

div.head: "PLENTY OF NARROW ESCAPES."
div.p: "PLENTY OF NARROW ESCAPES."
Artillery Sergeant Writes Of The Perils Of Observation Duty.

Sergeant J. Patrick Hollerinn, who is at- tached to the 10th Siege Battery of the Royal Field Artillery, in the course of a letter fisorn "Somewhere in France" to his cousin, Mrs. Reardon, of 11, Stanley-street, Friars' Gmen, Warrington, says: "The struggle we are engaged in is terrible. . . . I do not know the minute when I may be sent into the next world, and I put my trust entirely in our Heavenly Father. . . I have had plenty of sarytw escapes, my latest being only last night (Jtm° 4th.) Then it was that six of us were retuln- ing from our observation post when the Ger- mans commenced shelling the road down which we were going. To go on was to walk into a death trap; to go back was to walk into another.

div.head: Cross a Shell Swept Zone.
div.p: Cross a Shell Swept Zone.

"The shells were coming "thick that we had to throw ourselves into the ditch which bordered the road, and which happened to be dry at the time. There we lay for over two and a half hours. When the shelling had abated ;we got up—or rather two of us did, for the other four were casualties.' Two of the poor arms were killed outright and the other two wounded, though, fortunately, not seriously. Still their wounds were such as to make khero cry with pain as we carried them to the asap- eat dressing station—about half a mile away. An incident like this does not represent a quar- ter of what I have been through. "A Very Risky Job."

"I would not mind if I had the awns obn:noes as has an infantryman of bowling over some of the enemy, but being an artilleryman I have not the chance. We have to go up to any observation post that may be selected and we are not allowed to fire on any German we may see in case we should attract the attention of the enemy's artillery, which would blow us up to the sky before we knew where we 'mere. So, you will see, I have got a very risky job pn. .. . When we are well prepared to make an advance I pity the Germans who try to stop us. . . . . Of course, we have every faith in our winning, but it will mean a great saoriftne of life!"

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. MEMBER.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A. MEMBER.
Collapses While In The AO Of Shooting A Sniper.

Private G. T. Yeates, Orford Cottages, Or- ford, writing from the' Cottage Hospital., Woburn, Beds., to Mr. B. Farrar and -his brother members of the Wycliffe P.S.A., Says they will be surprised to know that he is in England. "I was in the trenches," he explains, "and was in the act of haring a shot at a German sniper when I was, without warning, brought to the ground with a terrible pain in my left knee. My leg was put M splints, and I was sent away by motor and then on to Boulogne. The doctor said I was eufferin,g from chronic synovitis of the knee, and I went under an operation and had a shrapnel bullet taken from the back of my knee. Thank God I am much better. I am bedfast, but hope to be up -be- fore long. I suppose you miss Mr. James. I hope to have an hour with you before I go back."
Private Yeates was wounded some time ago it, the knee, and the bullet apparently had not been detected or boated.

div.head: TO HELP IN Y.M.C.A. ARMY TENTS.
div.p: TO HELP IN Y.M.C.A. ARMY TENTS.
Revs. Ogden and Pitt To Devote Their Holidays To "Tommy."

We learn that the Rev. IT. Ogden, mintster of the Golborne-street Baptist Church, has decided to devote his summer holidays to work in connection with the Y.M.C.A. efforts among the troops and the navy men stationed at Chat- ham, or who are training or may be tempor- arily quartered in the big military and naval depot on the Medway. Mr. Ogden would dearly have liked to have gone to Franoe with tone of the Y.M.C.A. tents, but it was, unfortulately, impossible for him to arrange the nectszary throe months' leave of absenoe. Conscqttpitly, he has generously. decided to forego his regula- tion month's holiday and to put in the rime doing what he can for the edificatiou and amusement of "the boys in khaki, boys in blue." Ile will engage in work at the ChattAam Y.M.C.A. uamp during the whole of the moth et August and a few days of Eleptember.

div.head: WORK THE TENTS ARE DOMES.
div.p: THE WORK THE TENTS ARE DOMES.

The work which he is voluntarily under- taking is of a varied description. Ile will assist in seeing Ito it that Tommy " aid "Jack" have a rendezvous where they *en pleasantly spend their scanty leisure in healthy and docent surroundings, where they can write their lettere home, where they ean have non-aleehelie re- freshments and tasty snacks, where they can listen to music and, if they feel like it, loin in a rousing chorus; in short, where they can kayo 'a jolly good time without resort to the quessieren- able kind of place whither "Jack" and "'l%in" are so frequently driven to seeking their pleasure. The Y.M.C.L. touts have proved 'a huge success in all our big army and Alavy centres, and the work at Chatham is coad.nefed on a specially extensive seale. Besides helping the soldiers and glicabra t-o spend their spare time pleasantly and free ffpm vicious influences, Mr. Ogden will have ether self- imposed duties, such as ministering to the viek and to the wounded, and in noimirrefing religious services. The Rev. C. P. Pitt, the minister et the. Elmwood-avenue Congregational Church, is, we understand, arranging to spend his gii*imer vacation in a similar manner.

div.head: PRIEST AND PASTOR AT THE FRONT.
div.p: PRIEST AND PASTOR AT THE FRONT.

Fcrur other Warrington clerics have 2.1.0) given themselves to the service of "Tommy." and at the moment they are "somewhere in France." They are the Rey. Father Lane Fax, of St. Alban's Roman Catholic Chumll--‘4O went out early on in the war—and the Rev. er. T. Jamee. of Wycliffe Congregational Church. and the Rev. W. Bracecarap, St. Paul's. -aict the Rev. 11. T. S. Collier. Padget&

The Chairman: Personally, I think it would be better referred to the next parish meeting.
THE RULE OF FEW.

Mr. Bottomley : Suppose this came forward at a township meeting and we didn't get more ratepayers present than we usually do, are we to be bound by their resolution? Mr. Westbrook: Wouldn't it be a good plan to get each parish meeting to pass a resolution saying when they want the net meeting to be held?
It was decided to refer the matter to the next meeting of ratepayers.

div.head: " PREPOSTEROUS " WAGES.
div.p: " PREPOSTEROUS " WAGES.
Roadmen Receiving 21s. With Cost Of Living Up 45 Per Cent.
An agitation for the increasing of the wages of roadmen—now earning 21s. a week—was instigated by Mr. A. Bottofilley, at Tuesday. s meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee.

Mr. Bottomley suggested that a recommenda- tion be sent by that eommittee to the Rural District Council, asking them to -.consider the wages being paid at the present time to the roadmen in their employ in the Stockton Heath area. He understood that they were working ten hours per day for 21s. a week, and he thought they (his fellow members) would agree that it was hardly a sufficient wage, and that a man could not live on it in these days. The Chairman (Mr. G. Pilling) said he didn't think the hours were as long as Mr. Bottomley had stated. The men worked, he believed, from seven till half past five, with, of course, intervals for meals. Mr. Bottomley contended that it was not a credit to a public body to pay any man such t wage as 21s. to-day, with prices as they were. _ _ _ _ _

Air. Dukes said that he agreed with Mr. Bottomley. The cost of living had increased about forty-five per cent. Personally, h, thought it was „preposterous to pay such a wage as 21s. He wondered they got men to work for them at all.

div.head: Guinea a Week and a Family.
div.p: A Guinea a Week and a Family.

Mr. Whitley said that some few weeks ago, one of the roadmen—a married man with r family—mentioned that the matter had been brought up at the Rural District Council. He understood that an adjoining Rural District Council had raised the men 3s. a week. The man he had just referred to mentioned that he was rapidly getting into debt owing to the low wage and the high cost of living. The Chairman promised that the matter should have attention. Mr. Bottomley added that no man could live on less than 255. to-day, especially if he were married, and it was bad enough for the single men.
Mr. Westbrook suggested that the Chairman and Mr. Mclntyre, the committee's represents. tives on the Runcorn Rural District Council, should press the matter at the next Council meeting.
The Chairman and Mr. Mclntyre both under- took to do so.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—The monthly devotional meet- ing. of the Wesley -Guild was held on Monday evening, presided over by the Rev. A. J. Morton. There was a very large attendance, which in- cluded members of the Bewsey-road, who paid a visit to Padgate and joined in the welcome to the speaker, the Rev. T. Gladding, one- of the late ministers in the Warrington circuit. The subject for the evening was entitled " A good soldier," and the reverend gentleman gave an excellent address, showing how essential it was for all to apply to themselves the qualities necessary in a good soldier, so that we might become good soldiers and followers of Jesus Christ. Mr. Turner, of Warrington', was the soloist, and he gave an excellent rendering of "Into Thy hands" and "Ora pro nobis," the accompanist being Mrs. W. J. Bate. Votes of thanks were proposed by Mr. W. Newton and Mr. T. B. Duckworth, supported by the Rev. W. T. Derry.

div.head: PEN K ETH.
div.p: PEN K ETH.

Year-old Bride's Sad Death.—On Thursday afternoon the funeral took place, at Sankey Cemetery, of the late Mrs. Thomas Atherton, whose death occurred on Monday under sad-cir- cumstances. The deceased was born 29 years ago at Doe Green, Penketh, and lived there until her marriage about a year ago, when she went to live at Garston. There was a large at- tendance at the funeral serTice in the Wesleyan Church, the parents, Mr. and Mrs. Molyneux, having been regular attendants there for about 40 years, and their family having also attended there. Wreaths were sent by the following friends and relations: Husband and baby, Mother, father and Bert, Edith and Fred, Joe and Lily, Molly and Elsie, Mark and Annie, Mr. and Mrs: D. Atherton, Uncle Dan, Aunt Margaret and family, Mark Atherton and family, George, Lizzie and boys, Aunt Lizzie and Uncle Sam. Eva and Walter, Aunt Ann and Marion. Aunt Annie and Uncle Jack, Fred, Zoe and Mrs. Ashton (Silverfield), Jack Ashton, Harry and S. Hannan, Mr. and Mrs. Green, Uncle Bill and Aunt Lizzie, Mr. and Mrs. W. Higham, Mr. and Mrs. Lawton (Liverpool), Nurse Pritchard, and a few old friends.

The Genuine Article. John Lane, the well-known publisher, said at a literary dinner in New York : • "As an editor I find nobody so persistent as the amateur contributor. If the amateur were half as ingenious in writing his material as in trying to land it, he would become a Dickens in no time. "An amateur said the other day to an editor I know: "'Allow me to submit this bear story.' "'My readers don't care for bear stories,' said the editor. They want something spicy.' "'But this,' said the amateur, is a story about a cinnamon bear.' "

div.head: Sabbath in Scotland.
div.p: The Sabbath in Scotland.
An Englishman tells this story of Sabbath. breaking north of the Tweed, Scotland. A brawny Scot was hammering away at the bottom of his wheelbarrow when his wife came to the door.
" Mon ! Mon!" she exclaimed, "you're making much clatter. What wull the neebours say?"
"Never mind the neebours," returned .the busy husband, "I maun get ma barrow mend it."
"Oh, but Donal', it's vera wrong to wurk on Sawbuth!" protested the good woman. "Ye aught to use screws."

div.head: COSTUMES & BLOUSES
div.p: COSTUMES & BLOUSES
Ear MM gar. TX4I ' FX4 9 . cao
VISITING TERRITORIALS.

Churehpeople's Splendid Part In Club-Providing. As we announced last week, the Lymm Churcheg have extended a fine welcome to the Northwich " Terriers " arrived in Lymm, hastening to make them perfectly at home and providing them with clubs. In the local Parish Magazine the Rector (Rev. G. B. Thurston) writes:— " A company of the 3rd/sth Battalion of the Cheshire Territorials is at present on a visit to Lymm, under the command of Lieutenant B. Armitage, the men being billeted in different parts of the village. The various Churches of the place have risen to the occasion and have made generous provision for the men during their spare hours. This notice is to say that the Newfield Mission Room is open every night from 5.30-9.30; newspapers and simple games have been provided, and arrangements made for writing letters. Refreshments will be served each evening at a nominal cost from ,eight to nine o'clock. By the kindness of the Headmaster of the Grammar School (Mr. W. B. Hawkins), the men will be allowed the use of the playing fields after school hours." Private Joseph Clare, of the Lymm Terri- torials, writes from the Front to his mother:— "Lymm people want to make the visitors as comfortable as they can—the same as when we were billeted in Northampton and the other places we were at in England. I only wish we were in the same position as they are again." Arrival of Band. This week the visitors' band has arrived in Lymm, and the martial strains are stirring up the township in surprising fashion. Each day the band accompaniet;the men to and fro drill; and also does much musical marching on its own account. On Thursday evening the band gave a series of selections at The Cross with a view to re- cruitiug. A good number assembled to hear them. Indeed the music is so appreciated that Lymmites in generfil feel quite downheartea at the prospect of their leaving again at an early date. One of the men is seriously ill with pneu- monia. He is under the best care. Two or three more Privates also have arrived. On Thursday evening Mr. W. Finch, of Wood- lea, entertained the men, at the Wesleyan Schoolroom, to a potato-pie supper, to whieh full justice was done. A capital entertainment followed. Particulars of to-morrow's church parade at Oughtrington will be found in our Volun- teer news. The men will be commanded by Lieutenants Milne and Armitage.

div.head: tiEws •
div.p: tiEws •

Lance-Corporal Reg. Hillier in England.—We are glad to state that Lance-Corpl. Reg. Hillier is progressing favourably after being wounded in. the fighting in the region of the Dardanelles. He is now in England—at Netley Hospital, where he has been a fortright.

Red Cross Hospital.—Under the care of Sister Colburn and her staff there are now seventeen wounded soldiers in Brookfield," the Red Cross Hospital. Corporal Andrews has left this week, but there are as yet no new arrivals., All the patients are going on very satisfactorily.

British Music.—Voluntaries by British com- posers are to be played by Mr. William Cooke at the Parish \Chun& this month. Those selected are: Barcarole, W. Sterndale Bennett; "March of the Israelites," Michael Costa (by request); Carillon, William Faulkes ; Reverie, B. Jackson; Scherzo, C. F. Abdy Williams; Molto Adagia, J. Makinson Fox; Sonata, E. div.head: CAPTAIN T. liID6WAY.
div.p: CAPTAIN T. liID6WAY.
Pays A Brief Visit Home From The Front.

Captain T. Ridgway, of the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, the son of • Mr. and Mrs. T. J. Ridgway, of Wildersmoor, Lymm, and an exceedingly popular and re- spected gentleman—paid a brief visit to his township this Week. 'After 'leaving .the Front the Captain arrived in London on Monday, and there he remained for a day. On Tuesday evening he reached Warrington, whence he motored on to Lymm. Here a large assembly awaited him on Booth's Hill—for the news had somehow spread round the Village. . The waiting enthusiasts, :however, were sadly disappointed, for the Captain, quite unaware of the fact that everybody was so eager and anxious to see him, todk a different ,route home to Wildersmoor, where he arrived 'without in- terruption.

• Yesterday morning Capt. Ridgway returned to London after this short, but happy, respite, and to-day he is expected to return to France—in which country he has already seen five months' arduous military service.

div.head: Ilvetor Gives Advice And Diffuses Optimism.
div.p: Ilvetor Gives Advice And Diffuses Optimism.

The Rector of Lymm (Rev. G. B. Thurston) writes another long letter upon the Government in this month's Parish Magazine. He says : " Many things have taken place since I wrote a month ago as a result of the formation of 61 national Government that had lust been com- pleted but had not had time to put forward its programme, There is no doubt that the first and chief effect has been a national awakening, and that we are no longer a nation unmindful of the task that lies before us. . . . We cannot 'be told .too often of 'the things that belong unto our peace' while there is time to seize upon them before 'they are hid from our eyes.' There are three tasks lying immediately before the Government, each of. which will require careful and delicate organisation, and in two of which every loyal citizen can help in no small degree. The first, which we must leave to ex- pert hands, is the provision of an adequate and constant supply of munitions of war. This is absolutely essential both for the purpose of reaching the goal towards which we have set out—an honourable and lasting peace—and also for the preservation of valuable lives of those who are fighting and preparing to fight our battles. So far as reports can be relied on the Ministry of Munitions is making satisfactory progress, and the shortage from which we were suffering is rapidly being overcome. National Register.

"The two matters in Which we can all help are the provision of a national register and a hoarding by thrift of the national resources. It is evidently going to be decreed by Parliament that a register be made forthwith of all men and women between the ages of 15 and. 65, with particulars as regards age and employment, and what special forms of labour persons could engage in. This makes a very distinct advance on the somewhat ineffective result of voluntary effort on which_ we have hitherto relied, and it will bring much comfort to many who are only waiting to be told what the country requires of them. . . . Because we do not live under a perpetual semi-martial law like our enemies, it by no means follows that we are a badly organised nation, especially when we are in earnest about thp matter we have in hand. There need be no talk of conscription or com- pulsion; those are not ways we have been accustomed to, nor are they terms that find special favour among us; but it must be a very small minority indeed that is not prepared to do his or her duty when that duty is put clearly and reasonably before them. Call For Economy.

"The other thing in which we can all help is in the strict practice of economy for the duration of the war. As the Premier said in his Guildhall speech, 'waste on the part ether of individuals or of classes ,cas nothing short of a national danger.' We shall have in•ii,y prac- tical opportunities of learning lessons in politi- cal /economy through suggestions in the ne papers during the next few Jays-the .f,m Las of food which are extravagant and thoie that are economical. Our own sense of self-pm.ervation will lead us to take note of these, and to order our expenses accordingly. For with such pos- sible saving is allied the money nee-•,=sities of the country in carrying on the war; the two go together and cannot be separated. .. . One hardly likes to recommend the war loan cs an excellent investment, though, indeed, EO• it is; the main point 'is that the money must be obtained. Facilities have been given by which all can help by investing sums as small as five shillings at a time. Hence it will be seen that the curtailing of expenses means not ontv saving for the person concerned, but a direct con- tribution to the loan for carrying on the war to a successful issue. Pessimism In Certain Newspapers.

"Before I leave this subject I should like to say a word about the tone of pessimism that has been so common in certain newspapers dur- ing the past month. Because signal success is not immediately forthcoming for the Allies it by no means follows/that they are not doing quite as well as even the most sanguine might have expected. From all that one can gather there is no cause for such pessimism but rather the reverse. Granted that we have opposing us a strong, well-organised and thoroughly pre- pared foe, it is extraordinary how well the Allies have done; the future is merely a matter of time and of patience; the cost may and probably will be great, both in men and in material, but the outcome, can hardly be in doubt if the country as a whole is determined to concentrate on the task before it."

In the Parish Church Vestry on Monday evening the Rector presided over a well- attended meeting of the Lymm branch of the C.E.Y.M.S. 'The assembly included Messrs. C. div.head: "TERRIERS" SUMMER SHIRTS.

Lymm Lady's Patriotic Effort To Supply Needed Comforts.

The July Parish Magazine contains the following paragraph : " Intelligence has reached ,us, both through Lieutenant-Colonel Groves and also from our local Territorials, that there is need for the comfort of the men at the Front of khaki- coloured cotton skirts. Mrs.. Groves, of Dean's Green, is 'making an effort to supp).y •five hundred of these—about one hundred are being made locally, and the balance of four hundred have been ordered ready made. The total cost will not be less than fifty pounds, towaids which Mrs. Groves has received, chiefly from her relatives, thirty. "The remaining twenty pounds should be secured without delay. Would those who are prepared to contribute, large or small sums. kindly communicate as soon as possible either with Mrs. Groves or with the Rector?" ,
Football Decision.—The Lymm Wednesday Football Club has decided not to enter this season the Manchester Wednesday League— owing to the majority of its players having enlisted.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
div.p: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
RADDON COURT.
Its Work And Its Needs—And The Support Received.

Miss Sylvia E. Broadbent, vice-president of the Daresbury Division, British Red Cross Society. writes The Daresbury Division up to the outbreak of war was supported financially by the sub- scriptions of members and associates and adherents, and the work of the society consisted mainly in the training of voluntary aid detachments.

- In August, when it was decided to equip and open a hospital at Raddon Court,. an appeal was made for further subscriptions and donations, which was generously met by the public. Since then gifts of money and things in kind have been constantly received, and I wish to take this opportunity, through your kindness, of thanking all those who have helped in the support of the hospital. and in the provision of extra comforts and pleasures for the patients. The list of those who have given money and presents is so long that I may be excused from giving the names, and hope that all will accept -the hearty thanks of the committee of the Daresbury Division, and the staff of thc hospital. The gifts on Pound Day, often amounting to about .£lO, are a substantial help to the house- keeping funds. With the increase in prices of food, coal, gas, &c., the balance in hand must necessarily decrease. I therefore appeal for further subscriptions and donations to enable us to carry on the work of tending 45 wounded soldiers. _ _ _

I wish, also, to thank those who lend their motor cars to take the men pleasure rum, and to appeal for further help of this kind; also, thanks are due to the managers of the theatres and picture palaces for free performances, and to all those who have provided music2l and other forms of entertainment, including some charming dancing by children. A pleasing incident took place on Tuesday last week, when the children of St. Alban's Schools came laden with gifts of fruit, flowers, eggs, &c., which they had bought from their own savings. They handed fruit and cigarettes to the patients, who were amused and pleased. The hospital is quite full and the patients are making good progress, the fine weather enabling those who are allowed up to be much out of doors.

div.head: TO 111AKE--' GOOD COFFEE.
div.p: TO 111AKE--' GOOD COFFEE.

In the first place, the coffee must be of good quality, freshly roasted and freshly ground. Coffee that has been kept in a bag for several days loses most of its fragrance and tastes flat and uninteresting. When it is not possible to buy freshly roasted coffee every day or two the beans should be kept in a tightly shut tin, and before grinding placed on a plate in the oven for a few minutes. Some specially careful house- wives think it behoves them to try to roast the coffee at home, but this is not advisable. Coffee is roasted in a cylinder over gas or charcoal, and is rather a tiresome process, needing great care, as the beans catch very easily. If, however, it is necessary to roast at home, use a new, clean iron frying-pan placed over gentle heat and keep the -beans constantly moving.. But even when the coffee is good and fresh, it may be that the water is so hard as to spoil the result. Good coffee cannot be made with very hard water, and therefore in some places it is necessary to use distilled water for coffee-making. Again, different blends of coffee suit different kinds of water, and it is well to consult a coffee expert on the subject if there is reason to suppose that all other details have been attended to and,yet the coffee is unsatisfactory. But granted that we have water of no unusual hardness, fresh coffee of good quality, roasted not more than two or three days ago, freshened up in tfie oven, and newly ground, what next? The average cook fails in making coffee because she does not use enough. One cannot quarrel with the Eng- lish cook for economising, as a rule, but coffee she is apt to treat too much like tea, whereas for good cafe an lait one heaped tablespoonful should be allowed to two-thirds of a half-pint of water for each person. This allows of two portions of strong coffee, the cup containing about one-third of coffee and two-thirds of hot milk. For after dinner coffee less than half a tumblerful of water should be allotted to each tablespoonful of coffee. If the cups are very small use a little less coffee and just the cupful of water.—" Queen." if
