div.head: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
div.p: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
IN AND 01:1"[HE TRENCIIEg.

The Lymm members of the sth Cheshires at the Front re-entered, on Thursday ,night of- last week the trenches, and at ,present they are in them. They have, however, had a few days in dug-outs just behind the actual firing- line. From all "accounts they are having a lively time; but luck is with them. They\thave lost two men, it is true; but that is not due to the enemy. One--Private Geol-ge Taylor—has been so unfortunate as to slip in the dark and wound himself. Private John W. Jones has had a nervous breakdown, chiefly as the result of his seeing his mate shot when talking to him. Both live in Rush Green.

Private Percy Clare writes on Sunday, July 4th, to Miss Bessie Cross: lam writing while in our dug-outs. We are just behind the trenches, but our battalion are in the it-en...hes. Our platoon and another are in the dug-outs. We are like the working gang; we •larry all sorts of things to the trenches every night, and take the food up to the lads in the trenches. It is a rather risky job, as bulhts are flying all about us as soon as it comes lark; and they try to shell us in the daytime. I ant pleased to say they have done us no harm yet; but I am sorry to tell you that on the second day we came up this time we lost two offiflt3r3--both out of our company—one wounded and the other killed. ,So you see one never knows what is going to happen. . . It is a nice ,morning; it makes us think about you at home. . , The ..mtly church or chapel we go to is in the tleldi with shells flying about; but it answers the same purpcse. We have a Sergeant who can speak l'rench, so we take our cards to him and he tells Its what they say. I don't expect we shall get away from the trenches for a week or two vet. . . . Some more of us are going .mc leave this ucelc or Monday from the trenches. It will , come our turn with a bit of luck soon."

Writing earlier, the Pri cate said: "We have to go up to the trenches at night when we are on what they call our few days' rest. Last night (Saturday) we left our camp at half-past seven and got there about ten o'clock; so you see it takes us over two hours to go. And then we had three hours' digging trenches to do, and then walk back with a spade. So it was not far off four o'clock when we got back. Well; we had to be up at eight for breakfast; and then we have two full hours' drill. So you see it is little rest we get. I think they take us for horses; but never mind, we can do it." • We Shall Win This Match.
To his mother, Mrs. G. Davies, Private P. Clare writes :

"When we start work at night there are such a lot of stray shots knocking about; we are among them pretty fairly on this job. Well, keep your heart up! We are all keeping in the best of health. I am writing these few lines in my dug-out (Saturday). I am on guard to- night and to-morrow, so I shall not be out with the boys to-night. They have about three trips to do. We are just behind the trenches, and we have to go down to meet the transport waggons; and then we bring the stuff up to the lads in•the trenches—our battalion, but not our platoon and another. We have to carry- things up every night; it is far more dangerous than being in the trenches. Bullets are flying all about; it is really marvellous how so many get about without being hit; but thank God we keep missing them. 'Captain Hartley and Harold will be surprised to hear we have lost two officers. . . We shall be home for good before long if we have the luck to pull through. I don't think it will go on another winter. . . . How is Billy Poltal iping on? If you see him just remember me to him. Tell him I think we shall win this match; it is a stiff one, but we have got a guod team out now."
Yesterday word received from Private J. Clare _

ran: "By the time you get this I think we shall have W. Hadden and Jack Thomason with us: I had a letter from Ernest Hadden ; he said they had left for France. The Colonel made a speech to them on the station before leaving, and told them they were going to one of the best batta- lions in France, and I don't think he is far wrong! The weather at present is fearfully hot, and we get very thirsty. So could you send me some lemonade powder? It is not safe to drink too much water."
Corporal Jack H. Moston write: "We are all going on all right. . . I suppose by now you will have seen Sergeant Harold Claro and know all."

Captain G. W. C. Hartley and Sergeant Harold Clara set out on their return to the Front on Monday morning. They had a quiet send-off; everybody was sorry to see them go. Corporal Ernest Clare happily was able to come over on Saturday night from training in Essex to see his brother. The Corporal is a member of the second division of tho 1/sth Cheshire Territorials.
According to letters received in the region of Newfields, two other local 'Terriers" expected to arrive home for three days on Thursday night. They have not arrived, however.

div.head: PRIVATE GEORGE TAYLOR.
div.p: PRIVATE GEORGE TAYLOR.
Accidentally Hurt By Slipping On To Bayonet:

Yesterday morning Lance-Corporal Fred Kay wrote to Mrs. George Oldham, of Itush Green, to tell her that. her son, Private George Taylor, had accidentally wounded himself. The letter, which was dated Monday, ran: "It is with the deepest. regret that I have to inform you that your son, .George. was wounded last night. We had been carrying up to the trenches, and in stepping over a trench he slipped and fell on a bayonet. He was bandaged up and we took him to the dressing statign. He Will- be in hospital now somewhere down ,the line, where he will be well looked after. I don't think the wound is very serious. In a few days I expect he will be in England; then you will soon have him at home. The Rush Green lads seem to be amongst it, don't they?" • Aged 23, Private Taylor as a boy attended Onghtrington Church and schools. He is em- ployed at Heatley by Mr. Sam Davies, hay- cutter, and has belonged to the Territorials for nearly two years.

div.head: PRIVATE -JOHN W. .JONES.
div.p: PRIVATE -JOHN W. .JONES.

Health Breaks Down In The Trendies. On °Wednesday, Mrs. Robert, Jones, of Rush Green, heard through the medium of letters from •his mates, that her. son, Private John William Jones—of the local. Territorials—was lying very 'ill in hospital. He has had a physi- cal breakdown. One of the letters said that "he had not, been himself since his mate, Jack Guest, was shot in front of him; but last Friday dropped in the trench, and the doctor could not say what was the matter with him until he got in hospital. But he was very ill." He has not come over to England.

Corporal Fred Kay writes: "Jack Jones went to hospital sick last Fridai. . . . We shall be wondering whose turn it will be next." - Further word says that Private Jones' face and body were very much swollen. In peace times Private Jones is a fireman at the Partington Paper Mills, and attends the Lvmm Wesleyan Church. He has been a " Terrier " now for nearly two years. Aged 21, he was educated under Mr. 0. G. Smith, at the Oughtrington Schools.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
Month's Baptisms, Marriages and Burials.— During the month at the Parish Church four infants -were baptised, ten persons were married, and four funerals were conducted.

The Choir Excursions.—The choir boys at St. Thomas' Church are to have their annual ex- cusion as usual this year, but the date and the rendezvous have not yet been fixed. The choir men, however, have decided to dispense with their, excursion, owing to the war.

The Tramway Shelter.—The clerk to the Cheshire County Council has written to the clerk to the Warrington Town Council with reference to the shelter at the Stockton Heath tramway terminus, agreeing not to require the removal of the shelter, unless the site is required for a public purpose, and then only after six months' notice.

The Parish Council—The monthly meeting of the Parish Council on Tuesday evening was presided over by Mr. W. Mclntyre. Those present included Messrs. C. Dukes, J. McDermid, A. Bottomley, J. Whitley F. Rose, H. J. Westbrook, J. H. Clarke an cr E. Brad- shaw .(clerk).

Memorial Service.—A. memorial service for those who have fallen in the war will be held at St. Thomas' Church to-morrow afternoon, starting at 3 o'clock. Representatives of the Parish Council, Parochial Committee, and the local unit of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment will be in attendance.

Special Services.—Special services will be con- ducted at the Wesleyan Church to-morrow by the Rev. G. H. Cowles, D.D., of Australia. The Rev. Cowles will preach morning and evening, and address the young people in the afternoon, when Mr. G. Davey-Smith will preside. The col- lections 'throughout ,the day will be for the Trust fund.

"There Were Present."—Mr. Geo. Pilling presided at the monthly meeting of the Stock- ton Heath Parochial Committee, at the Coun- cil Schools on Tuesday evening. There were also, present: Messrs. J. H. Clarke, H. J. Westbrook, W. Mclntyre, F. Rose, J. Whitley, A. Bottom- ley, J. MeDermid, C. Dukes, S. Wright (sur- veyor) and W. E. Hough (Clerk). Alleged Big Gas A ccou nts.—Mr. J. Whitley, at Tuesday's meeting of the Parochial Com- mittee, in the Schools, said that the lighting accounts for the half-year, seemed, practically as high as usual, although quite a lot of the street lamps had not been lighted. The number of lamps that had been lighted were not stated. The Clerk said that an allowance of 05 had been made for the lamps not lit.

The Fish-and-Chips Fiend !—A complaint with regard to rubbish in the streets was made by Mr. J. Whitley at Tuesday evening's meet- ing of the Parochial Committee. One cause, said Mr. Whitley, was the sweeping of rubbish from some of the houses into the roadway. Someone said that fish and chip papers added to the disorder.—Mr. Dukes: Those who buy chips on Saturday night and eat them in the streets, can't see the wastepaper basket. (Laughter.) Presentation to a Sunday Sc.iool Teacher.— Recently one of the teachers in St. Thomas' Sunday School—Miss Elizabeth Blackbrirne— was married to Mr. Joseph Welding. of Latch- ford, the ceremony taking nlace in the Parish Church and being performed by the Vicar (the Rev. Jas. Collins). The teachers and scholars of the Sunday school made Mrs. Welding's nuptials the occasion for making her presents— the former giving her a silver cake basket and a butter dish, and the latter two nice silver photo frames.

Motor Cyclist Fined.—At 1-he Runcorn. Petty Sessions on Monday, Walter Napier Slater Jackson, of Heatherlea. Grappenhallro& Stockton Heath. was fined ss. for having the number-plate of his motor cycle obscured at eight p.m. on the night of June 23rd.—The evidence of P.S. Robinson was to the effect that he saw prisoner riding a motor cycle at the foot of Delph Bridge with a lady on the carrier, the hack number-plate being, hidden by her dress. He stopped the defendant, who said he was sorry and did not know about it. Later in the evening the defendant offered him half- a-crown, again expressing his sorrow.

div.head: MORE CRITICS WANTED.
div.p: MORE CRITICS WANTED.
VII Don't The Ratepayers Attend The Parish Meeting?
ALLEGED LACK OF INTEREST.

Mr. Bottomley said at Tuesday's meeting of the Stockton Heath Parish Council that the last two or three parish meetings had been very badly attended indeed, and proposed that in future only one meeting per year be held in- stead of two. Such meetings were not called for the Councillors to do businelik_ They were called so that the parishioners .could have a chance of criticising their actions, yet at those meetings there had been very few present except members of the Council. He did not think they were justified in spending money on a meeting that was attended only by a few of the rate- payers. If they (the ratepayers) were in- terested in the work, it was a simple matter. Parish meetings could at anytime be called by, the Chairman of the Parish Council, by any two Parish Councillors, the Chairman of the Parish meeting, or any six parochial electors. Mr. Westbrook expressed himself in entire agreement with Mr. Bottomley, and seconded.

div.head: LITTLE OCCASION FOR CRITICISM.
div.p: LITTLE OCCASION FOR CRITICISM.

Mr. McDermid moved that the matter be deferred till the next parish meeting. lie thought it would be undemocratic if they were to do what was suggested without consulting the ratepayers, after the latter had said there should be two annual meetings. He thought the main reason why the ratepayers had not attended the meetings in larger numbers was that there was very little occasion for criti- cism. Mr. Rose wanted to know whether any rate- payer was entitled to attend the Parish Coun. cil meetings., The Chairman : Any of the four statutory meetings. Mr. Clarke said it was time and money thrown away to hold meetings when no one attended thorn.

Mr. Dukes seconded Mr. McDermid's motion. He remarked that they did not want the rate. payers to think that an opportunity for criti- cism had been taken away from them. The matter ought to be kept open till the ratepayers had an opportunity of voicing their opinion.
CRANKS AND ALL!
Mr. Rose (in reply to a remark referring to "a few cranks"): We're here to represent the cranks -
Mr. Westbrook: I object. (Laughter.)

Mr. Rose: As well as the other ratepayers. We're here to represent the ratepayers, never mind what kind they are. (More laughter.) Mr. Bottomley said he didn't think a resolu- tion passed by the parish meeting on the mat- ter would be of any standing.

Mr. Westbrook aid he wiis inclined to agree with Mr. Bottomley. That/ is to say, it would not be binding in the statutory sense. But it would be morally binding. The Chairman: Hear, hear. Shall I put the matter to the meeting? . lir. Dukes: I think if we could avoid, a de- cision it would be better.

div.head: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE'
div.p: CHURCH LADS' BRIGADE'
Declaration Of Its Purposes
And Achievements.

The Church Lads' Brigade has, through itg, Governor and Commandant, Field Marshal Ler° Grenfell, been making an appeal for funds f.°l the part it is taking in providing men for toe Army, for home defence, and, in a lesser degree' for His Majesty's Navy. At such a time as this, when the greatest neede must be served first, and all things done decentlY and in order, it seems to be right that tbe Church Lads' Brigade should make a pub 11° declaration of its purposes and achievementB' Since its foundation nearly a quarter of a ceo; tury ago, not fewer than 450,000 lads have 119" the advantage of the high standard of religi°as. moral, and physical training which its organisa" tion affords, and although designed as a ligious rather than a military agency, there , at this time of our Empire's stress and Perla some 100,000 of its ex-members from home an overseas serving with the colours. div.head: The. Charge.

MANY SOUVENIRS.
.A: Warrington Private in the Territorials, wziting to his wife, gives a vivid description of the doings on the day of the charge. He saYS

"My story on the battle for three lines 'of trenches held by the Germans, at a point I am unab,le to state, but t hope you read about it in Your papers. Never in all mylife have I experi- enced anything like it. Plainly speaking, it was hell, and I am Proud that I am able to write an account to all my friends. I was, like all my comrades. who have fallen, expecting my turn to cOme. I am going now to give my story to You and explain everything from start to finish.

div.head: AN EARLY MORNING TRAMP.
div.p: AN EARLY MORNING TRAMP.

"On June 15th we had orders that our Brigade • Was to act as support to another Brigade, and we , had orders to get a plentiful supply of rations, because we were told that they did not know how long we would be on the job. Well, the evening eatoe for us to proceed to our destination, and 1. we had eleven. miles of country to tramp. We were very tired indeed before we got there, but ' made not the slightest difference. Our work of mark had to be done, and we knew it, et) we kept on the best we could. By this time the weight of our equipment, pack, and food, rifle, te*, was getting very uncomfortable, but that was a case of having to put up with it, any bow. t)Il nearing our trenches and the crowds of men about that were to take part in the charge, it get to the Germans' eyes. Seeing so many they !brew, up lights galore: Then we knew that they did have an idea that we were massed (we were massed, too, there would be about thousand or more of us), so they Eitarted at ace With their artillery and sent many great high "Plosives at us, putting the wind into us before Rot into 'position. They kept this up, -4ltheugh it had pot broken daylight then. A great lot of time was spent by us in getting into. , Fosition in 501110 very small trenches that had 'been:made purposely to accommodate us for the .aseault. 'Time grew on, we were all eager for Ole comrdencement, so we all 'got into position, and the Germans were still throwing these great aliens at us. At a quarter to three our artillery Faye them a few shots in return, and it seemed te.quieten them a little.

div.head: POURED SHELLS AT EACH OTHER.
div.p: POURED SHELLS AT EACH OTHER.

"Then the fatal hour came for the artillery 'Which had long prepared for this attack. At a quarter past three our batteries opened fire, Which is always done before a charge. T.hey Simply blew their trenches and men to eternity. Oh! the sound of the artillery on both sides will always live in my memory. It Was marvellous how they poured shells at each Other. It seemed impossible for anyone to live !II such a shower of shell and explosives. Our '2,ni obardment lasted exactly one hour. Then ; I'. e assault had to start. Directly the batteries petl the 3unlp,d ov men in our first line of trenches charg,d yr the parapet and with fixed bayonets .Many st:he Germans, who fled like wolves. bayonete:iYed in the trench, but those were there „ei`t! or taken prisoners. We believe • a 80 prisoners taken.

THE CAPTURED TRENCHES. well, this first attack our chaps, who ',were absolutely in rear of all, went off under rrible shell tire until they readied the Ger- 'l.llan trenehe,) IS rt. them, s O eager were they to have a dig Well, the first German line of rench wa taken sem as easily as going to bed, e 500 men leaving it. The feeling of all men was for victory at any cost, and they Fot it too, but while all this was going on, the taking of trenches, the German artillery was POaring shells on our support trenches. You 4e. as one line of trench is left to go forward, 1' 1! It was heart-rending to see 'lna of the trenches strewn with dead and • ,ag• The shell fire was the greatest cause I helped one poor fellow .and gave him • urink. It seemed the last few words he would ;TY, but on going past the place I saw him some ti °la's after I saw that he was still living, BO I ,sald e Have a drink. Our line has been sue- and if I could I would take you out to •0 dressi nis station myself.' I would, but no ltne had to take any wounded out at all, all ad th to t e ge away if it was possible for them, ,e 0 taselves. Not being a first aid man, 1 4„11,1d not tackle a wound like it, but I went Rot one who soon put him all right.. He •there fully twelve hours that I knew of. - ere were cases far worse. It was sickenirig to,,,ee the stream of wounded; all seemed to e one way down a communication trench. ;but rilastered all the trenches we had to take, tetali,n the afternoon we lost one. This was it is -"I very soon,and we still held them,though. Ne;jois .cost our side a great loss of life and Ivithild"l. The artillery of the Germans is, doubt, splendid. They are a. really 1371 a lot, ana one must admit it. The way they tewped shells of all sorts into us was awful. a good job that we were well entrenched, Intel° Would have suffered much .more. They 'slll.4l)ed these great heavy explosives and %airOnel shell fully 18 hours on us. It is that it was worse than the fight for Neuve I was very Of I indeed to knt)vi . we were to be relieved the same evening.

~FATEFUL FORTY-EIGHT HOURS. 1 NI I Was absolutely tired and weary, fatigued with such strenuous work and no c)t. .°l' 81 in between. There was no time )1":34e:111'elrd be, -e e were just 48 hours away, and it Nekw4.°llK. I can tell you. We .had the 11 mile )t, bl,r•Wolk, and I don't know how I managed. !itizl,l did; a mil, or rather or of the travel- kif,:utohons met us after we lad walked six 141)let--,APr 80, and they gave us hot tea. div.head: UNPRECEDENTED.
div.p: UNPRECEDENTED.
Officer Says Such A Fight Was Never
Fought.

"An officer of a Lancashire Territorial Battalion•in Franders," writing to the "Man- chester Guardian" evidently with reference to the charge in which our Territorials took-part, says:— " Literally we have fought such a fight for a day and a night as has never been fought be- fore. You in England will probably only read in the papers amongst other things that the British took three lines of trenches east of a famous town, and people will probably say:— 'A few more hundred yards! What's the good .of it?. Why don't they get a proper move on?' Well, our general has just addressed us, and his exact words- were : "'Men, when I came out here a few months ago I said to myself, 'I have been in the army 28 years, and I think I know all there is to be known about war.' But I found I was wrong. Again, a week ago, I said, I think now I know all,' but I learnt last Wednesday that I did not even know what shell fire 'was like. Men, I have learnt many things since last Wednesday, one of which is that the can never be broken; indeed, that the —th Brigade can neve' be broken.' . • •

"That's something from a General. But what a cost! We came out the best, yet our battalion lost ten officers and over 250 men. We have been shelled for 231 hours without stopping —shelled with every conceivable sort of shell, from an eight-inch howitzer down to small field-guns. I have talked to xnen one minute, ,and the next they were merely not there—gone completely; I have been buried under faller earth, deafened by explosion, choked with dust, blinded, and my nerves all but shattered. Wa have, charged the Germans at the point of the bayonet; we have been gassed; we have stood in the open and rallied out men while machine- guns have swept the ground and we have rot notiCed them; we have held them all liay, and, under a rain of shot and shell which VIM even worse than Neuve Chapelle (although ever a smaller area) we advanced and accomplished our purpose.

"But if, as I hear, there are young men in England who, while they are not ngaged in Government work, still have not joinel any- thing, tell them what we are doing out here, tell them we are willing to hold on to the last man if necessary, and we can win—are winning slowly,—but we want more help., What are they doing?"

div.head: MARKET GATE DESOLATE?
div.p: MARKET GATE DESOLATE?
Sergeant Asks Has The Charge • Brought In All Slackers ?

, Sergeant E. J. Widocks, Inachine gun secti'...n of the Will ringtun Territort ils, aud a car-driver when at home, who took part in the charge on June 16th, writes to Councillor Henshall as follows, carefully noting that the date of his letter, July 2nd, is Walking Day:—

"Dear Mr. Henshall.— "As our ' friends ' on the Opposition Bench are at present rather quiet, I thought I would collect my scattered thoughts and write you a few lines. I received your very nice letter a short time since, and your parcel came to hand last night (July Ist), and is now reposing in security in a dug-out on the ramparts of the most talked of city in the war area. We are going to start on the contents to-night for tea, and if they are as nice as the last—well, please accept the thanks and good wishes ,of the machine gunners—all that are left of us. I sincerely hope you and Mrs. lionshall are well. Am glad to say I am 0.K., and that is some- thing to be pleased about after what we have passed through lately. Not Swanking—Not 'Arf.

"You will know by now about the old Battalion being in the big attack on that eve) to be remembered Wednesday. And, doubtless, you will have seen what the General said about us after it was , over. Of course, we are not 'swanking' about it—not 'an. It is sad to miss such a lot of familiar faces, and the wonder is that all of us,did not go west. It was a terrible ordeal, as it lasted about 22 hours—the boys being shelled incessantly all that time, but they all behaved splendidly. I had five of my regu- lar section hit—happily none being killed. We had some very narrow escapes, especially late in the afternoon, when the Huns, thinking we were tired of high explosive and shrapnel shells, sent us some gas shells for a change. They are vile contraptions, and if civilisation can invent such deadly things, I think if the clock was pu back about 200 years we should be much better off. The fumes of the gas are very similar to holding your mouth over the exhaust of a petrol engine. They send a gas shell to make you run out of the dug-out, and then they let go a shrapnel shell to catch you when you get out, so you see there is method in their mad- ness ! I think it proves that they are a beaten nation, determined to be as cruel as possible, until• they are finally crushed. I should imagine Market Gate presents a desolate amiear. ance now all the slackers ' have rushed to the colours since they read of the way the old 4th behaved! What ? You mean to say that there are still young men at -home who are eligible for military duties.? Surely these must be women masquerading in men's clothing—and yet the women are doing all they can. If all that could would only come, we should be home amongst you all the sooner. Just look' what they are missing—a free trip on the Continent, food and 'sleeping accomniodation' for nothing, and money given to them to spend—and several othel free -items included—those they get from the other side. '

"I am glad to know that Warrington is still going on in the same old style, and that all friends are well. I and the others in the Battalion are getting leave in our turns (3 clear days in England), so I hope to see you at no distant date. Don't be startled at the sight of a poor old motorman wending his way along Knutsford-road—he may possibly condescend to ride on a tramcar, as I believe they are free to soldiers! . . .

"Excuse me. I had to leave this for a bit as our friends' have just said 'Good morning' to us with half a dozen souvenirs, encased in steel cases, but no damage being done, I will resume my attempt at a letter. Aeroplanes Are Plentiful.

"There are several aeroplanes overhead, but we seldom notice them now, seeing so many of them, and yet about four years ago I lost a day's wages, paid for two tickets to Blackpool, food and places of amusement, and 4s. to go on the flying ground to see them fly, but, alas! the •black flag flew on the Tower all day—de- noting "'there Will be no flying to-day." If I could ju§t have peeped into the future! Look at what I could have saved! Now they are up here the *hole day long, and' we won't chance getting a pain in our necks. We have seen several. German 'planes brought down by our airmen, who are the coolest and best in the' world. Aeroplanes play a most important part in this great struggle. It is so difficult to move troops about without some. aviator seeing them. Our aviator's here don't wait for the sun to come out and the wind to go down—they just go up in any weather almost. I am writing this on the outskirts of a very famous city, talked of by all—a city of desolation and ruin—called . I nearly said it, but 'why press' me to tell you.' Will you please remember me to all friends at the good and ancient town, and to Alderman Bennett, Councillors Archer, Wilson, Chrimes and all the rest? Hoping to see you soon, I 'will now. conclude this epistle and remain
"Faithfully yuurs, "E. J. WIDOCKS, Sold."

div.head: TOWN PROUD OF THEM.
div.p: TOWN PROUD OF THEM.
Mayor's Sympathy With The Relatives Of Killed In Great Charge.

At the commencement- of the monthly meet- ing of the Town Council on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) paid official tribute, on behalf of the Corporation, to the gallantry of . Warrington's_ Territorials.
f think," said his Worship,. ``ll-in-Wsay in the name of every member of this Council and of every reßdent in.thejown that..we are proud of the bruve dame of.. the .4tb„ South

Laneashires hi'. the great battle, fought a week or so ago. (Hear, hear.)' I am sure that we, one, and all, regret the serious losses which were suffered. I have personally written to all the families, of whom I could get to know, who have • lost relatives, offering them my, con- dolences on behalf of the town. (Hear, hear.) I am sure we all feel sorry for those who have been wounded, and that they have our sym- pathy in their pain and our best wishes for speedy and complete recovery. (Hear, hear.) The town, I am sure, should be gratified by the fact that Colonel Fairclough and Major Cros- field have been mentioned in dispatches for their gallant conduct—(applause)—and -by the fact that one of our townsmen, Sergeant Tom Widd, has received the Distinguished Conduct Medal at the hands of his Majesty. (Ap- plause.) I have written- to Mr. Widd, sen.' con- gratulating him on the honour obtained by his son and stating that I felt quite sure that War- rington would be proud of him, and of her, other gallant sons." (Applause.)

div.head: INDIAN LANCER'S TRIBUTE.
div.p: INDIAN LANCER'S TRIBUTE.
Sorrowful But Proud.

Driver W. Timmins, A.5.C.,7 attached 30th Lancers, Indian Expeditionary Force, writes:— " It is with profound regret that I read of the untimely but honourable death of the heroes of our town in your esteemed paper'of 26th June, 1915. These brave men, true sons of the country, sacrificed and laid down their lives for the uplifting of their Motherland. While showing my deep sorrow I am really very proud of such men who think their lives a trifling matter in view of the need of their country. England must be proud of such sons, cheer- fully facing death in 'trenches. This much I can say, of my personal experience: I have seen the Territorials going to the trenches in such a fearless manner, as if they were walking through the streets in London. What could be a better proof than this of the loftiness of the soul of a nation?

div.head: KILLED.
div.p: KILLED.
PRIVATE J. E. BANNISTER.
Well-known Liberal Gives Ills Life For His Country.

Private glohn- Edward Bannister has been killed in action. The news was received on Saturday by his mother at Bolton. She has heard nothing', however, as to the precise details of how he came to give his life.

Private Bannister, although having spent much time in Bolton, was really most closely connected with Warrington—where he was much respected. Aged about 36, he came to this town many years ago as a forgeman for Messrs. •Pearlon and Knowles. He had also worked for Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., but he was working at the Dallam Forge at the time of mobilisation.
lie joined the Territorials five months before the outbreak of war, and he had been at the Front since February.
Liberal and Catholic.

A member of the Liberal Club, Private Bannister for a considerable time had taken a prominent part in local politics. At the club he took an interest in, bowling and billiards. He also belonged to the League of the Cross, and attended St. Mary's R.C. Church. Whilst living in Warrington he lodged at 32,
playing the trombone in the battalion band. He worked at Messrs. Crosfield's soapery, where his father has been employed for up- wards of forty years.

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD SAYS "A FINE LAO AND VERY BRAVE."
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD SAYS "A FINE LAO AND VERY BRAVE."

Dated July 6th, the following letter has been received; from Major Geo. Cresfield:—" Dear Mrs. Chalmers,—l am very sorry ,not to have replied to your letter of June 24th before this, but I have been away on leave and only got your letter yeaterday. We have now learned the sad news that your son succumbed to his wounds in hospital on June 18th—where, we do not know. Your son was engaged in bringing in wounded when he himself was wounded. He' was a fine lad and very brave, and I know how much Surgeon-Lieutenant Law feels his loss. I can only offer you my sincerest sympathy, and I am sure that you and your husband will bear up as bravely as you can for the sake of our country and the noble cause for which we are fighting."

Memories of the Charge.

. In a subsequent letter he recalls memories of the charge, and says that about ha.. a dozen of the drummers got hit. "The Scots ' " he adds, "went .for the enemy fine . . . and our fellows didn't half give it 'em! We captured about two hundred Germans. Not bad waei it?" Writing later he announces that he is in hos- pital at Rouen, 'and say that the only grumble he has to make is that he cannot get any "cigs." " That " he adds, "is the worst part about it. Our Battalion caught it pretty hot, but not half so hot as some ,of the others. .. . The Germans shelled us as we were coming up.. . . but 'there was a rush for their trenches, and the Liverpool Scottish, the Royal Irish Rifles, the 11.A.C„ ourselves and two or three more lots got the first trench and then we simply walked to the second line of trenches. We not only had a bit of bayonet ocroise, but bad to fight

in his back, the result of a chain accident he had at the works some time ago. " I shall not be able to get any more souvenirs yet" he says. "I had a good one the morning I was wounded—a German helmet, but could not manage to get it away—l was glad to get -away myself, Wilkie. There were Germans everywhere—all sorts and sizes, young and old. . . . I received your letter and paper; it is quite welcome to have a little news. . . . I haven't been able to walk for three weeks, but I am pleased to say I am now able to knock about a bit, and am doing fine. I hope to have a look at you all very shortly. " It was during the bayonet charge that I got a shrapnel wound in the right upper leg. and then the trench came in on top of toe. I lest two German helmets when I was buried—but never mind, better luck next time.

"The people of Ireland are extremely good to us—nothing seems too much for them to do for us. Private gentlemen send their motors round for us and we have tea at their houses* I went out for tea and a 20 mile/ride last Sun- day. It was a treat—right opposite Belfast Lough—but after all, Wilkie, there's no place like home.
"Remember me to all Square Mill and all in- quiring friends."
PRIVATE J. E. WILSON. Wounded.

PRIVATE J. BOND. Reported Killed, but now in Hospital Woundel
Private Joseph Bond, 5, Worrall's-row, Sankey Bridges, an employe of the Cable Co., and goal.

keeper for the Sankey Football Club, was re- ported killed, but has since been reported as only wounded. He is at present in hospital at Cambridge. From there he writes to a friend in Warrington to say that he will shortly under- go.an operation in order to have a bullet taken from his stomach.

div.head: PRIVATE JOHN T. TAYLOR.
div.p: PRIVATE JOHN T. TAYLOR.

"Will Be Able To Conic To England In A Few Days." Private John Thomas Taylor, of 13, Naylor- street, Warrington—whose photo and story we have already given—writes this week to re- assure his mother of his safety. It will be recollected that at first he was reported to have been killed in the now historic charge. Mrs. Taylor has also received the following: "13 General Hospital, Boulogne, 2nd July, 1315. —Your son is going on very nicely, and the doctors think he will be able to come over t( England in a few days' time. He will let yor know which hospital he gets to.—Yours sin- cerely, Sister Grandjeau."
Sankey Bridges, as we reported last week, has written to his mother, saying that he was hit in the arm and shoulder. He is a single man, engaged at the Whiteeross Works.
PRIVATE E. HOI7LSTON. Not Missing.

div.head: PRIVATE J. LOW E.
div.p: PRIVATE J. LOW E.
One Of Tour Brothers In The Territorials.

Private Joseph Lowe, whose home is at 117, Lovely-lane, was originally' reported as missing, but, .greatly, to the relief of his relatives, is now reported as wounded, and, he writes, making a good recovery in hospital at Cambridge. Private Lowe is a single man and is 22 years of age. He has been in the Territorials since he was 17 years of age, and was among the first to offer himself for active service. He received his education at Heathside Sthool, and, as a boy, attended the Friars' Green Primitive Methodist Sunday school Prior to`the war be worked on the oil plant at Messrs. Crosfield's soap works. He belongs to an intensely patriotic family, and has no fewer than three brothers serving in the Army—one of them actually at the Front, and the other two in training and eagerly look- ing forward to going out !` to do his bit. All are in the '! Terriers."

div.head: PRI\,VIE WILLIAM ROWLAND.
div.p: PRI\,VIE WILLIAM ROWLAND.
Doing %%Tell In Fourth French
Hospital.

To say that he is now in another—his fourth —French hospital, and is going on quite well, Private William Rowland writes home to his wife at 26, School Brow. , It will be remembered that the Private—who is 29 'years of age, son of Mr. Daniel Rowland, of 28, School Brow, and a painter at Messrs. Crosfield's—was slightly gassed, and also buried in the trench by a bursting shell which caused him a slight contusion of the back. At first he was reported as missing after the chatge, but in last week's list was included amongst the wounded.

div.head: STILL MISSING.
div.p: STILL MISSING.
PRIVATE ARTHUR MONKS.
No News Of A Man Who Was Missed
After Charge.

Still no tidings are to hand concerning Private Arthur Monks, brother-in-law to Lance-Corporal 4stle, of 9, Cobden-street, who was himself wounded in the big charge. Private Monks has been officially reported as missing,, and an old friend, Private Joseph Laycock, has written to his relatives to say that he has made every possible inquiry as to Arthur's whereabouts, but has been unable to find the slightest trace of him. lie was in the trench When a German.shell burst close at hand and buried the writer of the letter,
PRIVATE THOMAS SMITH.
Last Seen Just Before A Shell Burst
In The Trenches.

No news has yet been heard of Private Thomas Smith, who was posted as missing after the glorious charge made by the Territorials on the enemy's trenches. Private Smith's relatives live at 70, Forshaw-street, and are, needless to say, anxiously awaiting tidings of him.
"Looked Round For Tom—But Could Not See Him!"

The last heard of him was through the medium of a letter written to his family by a comrade, Private Joseph Laycock, who said ' " Toni-and I were in the trench together for a long time, and then we got separated in some way, but Ile was not far away from me even when we did part, for I managed to speak to him. That was before the Germans started shelling our trench. I managed to catch sight of him just pefore I got hit and buried. When I was got out I looked round for 'Tom, but I could not see him. The shell which threw up the earth that buried me dropped just about where he was. . . . I went to help some of the lads out. One of them told me that Tom was just against him when the shell burst right close to him (Tom). I had a good look round, but could find no trace of Tom. I also made inquiries at the dressing-station, but nobody had 5,--11 him there ''
PrivAte Thos. Smith, hopes of whose safety are still entertained, is a widower anil had been
_ t•adO

in the Territorials about seven years, latterly eerving in the machine-gun section. He has brother also serving with the "Terriers." The missing private had, as a matter of fact, left the Territorials shortly before the war broke out, but when the call for men came he immediately rejoined. He was educated at the Heathside School, and was employed as a wire- dfawer at the Whitecross Works.
PRIVATE THOMAS SMITH. Still Missing.

div.head: PRIVATE ERNEST SMITH.
div.p: PRIVATE ERNEST SMITH.
"The Happiest Lad On Earth."

Private Ernest Smith, who was wounded in the charge, writing to his. brother, John, Ammunition Column, Birmingham, from Wel- lington Hospital, says he is keeping in the pink of health and doing champion. He hopes td be on furlough shortly; and continues:— " I am the happiest lad on earth now and hope they look after me same as they art doing."

div.head: PRIVATE E. LITTLEVt 00D.
div.p: PRIVATE E. LITTLEVt 00D.
Writes A Cheery Letter Home From Hospital.

Writing from hospital at Rotten to his mother, Mrs. Jolley, who resides at 14, Tilley- street, Private E. Littlewood, who Irak, wounded in the big charge, says, under datt. July 7th: "I am glad to say my deafness has almost left tue,-but my legs remain very pain- ful. Still, I am better off than some of the poor chaps here I hear that Bob Chadwick has been home on leave. He was the last one to speak to me as I was leaving the firing-line after being hit. We were al- ways together when we were out of the trenche: and we wished each other luck jitst before wc went into the charge. . . . We are having very hot weather here. . . . I am in hope of seeing you for a day or two when.l get wel enough, for I hear that those left of oui battalion are getting home leave. Whiling Away the Time With Song and Game

"In fact several of the boys have been horn' and have got back again. It must put nev life into them As I am writing I can see some of our boys playing cricket, bu" I am afraid that I shall not be able to pla:. that or football again, or go in for any of rn;, old games. But, never mind! Any way, shall be able to look ons: A concert has ills' started. We. get all the latest songs out hen. as well, of course, as all the old favourites and even now somebody is rattling out `Let'. all go down the Strand' on the piano! We ar to shave When the B'hoys Come llarchint Home Again!' and 'Your King and Countr; Need Yell!"

div.p: WAR ITEMS.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
The Staff of Life.

This week's reduction in the price of bread by Warrington bakers induced certain reflec- tions on the subject generally. Inevitably one turned over the old argument that millers should abandon the manufacture of white flour, retaining all the ingredients held to be essential to the -formation of bone, teeth and muscle. For years and years we have been told with wearisome iteration that the snow- white bread, of beautiful appearance, to which the average housewife is so partial, is far from nutritious. We are assured that what is technically known as " offal " is most valuable, really containing the richest and most nutritious portion of the grain. A Via Media.

It is conceivable that some may be ready to combat this, but I well remember the intro- duction of the fine Hungarian flour not far short of forty years ago, and do not hesitate to attribute thereto the strong prejudice in favour of that article which prevails all over the country. Undoubtedly wholemeal does not suit many people, and it would be well, particularly now that we are being earnestly exhorted to make the most of our available resources, if extremists -could agree upon a compromise that would be acceptable to the generality. I well remember how, years ago in "Macmillan," Mr. Francis Fox reasonably enough suggested that millers should aim at rejecting the bran (suitable only for stuffing dolls and pincushions, and as a mash for horses) and retaining in the flour some of the inner coating of the grain and fine " mid- dlings" together with the germ. A Queer Mixture,'

I once spent over three hours on a tour of inspection of a big, up-to-date corn milli and was especially struck with the appearance of the foreign grain at the point of delivery, prior to the separation and washing,processes. I noticed among it lumps of iron and gone, lengths of dirty rope and string, sand, soil, etc., etc. It was quite a revelation to me. Of course, the wheat was thoroughly cleansed of all such 'substances before it was passed as ready to be ground, the result of the pre- liminary process being a curious heap of mis- .cellaneous rubbish. This by the way.

How to Increase Fertility. From time to time I have met with alarming statements to the effect that the Chili nitrates were becoming exhausted, and that, as the wheat-producing land in the world was being gradually used up and the nitrates in the soil were diminishing, the situation involved, a tremendous problem. Sir Wm. Crookes, an eminently sane authority, observed a while ago: _

-" The, amount of wheat per acre over the world is about 121 bushels; by manuring arti- ficially with nitrates we can get up to 25 and 30 bushels, but, of course, that costs money. If we are only going to get 121 bushels per acre, all over the world we shall not have wheat enough to supply the wheat eaters of the world in about a generation." Plainly the only way of meeting the diffi- culty was by increasing the fertility of the soil, and he proposed a method of fixing the atmospheric nitrogen--by means of a high- tension electric current system, as a matter of fact, his conclusion being that if nitrates can be obtained from the air the fertility of the land can be increased to almost any, extent.

At a period when the wheat supplies usually drawn from abroad are being largely held up on account of the war, the foregoing may pos- sibly in some interested quarters be welcomed as a timely reminder.

div.head: Consumption.
div.p: Consumption.

Last week's allusion to the phthisical patients at the Borough Isolation Hospital set me thinking of the serious handicap imposed upon such sufferers. If, for instance, anyone submits a personal proposal to a life assur- ance company, he or she will be promptly asked if there is consumption in the family, and upon the answer to this the result de- pends to no small extent. It is therefore re- freshing to recall that at least one tuberculosis physician (Dr. Morris) ridicules, as " all stuff and nonsense," the idea that consumption runs in ,families. In the paragraph to which I have referred there was a report as to the number of scarlatina patients under treatment at the institution just mentioned. Well, scar- let fever is not transmissible from generation to generation; it does not " run in the family" in that sense, and Dr. Morris's argu- ment is "no more does consumption." He puts it that it is very often in the blankets, but never in the blood; it is very often in the

carpet, but never in the constitution. Babies are not born with consumption even if their fathers and mothers have it. This is sup- ported by other authorities, the observations of school medical officers since the establish- ment of clinics tending to confirm it. Some have sensibly urged that it ought to be part of the curriculum of every school to inculcate habits of natural breathing; no doubt the fight against consumption—which, sooth to say, is
,- meeting with• encouraging success—would 'be- come appreciably easier as a result.
The Temperance Phase.

Last night's B.W.T.A. meeting in connec- tion with the pledge-signing campaign of the Citizens' Temperance League had a distinct bearing on the above important subject— although, to be sure, the promoters relied mainly on the Royal example in the appeal for adherents. I read that Paris has a higher death-rate from tuberculosis than any capital in the world, and the doctors there have laid it down that any one who wished to combat the disease must make as a definite part of his propaganda a crusade against alcohol. Our own Professor G. Sims Woodhead bears this out. I recollect his declaring from the platform that alcohol played an unmistakable part in actual predisposition to tuberculosis. This faculty (said he) was a very important one, because it converted a resisting body into a non-resisting body' which gave the bacillus power to do its work. Alcohol quickened the disease and shortened the life of every tuber- cular patient who had only taken a moderate amount of alcohol. Whichever disease they studied they found that alcohol was a predis- posing agent because it lowered the resisting power of the body and rendered the patient more liable to take the disease, and once hav- ing taken it the patient was less liable to re- cover from it. The Royal Example.

"Sign the King's pledge." That, as I have remarked, was after all the keynote of last evening's effort at the Bewsey-street gathering. The reference, of course, was to the special pledge taken by His Majesty and many of the Royal household since the out- break of war; but our King and Queen have always favoured total abstinence from alco- holic liquors on the part of the rising race. The reigning Sovereign has all along been a patron of the Band of Hope Union; Queen Mary formerly acted as secretary of a Church of England Band of Hope Union at Kingston- on-Thames; and their Majesties have brought up their children as total abstainers. W.E.A.

The annual report of the Warrington Branch of the Workers' Educational Associa- tion reminded me of a saying of Charles Kingsley's which at least one influential sup- porter of that movement has made effective use of. "Workers of England," counselled the prominent Christian Socialist, " be wise and then you must be free, for you will be fit to be free." That, we ;are assured and clearly perceive, is advice that workers all over the • country are acting upon, and will keep specially in mind for the future. Mem- bers, of the NV.E.A., in Warrington and else- where, are (as one friend ekpresses it) devot- ing their leisure time to the acquisition of knowledge, not that it may raise them out of the sphere to whictt they belong,, but that it may help them to live more nobly, intelli- gently, and happily in that sphere. Of a truth, to those whose mind is their kingdom, outward circumstances are of comparatively little consequence.

div.head: THIS WEEK'S ESSAY: A STREET IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: THIS WEEK'S ESSAY: A STREET IN WARRINGTON.

111 Y DEAR CHILDREN,— This week I am giving you a very easy com- petition.: A/ few lines about any street in War- rington (or of the town in which you live) are all you have to write. Then send them to me by Monday. I am glad to say we continue to have a good number of entries for our com- petitions; and this I hope you will keep up. I am keeping a very interested eye upon every one of you; and if you do not see your name printed .do not think you are out of the swim," because I am watching your progress most carefully and kindly. Be, encouraged! In this week's essay you have, of course, perfectly free choice; You can write on a big street (such as Bridge-street, Sankey-street or Church-street), or that in wnfct. . your school stands, or that in which you live. And even if you write about a road or lane I shan't mind ! So go ahead! "DURING THE RAINY NIGHTS." A jolly letter which has come to give me pleasure is this : "6, Milner-street, Warrington, 29th June, 1915,—Dear Uncle ed,—l was greatly surprised to find that I had won the com- petition. I safely received my book, called 'Swift and Sure,' with which I am greatly pleased. I do not know how to thank you for it; but I can tell you it will interest me during the rainy nights which are 'becoming a bit frequent. Again greatly thanking you— I remain, your affectionate nephew, SAM BACKHOUSE:' Thank you, Sam,
"You velly pleased, me

div.head: LORD HALDANE'S VINDICATION.
div.p: LORD HALDANE'S VINDICATION.
Foolish Ingratitude.

History, says the "Daily Chronicle," will recognise Lord .Haldane as one of the two indis viduals (Lord Fisher is the other) to whom the nation is most indebted for the initial pre- paredness which enabled us to keep the war from our own territories and to discharge far beyond the, letter of any promise our undertak- ings to our Continental friends. When he went to the War Office ,he found it an Augean stable, which half a dozen Herculeses had tried in vain to cleanse. We had then but a single Army Corps, and that only on paper, and no sound system for expanding our active Army, or filling up its gaps either in officers or in men. He created the General Staff (we had none before) ; he created the Expeditionary Force (we had none before); he made all the plans for its tran- shipment 'last August; be created the Terri- torial Force, whose praise is now in every general's mouth; he created our first effective system of artily supplies, which has made ours the "best-fed army in history "' • and he made possible the re-creation of our Amy Medical Service upon a basis whose success is the envy of every other belligerent. After rendering these extraordinarily services he was allowed to be attacked as a " traitor " by the scum of the Press; charges were made against him which every single member of both Front Benches knows, and has always known, to be the craziest. moonshine; and finally he was let pass into' private life. A worse instance of -democracy's" weakest side could hardly be found. It is diffi- cult to think of the episode without shame, or discuss it without passion. Whether one con- siders the ingratitude or the abysmal folly of it, both are amazing. But Lord Haldane him- self betrays no touch of resentment. " I am as keen as ever I was," be said, "in a private capa- city to do everything that is within my power to serve the State. We have all to go into the trenches just where we are sent. 'Who dies if England lives?' "-
velly pleased "—as the Chinamen say. Nephew Thomas Ashton also pens a pleasant word :

"76, Stott-street, Warrington, 4th July, 1915,—Dear -Uncle Ned,—l was very pleased indeed when I saw my letter and essay neatly printed in this week's Examiner.' I wish the young lady who was last week's prize winner luck and prosperity.—l remain, your loving nephew, THOMAS ASIITON."

Nephew Fred Walker (who sent a capital essay last week saying he would choose to be Admiral Jellicoe, asks for his number. It is 455, Fred. .1 was sorry your essay came two days late to be judged. 457, Nephew ALFRED LONG, writes a week ago: "I hope you will occept the thanks, which I send to you in these few lines for the congratulations which I saw in our Corner to-day." I do accept them, Alfred. Niece Lucy Carey tells me: "I will remember my number, 365, be- cause of the days of the year !" A smart idea, Lucy! lam very glad it struck you; it shows you are a bright girl. Niece Ida Whitby writes a neat and polite note to ask-for her number. It is 445, Ida. By the way, you are not the only Ida in my family. 429, Niece Ida Barlow, of 50, Lancaster-street, is another.
Niece MARIAN BARTON sends me a letter: "I am sorry that I have neglected writing to you; • and I will be very much obliged if you will let me know my number."
~ I am glad to see your intere—st in our Corner, Marian. You will find your number lower down; and so will Niece MONA ARCHER, who has asked for hers.

To Niece ADELAIDE GRlFFrins I woild say: "I quite understand your misfortune, and hope that sickness in your home will soon be a thing of ,the past. It was grand of you and your sister to do your excellent part, and I prize your letter
The ntmibers of my three Birmingham nieces are: MARIE ROBERTSON, 452; MINNIE ROBERTSON, 453; and KATHLEEN ROBERTSON, 454. Don't forget them, girls!

div.p: THE EXAMINER, S ATURDAY, JULY 10, 1915.
WOMAN'S WORLD.

Gifts From Afar. An unofficial native inhabitant of the Federated Malay States has presented an aeroplane to the, British Royal Flying School, which gift has been gratefully accepted. The members of the Sierra Leone Bar, and others entitled to practise before the Supreme Court of that country, have sent a donation of one hundred guineas, which will be handed over to the Prince of Wales' National Relief Fund. The Jefferson Medical College of Philadelphia have offered the Allies a complete medical and nursing unit for a hospital of a thousand beds. The President of the College is now in France conferring with the French and British medical authorities as to the most convenient place for the establishment of the hospital. Thirty physicians, several of whom are specialists in bacteriology and other branches of medical science, have offered their very valuable ser- vices.

The Tango, As Training. g Only a year ago Paris was dancing the Tango, almost as if the life of the nation depended on the exertion of the dancers. All classes took the fever, as did the stranger within the gates. for Americans danced as enthusiastically as Parisiennes. At public and private balls, ladies of the highest rank danced for many hours, seemingly without fatigue. Now these same patricians, Americans, and other foreign ladies, are nursing the wounded with a devotion and energy almost unexampled. It is said that the dancing hardened the muscles of the body and limbs, and that the exercise was a useful, pre- liminary to the hard work and training neces- sary to qualify as nurses. The Parisian Red Cross nurse, unlike her British sister, seldom, if ever, wears her uniform in the streets; she puts it on, and takes it off, on entering and leaving the hospital. Buy Medium Skirts.

Many women have, this year, very wisely continue& to wear their narrow skirts, until the sales provided the opportunity of buying new models at greatly reduced prices. Others have, with more or less success, brought last year's gowns and costume skirts up-to-date by means of tunics and over-dresses. in the case of the former, and broad pleats, laid on the front, or gores and kiltings, cleverly let in at the sides in the latter. A word of warn- ing may not come amiss anent the buying of new suits and gowns. The extremely wide and short skirt should be avoided, for it suits only the young and slim, and it is highly improbable

that this style will remain in favour for any length of time. Modes are at present in a very transitory state. Time alone will decide the fate of the various shapes now on trial, but it is quite safe to predict that the medium skirt will eventually triumph over its rivals. Just at the moment the wide gowns of 1870, or those of even a decade earlier, might be worn with only the slightest alteration, and as far as the shape is concerned they would be in the fore- front of fashion. Fashionable Combinations of Materials.

Another pitfall, more especially for the amateur dressmaker is provided by the dress of two materials and colours, which to prove a success requires very skilful handling.. Two material gowns when artistically designed, are very charming, hence their popularity, but many combinations, attributable at a glance to the amateur are, seen in the streets, and are anything but, pleasing or attractive. Like the wide skirt, the dress of two ,fabrics and colours must be extremely well carried out to be suc- cessful. There must be no exaggerations in either, or the effect is grotesque, rather than charming. Muslin and taffetas, figured delaines with plain cotton crepes and foulards and fine cloths, or foulards and plain silks, mingle well. Small checks with plain materials are more easily combined, and when used alone give little trouble to the amateur. Stripes again which are so smart and universally worn, require careful manipulation, whether used alone or with plain materials. The Useful' Coat-Frock.

A most practical fashion, due probably to the demand for useful clothes, is the coat-frock, which has found instant favour, and bids fair to have a vogue for some time to cAne. At the first glance it is difficult to distinguish this newcomer from a dress, or a long coat worn with a dress. Being simple in design, and in one piece, it is, quickly put' on, and makes an ideal morning dress in serge, tussore or linen. Some of these coats are masculine in cut, more especially when long and finished with a. belt, usually of the same material. The skirt flares out at the hem, and useful pockets decorate the coat portion. In fact pockets 01.3 very much in evidence this season, both on dresses and (Inds, and means have been found to render them quite decorative. The " pat.+ " variety is pre- ferred. It is of good size and b _mind with a con- trasting colour, or adorned with the trimming used on the dress or suit. B•ttbns, of coutse, are not out of place in this c,Juttection.

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.

American Generosity. The sympathy shown by America to the Allies, in this terrible war, has been not %ly practical, but unexampled, In its splendid generosity. On the outbreak of hostilities American women married to British subjects met in London to 'discuss what they could do to help, and it was decided that caring for the wounded must come first. Mr. Singer, an American, offered his beautiful house at Paignton, which was , speedily perfectly equipped as a hospital, from the money raised by American ladies; and their war relief fund has borne every expense up to the present. In addition, six motor ambulances have been given to the War Office for service at the Front, and two workshops , for women have been opened. In conjunction with the Society Of American Women in London, another depot at Victoria finds employment for educated women in dis- tress through the war. All the organisers and workers in hospitals and depots voluntarily give their services.

Women in Munition Works. Although some thousands of women who registered at the Labour Exchanges expressed a wish to be employed in munition factories, so far few have been taken on. The decision not to admit them is doubtless a wise one, for the workshops with their furnaces, and heavy machinery are no fit place for women. The toil is excessive, the pay for unskilled labour very little, and the heat so intense that the men work almost without clothing. Besides which the processes of shell manufacture are exceed- ingly complicated. : Men serve an apprentice- ship of from five to seven years; women there- fore could not master •the intricacies in a few weeks. At the University of Sheffield a pro- fessor is training men from other trades to make munitions. His workshops are perfectly equipped as regards tools and machines required for shell making, but no women have as Tet taken advantage of this opportunity to learn war work, and the professor deprecates their employment, except in the case of a failure in the supply of men.

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes and Useful Suggestions.
Snoring. To prevent snoring have plenty of fresh air in your sleeping room. Sleep with your mouth closed and lie on your bide. Avoid sleeping on your back. • Freckles.

Freckles are caused by an over-production of pigment in the skin, which seems to be brought out in spots by the sun's rays. A small amount of lemon juice in glycerine and rose-water, applied night and morning, should remove them if used steadily. A good freckle lotion is: Alum and lemon juice, of each loz.; rose water, 1 pt. Bathe the face three times a day. It will probably remove the freckles, but, at the same time, it dries the skin, and, no doubt, if constantly used would CA.use wrinkles. Cheese Sauce.

Melt one tablespoonful of margarine in a saucepan (a double saucepan is best), then stir in one tablespoonful of flour, and mix well. When that is hot, add gradually a breakfast- cupful of milk, stirring well. While this is getting hot, grate or chop up finely, 2oz. of cheese, and stir it into the sauce, which will gradually thicken, and then be ready to use with macaroni, fish, ez.c. Fish Fried in Batter.

Some people prefer fish fried in batter. To make this take three large tablespoonfuls of flour and a sprinkling of salt and pepper, pour into it barely a tablespoonful of best Lucca oil, mix, then add by degrees half a tumblerful of lukewarm water; when quite smooth add the whipped white of one egg. Dry the fish as already described, dip it into the batter, and fry. Puree of Carrots.

Wash and scrape five or six large carrots. Cut the red part off into slices, and boil in salted water for a quarter of an hour. Drain, retura them to the saucepan, together with an onion stuck with cloves, pepper, salt, loz. of butter, and stock to cover them. Simmer till quite tender, then rub through a wire sieve. Heat up the puree, add 2oz. of butter, a pinch of sugar, a little grated nutmeg, ano stock to make a •thick puree.

Cabbage and Rice. Boil a small cabbage, and in another sauce- pan boil 2oz. rice; when the rice is cooked, drain, and leave it on the side of the fire till some of the moisture is absorbed; then drain the cabbage well, put in on a board, and chop it up, mix it with the rice, add loz. of butter, some salt and pepper, and stir bver the fire till hot. Now, boys! Don't forget that the very first thing you should do after joining our Corner is to enter the competitions! I shall look out for your names straightaway!
The winner of Our latest competition is Nephew Alfred Long,

whose neat essay runs:— " 79, Orford-avenue, Warrington, 3rd July, 1915v7-Dear Uncle Ned,—The 801001 I attend is Heathside Elementary, which is situated opposite Walker's Brewery in Golborne-street. There are six teachers and a headmaster, and by them nearly three hundred scholars are taught. Surrounding the school is a large quadrangle in which the pupils play, and in summer weather are taught how to keep themselves healthy by performing Swedish drill. The school con- sists of ten rooms, five on the, first storey, and the same number on the second. Six of them are used for taking classes in, three are lavatories, and the remaining one is the headmaster's office. The school is used for religious purposes as wejl as educa- tional ones.—l remain, your affectionate nephew, ALFRED LONG."

The second best essay was the following : " 56, Westbourne-road, Handsworth, Bir- mingham, 4th July, 1915. Dear -Uncle Ned,— Our day school is called ` Bookerproad Council School,' and we have a very patriotic schoolmaster. Two hundred and seventy-five old boys luive joined the colours. One of our 'rooms is full of Captain Scott's Expedition pictures, which are very inter- esting. There are over seven hundred chil- dren in the senior department, and it is the largest school in Birmingham. There is a laundry wheKe the older girls of the school learn to wash and iron. There is also a cookery room where we make all kinds of pies and difiners.—From your loving niece, MARIE ROBERTSON."
Upon so excellent a piece of writing I must and do heartily congratulate you, Marie. Also, I want to say that you are the neatest writer in our Corner.
Our popular member 381 Niece MONA ARCHER writes :

"11, lleatliside, Warrington, July sth. Dear Uncle Ned,—The school I go to is called Deathside Girls' School. It is situated in Kendrick-street. At my school. there are seven classes and eight teachers, including the head mistress. Nearly four hundred girls attend, and it seems like a large house when every girl is present. There are a lot more schools in Warrington, but I like Ileathside School the best. I suppose it is

because I have never been to any other.—l remain, your faithful Niece, MONA ARCHER." But Mona's is by no ,means the only • essay upon the Heathside Girls' School. This is what 443 Niece ADELAIDE GRIFFITHS has to say "22, Wakefield-street, Warrington, July sth, 1915. Dear Uncle Ned,—You ask me to tell you about the school I attend. • I attenct Heathside Girls' School, which is situated in Kendrick-street. It faces the Infirmary. It is a large sehool, although no boys attend, and is divided into two parts, one for in- fants and one for older girls.—l remain, your

loving Niece, ADELAIDE GRIFFITHS." Nicely done, Adelaide. Perhaps you will be interested to hear what 444 Niece MARIAN BARTON says—because she too attends your schools : "4, Wakefield-street, Warrington, July sth, 1915. Dear Uncle Ned,—The school I: am attending is Ileathside Girls' School. It is a • very large school, and is the second largest in Warrington. There are two parts in it, one for the infants and one for the big! girls. The girls' part is separated from the infants' by a large playground. I will now bring my letter to a close, as you only want' a short one.—l remain, your loving Niece, MARIAN BARTON."

That's quite right, Marian. Always remem- ber that I simply can't bear long letters—what- ever they are about.. Your note was just the right length! Thank you very much ! Nephew SAM BACKHOUSE—WhO is one of My best recruiting sergeants, and of whose friend- ship I am indeed proud writes : "6-, Milner-street, Warrington, July 3rd, 1915. Dear Uncle Ned,—l have been a regular Vender at Heathside School for five years. I have been well taught by the teachers, who are headed by Mr. Parker. I think I 'Cave been of very little trouble to my teachers; I am now in my last year of teaching, and am very 'interested in my les- sons—given by my present teacher, Mr. Edden. Heathside School has a Rugby and an Association football team. Several times we have won shields; the following are some: Association, swimming, and gymnas- tics One of our school's old boys has won a commission on the battlefield or bravery. I think we who attend Heathside School are .very proud of this.—l remain, your, loving Nephew, SAM BACKHOUSE." . •
Another very good entry was by my affectionate niece LUCY CAREY, whose letter rah
"68, Steel-street, Warrington,—Dear Uncle Ned,—l attend Beamont Council School and it ia a very fine, beautiful build-

jug too. There are some nice teachers there also. There are three divisions to the school; first, the infants' department, then the girls', and the boys' department on top of the girls'. There is a fish tank in the girls' department which is under my care. I get worms for them eVery day, and some extra on Friday. There is a big play- ground for the girls and infants, and another for the boys. We have a typewriter, and I have lessons on it. I write all my letters

of social correspondence. But you said pen me a line or two'; I will close now." Here is another highly commendable letter "5, Green-street, Warrington, July, 1915, "—Dear Uncle Ned,—You asked me to write a short account of the school which I at- tend. I attend the Evelyn-street Council School. It is the most interesting school I have ever been to, and it is a very large one. , We have a cookery at which girls eleven or more years of age may learn how to cook. . We have also baths, where we go for a cool and refreshing bath; they are only for the Evelyn-street school children. There is a place where the boys are taught to be car- penters. We have gardens all round the playgrounds. The girls are downstairs and the boys are upstairs, and we have different playgrounds. Inside the school there are eight class-rooms and a large hall where we all meet together for prayers.—l remain, your loving niece, IDA WHITBY." 456, Nephew Thomas Ashton's essay is as follows "The school I attend is situated in Hamilton-street, and is, therefore called . Hamilton-street School. The headmaster of the boys' department is Mr. Longshaw, whose residence is in Manchester-road. The . ,• school has done its duty by sending three of the staff as defenders of the Empire. In the girls' department socks, mittens, towels and sleeping helmets, &c., are being made and given to soldiers who are doing their duty."

A very patriotic work, Tom! So that taken all round the pick of our School Competition bunch show a fine variety of interest—indoors, outdoors, work, play and duty. These reflect great credit on every nephew and niece in the family of Your ever loving UNCLE NED.
THOUGHT FOR THE WEEK. He serves his party best who serves his country best.—RUTHERrUED U. Ilmcbs, 1877.

Baked Suet Pudding. When carefully made, baked suet pudding is a most palatable dish. To one cup of boiled milk add three-quarters of a cupful of sifted flour, and stir until smooth and well scalded. Add one cup of treacle, one teaspoonful of salt, and two tablespoonfuls of sugar. Make a mix- ture of one cupful of suet chopped fine, one quart of cold milk, one cupful of currants, seed- less raisins, or dried berries, and' add to the boiling milk and flour mixture. Bake slowly for six hours, and let it stand in the oven over night, or, if possible, until the fire goes out. Serve with butter and cream.
