div.head: Why Lovers Like'Hirti.
div.p: Why Lovers Like'Hirti.

Justice John R. Kelso, of Milwaukee, a suburb of Portland, Ore., is becoming popular as a marriage official. He is sent for far and near whenever any young couple in that neigh- bourhood want to be married. His popularity is said to be due entirely to his short and unique ceremony. This always appeals to the nervous couples. His ceremony is about as follows, after the couple have been brought be- fore him:
" Dp you people want each other?" "We do, we do," is the answer required
"Then, goodness gracious have each other, for nobody else wants you. You are married."

div.head: Painful Memories.
div.p: Painful Memories.

The best man thought he'd take a look around and see that everything was running as a fas- tidious bride would wish it, and up in the room where the presents were displayed, alone and unhappy looking, he came upon a youth; seemingly ready, like the wedding guest of the English poet to "beat his breast." Re was wandering about, looking at silver and cut glass without seeing them, and the best man hardly. knew how to approach him. _ _
"Er—have you kissed the bride?" he asked • at last.
And the answer told far more than its twa meagre words might have been expected to. It was, "Not lately !"

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular Language.
Loss of appetite in a child is by .no means always a sign of approaching disease, but it is, nevertheless, a matter that requires investiga- tion.

Children's Clothing. A well-known authority •on the care of chil- dren says-, respecting the clothing of the very young: "A rule to whieh there should be no exceptions, even in the very hottest weather, is that the whole surface of the body, from the neck down, excepting the hands, should be equally covered. The undergarment may be as thin as one pleases, but it should have long sleeves. The child is very little warmer in this way, and there is a decided protection against. draughts of air causing chilliness if perspira- tion has occurred."

Cold extremities seriously interfere with good digestion and sow the seeds of numberless ills: Many mothers are alarmed if the child has wet feet, and yet seem utterly oblivious to the dan- ger from continuous cold feet and legs. Little children just beyond the age of infancy who have not yet learned to express their feelings in words are especially liable to suffer from lack of care in this respect.—Mrs. Kellogg. The Care of the Hair.

Many ladies find they cannot wash their hair frequently on account of taking cold, and may welcome one or two recipes which will keep the hair clean, and at the same time promote its growth. A couple of handfuls of rosemary leaves steeped in a quart of boiling water, then Kept simmering until the fluid is reduced to about a pint and a half, is a simple way of pre- paring a hair-wash, and if the scalp is rubbed lightly with this, the hairbrush dampened with it and used for brushing the hair, it will not be necessary to have a real shampoo very fre- quently. Burdock leaves also contribute strength and vigour to the hair if made into a strong tea and used as a wash twice daily, but many ladies may not care for the recipe which follows, although an excellent one. In five pints of water boil 11b. yellow dock roots, then strain and add loz. powdered borax, ioz. ordinary salt, 3oz. gweet oil, and about a pint of bay rum, the juice of three onions, and enough burgamot or other scent to overcome the odour from the onions. Tincture of cantharides is the best-known remedy for the prevention of falling hair, and stimulating its growth, but cannot be bought separately with- out some difficulty, but if you take a bottle con- taining toilet paraffin, and ask the chemist to add a drachm of the cantharides to the paraffin, you will not find any difficulty in obtaining it. I will give a few more recipes and hints with regard to the hair, &c., within the next few weeks.—Maud, in "Farm and Home."

div.head: HOUSE FLY.
div.p: THE HOUSE FLY.
Common Pest That Is More Dangerous Than Enemy Bullets
WAR ENHANCES RISK.
BY C. E. PARKER.

While each one is doing his best to fight the Germans we must not forget the enemies in our own country. I refer to house flies, not foreign aliens; of the two the former are the more dangerous. House flies will this year be the cause of more deaths than all the Zeppelins likely to visit our shores. There are no Hague rules requiring delay and mercy in dealing with these enemies; we need have no compunction in killing at sight. There was a time, not distant, when it was thought that of the fly tribes only the biters, such as mosquitoes and tsetse flies, were dangerous. Non-biters such as house/flies (Musca Domestica) were considered innocent little nuisances, but not dangerous. Now we know these flies are disease carriers, with man- ners atrocious, and habits filthy. House flies are the principal means of spreading typhoid fever, infantine diarrhoea, consumption, and the like.

div.head: From Filth to Food.
div.p: From Filth to Food.

They wallow in spit, excreta and any other moist mess lying about, they flit and flirt from filth to food, and from food to filth, they alternately visit dung heaps and dinner table. Fancy these dirty little insects having a bath in the children's milk, or a dinner off a baby's teat! They carry dirt and disease germs on their hairy, sticky feet, and have the abominable habit of regurgitating the contents of their crop upon the food. A fly settles on a piece of sugar, but as it is impossible for it to draw up any of the hard sugar through its sucker, it moistens and renders a part soluble by sending up a drop of liquid from its croP. This drop is composed of the products of its previous meal. Bacilli from infected food may therefore be vomited upon human food and a portion left upon it. A fly as it flits about in search of food is continually tasting by the aid of its own vomit; an exceedingly dirty habit! But it is not alone through their manner of feeding that flids are dangerous and dirty, they pick up bacteria on the sticky pad of their feet, and on the longer hairs of their body; they deposit germs as they travel, or as they clean their legs —as they are very fond of doing—by rubbing them against each other. Then there is the excreta. Typhoid bacilli has been recovered from this three weeks after flies have been infected. This we know from records made in a camp where flies were in- terned for investigation. In South Africa the disease carried 'by flies killed more of our soldiers than the bullets of the enemy. Active steps under scientific guidance are being taken in France to reduce the danger to our troops. The danger is very great because there are there .all the conditions favourable to the develop- ment of flies. It will be a great triumph to science if this summer typhoid .can be warded off at the Front.

div.head: Attack Breeding Places.
div.p: Attack Breeding Places.

It is little use trying to tackle the problem by killing individual flies—although this is worth while—the breeding places must be got at. Descriptions of thy methods and the localities of these breeding places have frequently been described, but it is necessary to do this again and again because of its importance. Flies breed all through the summer season, for pre- ference in horse manure in heaps, also in decayed vegetable matter, and in any moist fermenting waste product; moisture and a degree of fermentation being indispensable. Perhaps the advent of the motor car by diminishing the amount of horse manure will help. We should never expect to find a fly squatting and breeding on a splash of petrol. Each female house fly lays about one hundred and twenty eggs at a sitting, and on the average has a sitting about every fourteen days. In hot weather it is said that a fly may see its grand- children in three weeks. There is therefore the possibility of a family of over five million in one season from one fly. Happily there are acci- dents in the fly family as in others which keep down the numbers. The eggs are laid in patches, little clumps of small white oval objects, which hatch out in from one to four days according to the conditions. The issuing maggot is about one-fourteenth of an inch long. After feeding for a day or two it has its first moult, when it casts a soft downy skin. After two or three days it moults again. By this time the maggots are about half an inch in length, of a creamy white colour. It then makes for some dry spot, say at the edge of the manure heap or in the adjoining soil, where pupation occurs, the body contracts and develops a hard barrel-shape outer case called the .puparium During this period, covering five to seven days, the colour of the case changes through bright red to a dark chestnut. Structural changes meanwhile proceed in the enclosed maggot, re- production organs develop, the wonderful sec- tional eyes grow, and wings are formed. When the process of development is complete, the fly, like a new aeroplane from its hanger, emerges from its case developed and full-grown. Note, flies do not grow in size after emerging from the puparium, the small flies which are often thought to be young house flies belong to an entirely different species.
Protect Food Stuffs and Wounds.

Flies are the companions of man as much as the dog and the cat, but it has not yet been dis- covered that they have any particular love for man as such. it has been found by marking flies that should the nearest human habitations be a mile from their breeding places they never- theless get there. Restaurants, camp kitchens, and the like, they are especially fond of,; and this seem q to indicate that it is the food more than the feeder that they are fond of. They will go as far, but only as far, as where they can find food` The dpportunities of town dwellers to kill flies in their breeding resorts may not be great. The back yard and'dustbin are the only possible breeding places. ,If refuse is not allowed to accumulate and is frequently removed there is little chance of fly breeding. It then becomes a question of defence from the flies that have developed elsewhere. Milk, food and fruit should be covered and if possible, as an additional safeguard, kept in fly-screened larders or meat safes. The access of flies to all excrement, to sputum, and to wounds should be absolutely prevented. If sties have no afeesskto disease germs they cannnt of cfrlrse carry them. All wounded men, sick persons and 'young children should, for this reason, be pro- tected from flies, not alone for their own sakes but also for that of others. Wire screens should be fixed inside windows that it is desirable to open. Creosote, carbolic avid, or "sanitary fluid" when heated drives off flies.

div.head: Fly Traps.
div.p: Fly Traps.

There is at the present time in the London Zoological Gardens a Fly. Exhibition. In this exhibition all the stages of fly development from the eggs to adults are shown alive under natural conditions. Fly posters illustrating the life history and the habits of the fly are shown upon the wall. In this Exhibition are number of skilfully devised fly traps, but most of these are too elaborate to describe. There is, how- ever, 'a very, simple one which anyone could make and which is said to be effective. .This consists of a drinking glass with a square of cardboard on the top. In the centre of this a hole is bored just large enough to admit a fly. The under side of the cardboard, and especially round the hole, is smeared with some sweet sub- stance such as honey; jam or the like. The glass is half full of water, or perhaps better as an additional- bait, sweetened beer. The. flies* at- tracted by the smell enter by the hole, are un- able to retrace, their steps, and fall into the liquid below.. I cannot say whether such a trap is fiiiire effective than the ordinary glutinous tapes which are in common use, but I intend to give it a trial, if this season I have an invasion of flies bred in my neighbour's dung heaps. If you cannot kill Huns, kill flies.

div.head: NEED FOR SAVING.
div.p: THE NEED FOR SAVING.
Everybody in the country ought to save ever" possible shilling because- -I.—The Government wants all the money it can get for the war and Lillis us to lend it all we can.

2.—By saving we use less goods. These goods either come from abroad and so by not using them we diminish the country's debt to othe) nations, or if they are made at home, by not using them we set free the work that makes them for producing things that are wanted for the Army and Navy and for those of our Allies, or for things that can be used for export. 151 helping to maintain our export trade we Pali part of our debt to other nations. This deb'' to other nations has grown very fast during the war. Since the beginning of the year the to' crease in Our imports and the decrease in (°t. exports have been adding to our debt to o.ther nations at the rate of nearly 22 millions a month, or at the rate of over 260 mons a year.

p.—The war is costing us over 1,000 millions 3 year. If weei pay for it by selling our invest- ments abroad or by issuing loans in other countries, we make ourselves permanentlY: poorer. If we sell investments abroad we shall get less interest from other countries. If we) raise loans abroad we shall owe interest to other. countries. If we pay by drawing on our stock of gold we impair the strength of our credit Os' tern and endanger our position as the world banker. The only way in which we can Pal without making ourselves permanently pooret is by importing less and exporting more. Thig can only be done if every citizen consumes loss goods that is to say—saves.

4.—Our export trade is already very twil hampered by the withdrawal of over two nur lions of men into the new armies and of a fur- ther large number of other men into the produc- tion of war materials. Consequently it is the duty of every citizen to save and to spend less on goods produced at home so that we may port more, and still less on goods that come from abroad so that we may have less to paY foreign countries.

s.—Nearly everybody spends more than he need on something—food, drink, tobacco. amusements, clothes or holidays. We can all save a little, and if all the millions of inhabi. tants of the country would save what they can the effect would be enotMOUS. 6.—Well-to-do people can all be. do most of cause they have most margin. Let them Te: -- member that the old idea that free spending is good for trade is always fallacious and is nof more untrue than ever. Free spending al luxury and extravagance has always been bi for trade, because it diverts money and worl from being used to increase the product'r power of the nation by building railways, pc; tories and ships, and by opening up land ic3 cultivation. Now it is brad for the nation 011, for the cause for which we are fighting becall:; it diverts money and work which ought to vd going into producing goods for the Army all Navy or goods for export.
- 7.—lt is everybody's business now to work 11° hard as he can, earn as much as he can, sret as little as he can, and put all the money tll5 he can into the War Loan.

div.head: LADIES WITH THE WOODS.
div.p: LADIES WITH THE WOODS.
Interesting Drive Played On A Private
Green.

Wives and daughters of the members of the Warrington Caledonian Association indulged in an interesting bowls drive on Thursday after- noon. The drive was held on the private green of Mr. and Mrs. Lockeibie, of Chester New- road, by their kind invitation. The prizes, which were given by the President of the Association (Mr. J. Davenport), were won by Mrs. Lockerbie and Mrs. D. Reid. Before the company separated they aceorded warm thanks to Mr. and Mrs Loekerbie for their invitation and to Messrs. J Robertson, Oxley and G. Marshall for assisting to make the event a success. •

div.head: Of Prizes.
div.p: Of Prizes.
MAJOR CROSFIELD'S THANKS.

The successful War Fund Handicap pro- moted by the Warrington Works Association, came- to a close on Saturday, when in the pre- scene of a large number of bowling enthusiasts and of many well-known local ladies and gentlemen, the prizes were presented, on the green on which the tourney had been waged— that attached to the Horse and Jockey Inn, in Winwick-road—and when also the proceeds, in three equal portions, .were handed overt to the representatives of three deserving causes, on be- half of which the event had been organised— the Territorial Equipment Fund, the Liberal Women's War Sewing Class and the Conserva- tive Women's War Sewing Class. The Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) had hoped to be able to platen the proceedings with his presence, as also hiid Sir Arthur Crosfield, Bart., whom Warringtonians were specially looking forward to seeing in their midst for the first time since his King conferred upon him his well-merited distinction. Unfortunately, however, both gentlemen were reluctantly compelled to dis- appoint the company. Sir Arthur's interest in bowling is well-known; as well-known in fact as is his Worship's interest in all the local efforts put forth in connection with the war, and pro- found regret was felt at their.inability to at- tend: In their unavoidable 'absence Mr. W. Peter Rylands kindly consented ;t0 attend and say a few words of thanks and encouragement, and to present the prizes.

div.head: WINNERS OF THE PRIZES.
div.p: THE WINNERS OF THE PRIZES.

The closing games were 'intensely interesting from the bowlers' point of view, and the par- tisans of the various semi-finalists and finalists cheered their respective favourites until they w .e,re hoarse, whilst the player who eventually emTrged top-dog came in for a specially rousing and sportsmanlikely-accorded round of applause. Altogether, nine prizes were awarded, the winners boing- 1, A. Gleave (clock and bronzes). 2, J. Coyne (smoker's cabinet).

3, H. Gatley (set of bowls). 4, H. Woods (clock). 5, J. Smith (set of brushes). 6, W. Atherton (order on the Manchester Tailoring Co.) 7, W. Barnard (order for a pair of boots on Councillor J. Halliwell). 8, R. Warburton (set of carvers).

div.head: FOOTBALLS FOR THE "BOYS" IN THE TRENCHES.
div.p: FOOTBALLS FOR THE "BOYS" IN THE TRENCHES.

Prior to the handing over of the prizes the Secretary of the Association (Mr. W. Patrick) had a few words to say. He announced that arising out of a hint contained in a letter which had been received from Major Crosfield (the President of the Association)—whose name was received with loud cheers—a collection had been made on the green in order to provide footballs for the gallant Warrington Territorials at the Front, and, as a result, the sum of £2 12s. Bd. had been raised. Whilst that was not a bad sum, he said, it was hardly as much as he expected, but he had no doubt they would be able to get more somewhere else. He then pro- ceeded to read a brief note from Mrs. B. Fairclough, the wife of Colonel Fairclough, who commands the "Terriers," and who, he men- tioned, had looked in during the afternoon, but had been unable to stay to the close as she had a train to catch. As she was the President of the Territorial Equipment Fund, added Mr. Patrick, the Chairman of the Association had had great pleasure in handing to her a cheque for £lO. which represented one-third of the pro- ceeds of the handicap.

div.head: What The Equipment Fund Has Sent Out.
div.p: What The Equipment Fund Has Sent Out.

The Equipment Fund had been the means of sending to the Territorials 6,912 pairs of socks: 1,560 shirts, 720 woollen helmets, 2,217 body belts, 1,007 scarves, and £lO worth of 'writing paper. If the handicap had been the means of doing nothing more than help in the good work which those figures represente.l, h thought, the holding of it 4ad been justified. (Applause.) Mr. Patrick then went on to announce that he had received letters of apology from the Mayor, Sir Ar,thur Crosfield and Mr. John Randall (who was the donor cf one of the prizes), also the receipt of a brief letter from the esteemed President :if the Association, Major Crosfield. The Mayor' wrote that he was unable to at- tend as he had previously arranged to go to Shrewsbury,

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD'S MESSAGE.
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD'S MESSAGE.

Major Geo. Crosfield's letter to Mr. PatriA read: "I was very pleased 'co get the news about the Warrington Works' Bow.ing Association, and to learn that they had been so succe,44fttl in so good a cause. On behalf of Colonel Fair- clough and the regiment I wish particularly to thank you and your committee, as well as the Association in general, for the handsome con- tribution of £lO. Colonel Fairclough asks me 'to say that he would be very pleased if out of the £lO you would buy four footballs and send them straight out here. Our brave fellows need some recreation after the hard times they have been going through. You ask for a message to the Association. Well, I will give them one, and it is this: They must do all they can to help in seeing this thing through, now or never, and to that end they must shrink from no sacrifice, great or small, so that only then shall be victory." _ _ _

div.head: WHY SIR ARTHUR AND LADY CROSFIELD
div.p: WHY SIR ARTHUR AND LADY CROSFIELD
WERE ABSENT.

Writing from his town house, Sir Arthur Crosfield, Bart., said: "I dearly wish I coulo join you on Saturday, and that Lady Crosfield could come too. But both of us for some time past have been engaged to take an active part. here [at Highgate] in a function on behalf of the Red Crosi funds, for which we are also actively responsible. It is, therefore, simply impossible for either of us to get away, and wish you would kindly tell our friends how much we regret it. If I were not tied by the leg here in this way I should most certainly have come North on Saturday morning, so as to be with you. I can only say 'Better luck next time!' and wish you all a most successful land enjoyable afternoon."

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD'S NARROW ESCAPE.
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD'S NARROW ESCAPE.

Writing to Mr. E. A. -Sanders, the Liberal Agent, on the same matter, Sir Arthur said: "The function we have organised on behalf of the Red Cross funds—a function which closes on Satuttlay—is a function of no small import- ance here, and as Lady Crosfield and I have got the thing updt is absolutely imperative that we should be present. If only it was possible for me to be in two places at once you may be sure

I should have allowed nothing to prevent me coming down to-morrow, but not having that faculty the thing is impossible, because my presence here is really indispensable. Major Crosfield is paying a flying visit to London, on three days' leave from the Front. Ile lunched with us on Friday, and I beg you to tell all friends' of the Warrington Works' Bowling Association that he is in first-class form.

div.head: Two Bullet Holes Through His Cap.
div.p: Two Bullet Holes Through His Cap.

"The narrowness of the escape he has had y 9 may judge from the fact that when he appeared here, in khaki, we noticed two ominous holes in his khaki-coloured cap, both of them caused by ballots. A narrower shave no man could have! It is only the briefest possible visit that Malor CrosEeld is able to pay this time, as he is obliged to start back for the Front on Saturday evening, or Sunday at the latest." Extracts from t'he foregoing letters were read by Dlr. Patrick, who also announced that he had been in etinnuttnication 'with Lady Greenall, who, however, was unable to be present as she left for Prance on Priday night. But for That fact she would have -been with them.

In doing so he said that both of the Associations had done good and useful work for the lads at the Front—the lads of whom they were so justifiably proud. (Applause.) If bowlers felt that they wanted to do more than they had already done—well, they had only to hand over the brass' and the 'Association would see ,that it xas Propprly applied. (Hear, hear.)

THE LADIES SAY "THANK YOU!" div.head: NORTHERN UNION FOOTBALL.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION FOOTBALL.
Shall Competitive Football And Players' Fees Be Dropped?

div.head: PLEA OF THE PROFESSIONAL
div.p: PLEA OF THE PROFESSIONAL
BY "CENTRE."

At the meeting of the Northern Union Com- mittee, due to be held on • Tuesday of next week, it is thought possible in some circles that a strong and influential effort may be made to revise the decisions with regard to the gam( which were come to at last month's assembly of the delegates from the various clubs con stituting the Union, among them, of course, being Warrington. At present the Cnio) authorities stand committed to two important and far-reaching courses of action. The first is that no football of a competitive character shall be played—unless it be that various of the clubs feel disposed to do what they can with a view to fostering purely junior football, with a view to recruiting their ranks in the days when the war shall no longer be with us—and that no payment shall be made to players for football services rendered during the duration of the war in any of the friendly games which it will be open for the individual clubs to arrange among themselves.

div.head: WAS THE COMMITTEE'S DECISION PREMATURE? •
div.p: WAS THE COMMITTEE'S DECISION PREMATURE? •

There is in more than one quarter a growing feeling that the decision arrived at by the com- mittee with regard, at any rate, to the first prin- ciple, wa.s premature, seeing that it was reached in June, and before they could possibly- foretell what altered conditions September might not bring forth. Those who take this point of view naturally call attention to the fact that man cannot live. by work alone and, not illogically, want to know if a man must have a few hours' leisure, does it really make a difference whether he spends them in watching a competitive game or a purely friendly fixture? It cannot to any extent—so those who take this point of view claim—be a fear of serious interference with war-work that has prompted the decision of the committee, for the great majority of the works that are actually engaged on the production of the all-important material nearly all close down either wholly, or partially, on the afternoon on which the League and cup games are generally held, whilst the legislature gives such wide powers to the heads of firms that find Saturday afternoon work necessary as would render it highly improbable that workmen would be so silly or unpatriotic as to disturb war-work in order to go and see their " fancy " on the foot- ball field.

div.head: NO REAL REASON FOR ABANDONMENT
div.p: NO REAL REASON FOR ABANDONMENT
SAY MANY.

That being so it is urged that there is no real and sufficient reason why the great majority of respectable working men should not be allowed to spend their half-day off, "as usual," in watching the grand old game which is so dear to their hearts. That point of view, of course, leads on to the second issue—that of profes- sionalism or no professionalism in war-time. And here, whilst views are divided into two opposite camps, it is probable_ that the majority may feel that these are not days when young men should be paid to play. There is, however, the professional footballers' opinion to be taken into account, and he not unnatur- ally asks why he alone should be deprived of reward for the services he renders in adminis- tering to the recreative-side of human desire, while the actor and the music-hall artiste, the singer and the cinema operator are still allowed to pursue their avocations, unrestricted Ind at their old salary. i•

div.head: PROFESSIONAL FOOTBALLER NOT
div.p: THE PROFESSIONAL FOOTBALLER NOT
THE ONLY ENTERTAINER.

Further, he points out that in the great pnajority of instances he is, during the five days of the working week in which be is not engaged footballing, rendering useful work to the community as an ordinary worker; some, thing which cannot be said of the " profes- sional " whose sphere, is behind the footlights instead of on the green turf. "Why should not the footballer draw his small pay just as the music-hall artiste draws his big one?", a promi- nent Northern Union player asks, adding "Probably in nine cases out of ten the profes- sibnal footballer has more dependents to con- sider than has the professional entertainer, to say nothing of other responsibilities which the touring performer wots not of! The decision to prohibit without distinction, payment for foot- ball services during the war will come particu- larly hard on many, amongst them men who have sacrificed what might have been good, per- manent jobs elsewhere in order to go to the town of the club for which they have been play- ing, and where they have only found second-rate fill-in-the-time jobs to help 'em to eke out their football fees and retainers."
F NOT "AS USUAL," NO NEED TO DROP
THE GAME ALTOGETHER.
These and other points of vievi are, we learn,

likely to be urged at next Tuesday's meeting by those who feel that, whilst, perhaps, we must not expect football quite as usual, should the war—as there is every prospect of its doing —extend over next season, there is no reason why it should be dropped practically altogether and the professional should be sorely penalised. Personally, whilst dearly appreciating an ex- hilarating game of first-class football, behind which there is the impelling power of strong rivalry and competition, I am disposed to leave the issue, unquestioningly, to the wisdom of those delegated to voice the views of the mem- bers of the different big clubs affected.

div.head: BIG INVESTMENT IN THE WAR
div.p: BIG INVESTMENT IN THE WAR
LOAN.

At a meeting of the Northern Rugby Union, held in Manchester, the officials for next season were appointed as follows:—Chairman, Mr. J. H. Smith: Vice-chairman. Mr. J. Lewthwaite; Honorary Secretary, Mr. J. Platt. It was decided to invest £3,000 in the War Loan from the Union funds, and £l,OOO from the British Playing Fields Society, the trustees in each case to be Messrs. J. H. Smith, J. Lewth- , waite and J. Platt.

div.head: ASSOC lAT lON.
div.p: ASSOC lAT lON.
To Keep The Game Alive.
The Management Committee of the Football League have issued particulars of the scheme they suggest for keeping the game alive curing the coming winter.

It is suigested that the forty clubs be split up into sections in order to obviate long journeys. Medals will be offered for each divisional com- petition. The scheme will come before the League at their annual meeting on July 19th, and also be- fore the Football Association later.

div.head: LUXURIES v. NECESSITIES.
div.p: LUXURIES v. NECESSITIES.

The tendency in every direction to-day is to give up the use of all luxuries, but the bicycle is by no means in that category. There was a time when the bicycle was purely a pleasurein- strument, but that day has long passed. The bicycle is now universally recognised as the handiest, cheapest and quickest way of getting about, and the hundreds of thousands of people who use it for going to and from their work could testify to that. Moreover, there is, this year, a great increase in the popularity of cycling holidays—short tours taken to relieve the strain of war work, probably largely in con- sequence of the shutting down of all cheap facilities on the railways and the national des- sire for economy—for there is no holiday so cheap 'as that spent on a _bicycle. The value of a good machine, which will stand everlasting wear, is more than ever a point for the public, as, for instance, the experience 'of Mr. L. Bay- liss, of 224, Waterloo-road, Wolverhampton, who writes that he has ridden his Raleigh "during the last twelve months in all weathers" and has found it most satisfactory. The British bicycle has made its reputation on its sound quality., and probably a very great deal of the • popu- larity of the bicycle amongst the whole people is due to the high standard which the Raleigh and other leading manufacturers have always -Bet.
ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKING MEN'S
ASSOCIATION.
THE OPEN MATCH AT NORTON.

The first open contest held by the Northern Anglers of Warrington for a number of years proved a great success, 257 entries being ob- tained. That at a time when one-third of the N.A.A. members are serving their country, it must be reckoned as very good indeed. The entries mostly came from out of town. This alone proves that open contests can be held with success. Why it was not appreciated better by Warrington anglers, we'cannot imagine, as train service and time of the match were arranged to suit all those who worked on till one o'clock. Probably the pollution scare had a great deal to do with it. However, we got through by sheer hard work by all the officials, and with the ex- ception of a scarcity of fish during the contest, everything went off excellently. I have been criticised respecting mji, report in last week's issue. Well. I try to state plain facts, and facts that will be understood by all anglers, and I again state that the canal was in good condition on the Thursday before the match. Mr. J. Cox was fishing off Mr. Wil- liams's meadow and took fourteen roach in four hours' fishing, all in good buckle. A native of Preston Brook—whose name I have not to hand, but angleis will know him by "the Green- grocer," who resides opposite the Red Lion Hotel—took twelve roach and one eel the same afternoon. After visiting the canal I came home and made out my notes, also publishing the letter from the Runcorn secretary, who, I take it, is the best authority on such matters. Now after seeing the canal and fish caught and the letter from My. Clare, I will leave it to readers of angling notes to say what other report could have been made. If I was asked my personal opinion on canals in this district it would be quite another matter.

div.head: SPORT.
div.p: SPORT.

'Mr. W. Peter Aylinds then presented the prizes, and went on to thank the Association on behalf of his wife for the cheque for the Con- servative Women's Sewing Class, • and congratulated Mr. Willett and his committee upon the success which had attended the handi- cap. Owing. to the ,terrible anxiety. Nvhish gripped them all at the present time, it'was impossible for them to take their pleasures in quite the ordinary way, but it was quite right that they should take their exercise and keep themselves in health• by. so doing, especially when, as that afternoon, that exercise was directed to helping the men who were fighting the country's battles. (Hoar, hear.) The times were terrible. As Major Crosfield had so truly written, they had to stick on, and to be ready to make any sacrifice that might be neces- sary in order that they might achieve victory. Things during the last month or so had seemed to be going slowly in, the arena of war, and there was no doubt that a slight wave of pessi- mism had been passing through the land. Per- sonally, he believed that there was no ground for that pessimism. (Hear, hear.) Seeking Victory For The Sake of Peace.

Ile was satisfied that those best capable of judging agreed with him on that point. (Hear, hear.) It was perfectly true that they had found themselves up against a stiffer proposi- tion than they had anticipated—though they always knew that it would be, a stiff one !—and it was equally true that at the Present stage of the summer campaign, from which they had been hoping so much, they found themselves, owing to lack of sufficient guns, unable to press home to so speedily successful a conclusion as they could have wished, the great attack which had been planned. But at worst, it meant only ' more delay—and that was bad enough! It did not, however, mean defeat, but only that they had a terrific job on—one which they were going to see through and do thoroughly. (Cheers.) "Let us set' our teeth." added Mr. Rylands, "and behave as the British have always behaved in ,previous wars, and all will yet be well. Our forefathers, a hundred years ago, fought for seventeen years, and we are not behind our fore- fathers in courage, determination or devotion to our country. (Cheers.) We do not seek victory merely for victory's sake,' but for the sake of peace, and we must be prepared to face any sacrifice, however great it may be, in order to achieve that victory and gain the end upon which we have,' with our gallant Allies, set our hearts." (Renewed cheers.) _

Mr. W. Peter Rylands having presented the prizes in accordance with the list given above, after which the proceedings closed with a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Rylands, to Mr. Willett and to the donors of the prizes. Mr. Fred Dean was the proposer and Mr. Nathan Cook the seconder.
CONSERVATIVE WOMEN WORK UP NEARLY A TON AND A HALF OF WOOL.

Writing subsequently to Mr. Patrick, Mrs. W. Peter Rylands again expressed the Con- servative Women's appreciation of the cheque which had been handed over to them, and added: "As a matter of interest I might men- tion that the Association has worked up nearly a ton and a half of wool, in addition to other , materials, since the war -started."

div.head: MUNITION SHORTAGE.
div.p: MUNITION SHORTAGE.
Lord Haldane, Mr. Lloyd George, And
The Cause. _ _ Lord Haldane, in a speech delivered this week said:
In the month of October, while he (Lord Hal-

dane) was still a member of the Cabinet, there was a Committee assembled by the Government which included Lord Kitchener, Mr. Lloyd George, Mr. Churchill, Mr. McKenna, and other Cabinet Ministers, and their attention was drawn' to the urgent necessity to increase the supply of munitions. The changed conditions had necessitated a very large increase. "We consulted General von Donop," Lord Haldane continued, "and afterwards we sum- moned the great munition manufacturers, and we plaCed orders withothem which they under- took to carry out, and which if they had been

carried out would have placed this country in a position of tremendous- advantage, and we should have had a very large surplus. We placed these orders. The munition manufac- turers did their best to execute them. But there arose difficulties between labour and capital which confounded all the calculations of ,the munition manufacturers, and that is the source of the trouble to-day. It is not General von Donop. The industrial conditions in face of such a demand were such that the great munition manufacturers could not complete them, though they 4id their best."

div.head: MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S COMMENT.
div.p: MR. LLOYD GEORGE'S COMMENT.

Mr. Lloyd George has authorised the issue of the following statenrent with reference to Lord, Haldane's speech : Lord Haldane's version of what took place some months ago at a Committee of the Cabinet on arms is incomplete, and in some material respects inaccurate. At the proper time it will be necessary to go more fully into the matter, though Mr. Lloyd, George hopes he will not be driven to do so at this stage. But he would like to point out that the very fact of this conflict of memory having arisen shows the unwisdom of these partial and unauthorised disclosures of the decisions of highly confidential committees of the Cabinet.

div.head: MATCH.
div.p: THE MATCH.

After a little delay in getting in duplicate I tickets to get the number ,of entries, the draw I was gone through in quick style, and off they went to their peg numbers. Special speed had -to be put on by those who had drawn over the 200, as they knew they were in for a good tramp, and they were chaffed by the more fortunate anglers as 'they Wilt by. The call of time was made by five minutes past four and soon there was a cry of "landed." It was stated by the bank walker to be inside the first half minute. Anglers around thought they were in for a good time, but they were doomed to disappoint- ment. Results show 52 fish- were caught in the match; 36 caught fish, and the total weight was 41b. 3oz. 9dr., or less than 2 oz. a man who caught fish. It was hard lines on Mr. Henshall, who took five roach in such a contest, to be beaten by one eel. The winners were :- 1, J. Holden, 7oz. 7dr., £5. 2, W. Owen, soz. 6dr.. .R 2 10s. 3, T. Stockley, soz. ldr., £l. _ _
4, E. Henshall, 50z., 15s. 5, A. Chambers, 4oz. 2dr., 10s. _ _ _

6, J. Rowley, 3Oz. 15dr., 58. Not a very good result for such an entry, but these things cannot be seen beforehand in angling contests. We have in mind other con- testa where there was more at stake, but they have been reported on and there is nothing to gain by a repetition, especially when societies are trying to enrol the novice.

div.head: NEW COUNCILLOR FOR WHITECROSS.
div.p: NEW COUNCILLOR FOR WHITECROSS.
Mr. George Dale Succeeds Councillor Hawthorn.
WITHOUT A CONTEST.
AN UNOPPOSED RETURN.

Owing to the resignation of Councillor Joseph Hawthorn, who had held the seat :or a nam- ber of years; a vacancy occurred in the repre- sentation of the.Whitecross Ward on the Town Council. But it has been speedily filled, Mr. George Dale, of 23, Lovely-lane, the nominee of the Liberal party, having been accorded the honour of return without the trouble of fighting an election.

Thursday was the day 'fixed for receiving nominations, and only two papers were handed in-to the Town Clerk—those of Mia Dale's, and he has accordingly been declared elected. The first of Mr. Dale's nomination papers contained the names of Messrs. J. T. Barton and Thos. Dale as proposer and seconder respectively, and of the following us assentors; Messrs. J. A. Hey- wood, Jos. Owen, Thos. Lythgoe, Arthur Edwards, John Griffiths, Wm. G. Robinson, W. Bibby and Ezra Eden. The names contained in the second paper were :—Proposed; Mr. Geo. S. H. Gilling ; seconder: Mr. Fred Atkinson; assentors: Messrs. P. Gleave, A. E. Lowe. A. R. Buchanan. J. T. Dolan, J. Flood, W. Corlett, H. James and D. Callaghan.
ber who was respected, it was Councillor Haw- thorn, who *as always gentlemanly and busi- nesslike.

Alderman BENNETT, in supporting, said he thought the Mayor had expressed the matter very aptly when he remarked that ,Councillor Hawthorn's manner was one which could well be copied with usefulness to the town. Coun- cillor Hawthorn always spoke 'with considera- tion, and was entirely public-spirited. His' loss was one which every member of the Council would feel very deeply. (Hear, hear.) • Councillor ROBERTS said that he, as Councillor Hawthorn's colleague' in the representation of the Whitecross Ward, would like to add his testimony to the .value of the retiring Coun- cillor's services, and also to pay tribute to his extremely pleasant personality. He had known Councillor Hawthorn since he was a boy, 'and he also, knew the Councillor's family, which was' held in the highest respect- generally and was particularly respected in the district in which its members lived. Councillor Hawthorn would carry with him in his retirement the good wishes not only of his more immediate friends, but also of everyone who had been brought into contact with him. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: ALWAYS HONOURABLE AND STRAIGHTFORWARD.
div.p: ALWAYS HONOURABLE AND STRAIGHT- FORWARD.
Councillor WILSON said the retiring Coun- cillor was always most honourable and straight- forward, and his resignation was a real loss to the town.

The DErtrrY-lIIToR (Dr. Joseph) thought the Council might console themselves with the reflection that Connelllor Hawthorn was still a young man, and, that it was possible that in the future he might see his way to take up the duties again. Alderman TINNION said he had known Coun- cillor Hawthorn intimately for a number of years, and a more hard-working and earnest Councillor he never knew. (Hear, hear.) He did his work in committee thoroughly; attend- ing often at great inconvenience owing to his business being ,in Liverpool, and when he Alid attend his advice was of great value and assist- ance to the Chairman of whatever committee he happened to be en. He did not talk for talking's sake, but with the idea of assisting in getting both, sides of a question brought out before a decision was arrived at. It was a great loss to the town that such an honourable, straightforward and honest gentleman should feel it necessary to give up his public work. _ Alderman JAMES EveNs said the resignation of Councillor Hawthorn would create a gap which would not be easily filled.

COUNCILLOR GEO. DALE

who lives at 23, Lovely-lane, being married and a family man, is not a native of the town, but he came to Warrington and lived in Whitecross Ward when quite a youth. He went away frir a period; .but 24 years ago retaened and, for the last 21 years, he has been employ (1,1 by Messrs. Jos. Crosfield and Sons, Bank Quay. As technical chemist and manager of the fuel department, formerly under Dr. Markel and latterly under Dr. Armstrong, the present technical director of the firm, Councillor Dale has had an active part in the Work which has reduced the output of smoke. at Crosfield's until black smoke from their chimneys is practically unknown, and the firm can lay ,claim to saving many thousands a year upon fuel that once escaped in the form of smoke. In this respect alone Councillor Dale will be an asset to the town, and he ought to find a seat on the Health Committee at the earliest pOssible date. That he is well up in his particular branch is clear from the fact that he has taken diplomas in seven branches of science, and obtained first-class honours in practical chemistry at the Warrington Technical S'eltiiol, under Mr. 'Ruddick. Councillor Dale takes a deep interest in social questions. lie was President of the Bank Quay Guild of Help, which long anticipated the War- rington Citizens' Guild of Help, and on the latter he has ben, since its ,nwigure.tion, the district head for\ St. Austin's Wa ed. He is also a member of the 'executive: Among other- offices he bolds are those of Vice-President of the Bank Quay Nlision and manager of Evelyn-street Council School.

Chorus Of Praise.

The Warrington Town Council on Tuesday night received with expressions of general regret the resignation of Councillor Hawthorn one of the representatives of the Whitecrosr Ward, and decided to place cn record their appreciation of his services to the town. Coun- citlor Hawthorn . conveyed his intention of r&igiiing through the medium of the following letter, which was addressed to the Town Clerk. and was 'dated July 2nd:— It is with sincere regret I tender my resignation as a member of the Town Coun- cil. It has been my privilege to be one of the representatives of Whitecross Ward for over eight years, and I have had much pleasure in the work, but recently, owing to business engagements, I have found it in- creasingly difficult to attend to the duties. especially at the afternoon meetings; and. as I do not wish to hold a public position unless I can devote the time to the work, I have decided to withdraw. My recent removal to Stockton Heath is also another reason for taking this step. In tendering my resignation I wish to thank the Mayor and all the members of the Council for the courtesy extended to me, and to the official,: for the assistance they have always will- ingly rendered. I enclose the usual fee.
THE RETIRING COUNCILLOR.

the trench for about ten minutes, but when I clme round I soon found my way out." • Wounded Help the Wounded. In another letter Private Littler—who before the war worked for Messrs. Fairclough, builders —wrote: "You could not make anybody realise what a charge is like, unless they had been in one. . . . You could see the wounded carry- ing other wounded out of the trenches—German wounded as well! When you are ,in a charge and get right on to the Germans you seem to go out of your mind and you,don't,know what you are doing." - PRIVATE R. J. BLEASDALE. Man Who Thought Top Of His Head Was Off. As recorded in our columns last week, Private Richard James Bleasdale, who is married and
PRIVATE R. J. BLEASDALZ. Wounded.

whose home is at 33, Dudley-street, was wounded in the trenches during fighting in the early morning of Friday, June 27th. Thirty-two years of age and an old Volunteer, he jvined the Territorials on the outbreak. of war. Writing to his wife to tell her that he was wounded, he said "All at 'once I felt Quzh a thud and I thought the top of my head was gone." Since then, up to yesterday, nothing. further had been heard from him. PRIVATE F. HUNT. Nature Of His Injury Still Unknown At Home. Upon inquiry of Mrs. Fillingham, 103, Sharp- street, an "Examiner" representative was in- formed that so far nothing further had been heard concerning the wound received by Private F. Hunt in the fight. on June 27th. Private Hunt, who, .as we reported in our last issue, made his home with Mrs. Fillingham, has been

about twelve months in the Territorials, and at the time he volunteered for active service was employed by Messrs. Rylands Bros. He has a brother serving in the A.S.C. PRIVATE W. RorniWELL. He is suffering from a shrapnel-wound in the ankle and is progressing favourably. He joined the Terri- torials at the outbreak of war and is at pre- sent a member of "A" Company. He is a single man, 28 years of age, and resides, in
PRIVATE W. ROTHWELL. Wounded.

pease times, with his parents, in Longford. street. Private Rothwell was educated at Hamilton- street School, and was employed, before the war, at Messrs. Cunningham's Brewery. Two of his brothers are in' the Army—Driver John, who is serving at the Dardanelles with the Royal Field Artillery; and Trumpeter George, who is in training with the Royal Garrison Artillery.

MISSING ! News Wanted Respecting Private John Brimelow. Private John Brimelow, son of Mr—and Mrs. Richard Brimelow, 22, Pickmere-street, who took part in the famous "Terrier" charge in Flanders on the 16th inst., is missing: He was reported in the official list as wounded, but the officials have not been able to locate the hos- pital in which he is staying; nor has he written;, or caused to be written, a word to his parents. Before this action he had been a regu- lar correspondent, being a good scholar, and his prolonged silence, now really a month, is caus- ing much anxiety. Probable Theories. Private. Houghton, a neighbour, writing to his friends after the battle, said : "You may inform Mr. Brimelow that John
PRIVATE JOHN BRIMELOW. Reported Wounded and Missing.

got wounded while we were taking the German second line. I don't know whether he was car- ried out or not, or whether he would be gassed, as they tried to gas us:" His parents think that probably he was gassed after being wounded and that his memory may have become affected. This is the only way they can account for Ws silence if he was only wounded. They would be glad to hear from anyone who has seen or heard anything of him in either a home or a foreign hospital. Private George Cliffe wrote to say that Private Brimelow was "wounded and still re- ported missing. He might have been picked up by a stretcher-bearer of another regiment." Private Brimelow, who is 22 years of age, worked for Messrs. Kenyon and Co., oil mer- chants, and had been in the Territorials four years. His father is. employed at Messrs. Crosfield's (extracting plant). ,

KILLED IN ACTION. PRIVATE GILBERT SAVORY lilt In The Head By A Shell Fragment. Mrs. Savory, of 4, New-road, Latchford, War- rington, has received news that her husband, Rifleman Gilbert Savory, of the Rifle Brigade, has given his life for his country. The news reached her first through a letter written by a comrade of her late husband's—Rifleman J.

favourite with officers and men alike, on account of his generous and open-hearted nature, and his death is mourned by us all. During the first few days of fighting he did some very valu- able svad brave work. On the day of our land- ing on the Gallipoli Peninsula we forced our way inland for about four hundred yards from the beach, and there we entrenched. During the night the enemy attacked us in thousands and after about two hours' fighting we began to run short of ammunition. A Perilous Mission. " There were only two alternatives. We either had to get more ammunition, or else retire, so the officer asked for a volunteer to go back or ammunition. Tom volunteered and went to the beach under a hailstorm of bullets, and came back loaded with ammunition. For this ser- vice he was placed on the Commanding Officer's Staff, as fire observer. A few days later there was a general advance by the whole of our divi- sion, and Tom accompanied the Commanding Officer, who was then acting as Brigadier- General. During this advance Tom again ren- dered specially valuable service, going back, under heavy fire, for reinforcements. 33 years of age, married, and member of the Warrington Adult School. DRUMMER lIERBERT PRINCE. Out Of Hospital After Being Wounded In The Big, Charge.' Drummer, Herbert Prince is only eighteen years of age, but he has seen six months' ser- vice at the Front, and has bled in his country's cause. He "joined up" in October last and sailed for France in February, He was hit on, June 16th—in the big charge—and a few days later he wrote to his parents, who live at 35, Leicester-street, to tell them all about it, ex- plaining that his wound , was not as bad as it

hard for the third and fourth trenches, and, of course, we lost alot of men." Meeting With Another Wounded Drummer. Still later, the wounded drummer wrote home to say that his wrist was nearly better, and that he had been discharged from hospital. He mentions that one of the first persons he met aftei he came out of hospital was another drummer in the Terra9.rials, John Lightfoot, who had been hit in the shoulder and was, like himself, well on the way to recovery. " Jack Ryder," he says. "who was another of our drummers, has died: That Only leaves six of us out here." Drummer Prince is an all-round sportsman. Prior to going to the Front he worked as an apprentice at the roll-turning under his father, Mr. Geo. Thos. Prince, who is a foreman roll- turner at the Whitecross Works. He was educated at the Heathside School and wor- shipped at St. Paul's Church, whilst he was a Cvporal in thei Company of the Church Lade Bbgade connected with that Church. • - . PRIVATE J. J. WILLING TO GIVE ANY ASSISTANCE. In accordance with the bylaw the Mayor declared the seat vacant, and went on to say that he was sure that they, all appreciated Councillor Hawthorn's sehicei to the Council. Councillor Hawthorn was always willing to give any assistance it was possible for him to give. and his manner was one which could well bo copie'd with usefulness to the town. Councillor Hawthorn was a great friend of his (the layoi's), and he' felt sure that he was voicing tile opinion of• the members when he said how sorry they weie to lose him from public work. (Hear, hear.) He moved that the Council's appreciation of Councillor Hawthorn's services be put on record, and that a suitable letter be sent to him. PUBLIC • AIIiUSEMENt. • •.• . • . • A "TRUMP HAND" 'AT THE HIPPODROME. The manager of the Hippodrome has a "trump land " this week. The " star " turn is provided by Harry Atkinson and Co., ia a musical novelty, "'The Unhappy Medium," in- troducing some wonderful imitations of musi- cal instruments. It is an extremely fine turn. Mi. Atkinson's illusions are amongst the best we can recall, and the .enthusiastic plaudits of the audience are well merited. Briff, Braff and Broff give us something quite in the front rank of comedy, tumbling. Their athletics are excel- lent, and they cause plenty of fun. Out of the rut of the .average conjuring entertainment is that given by Gene Gordon, the comedy magician. One is undecided whether the wizardy or the wit is the better. Cole Cliffe, a Yorkshire cerriedian, is responsible fur some admirable impersonations. His is a really funny) contribution, and is immensely and deservedly,popular. The Martini Trio present a most enjoyable musical act. So, too, do the Sisters Reeve, whose voices harmonise well. A first rate acrobatic performance is given by the Annytos trio, and the Bros. Bury " piwatorial comedians," in . their amusing speciality, "Fish Cutlets," complete a pro- gramme to be very highly recommended. Fine Fare Promised Next Week. What bids fair to be a specially attractive programme has been drawn up for pent week. The piece de resistance will be the screamingly funny sketch " Half-a-Dollar," which will be presented by Alan Borthwick and Co., includ- ing W. A. Haines is tits original part. The Five clovers, a troupe of Spaniards, promise something extra special in the way of gym- nastics and acrobatics, and the Real McKays will be found to be a clever Scotch juvenile troupe. Other turns will include Herd and Gard, "the limite in comedy musicians "; Mike Cray and Dog Dooley, in comedy juggling: Mary Moran, in "sobs, thrills and laughs," and The Stevan.os, "-original eccentric college boys," (S-..c. CHARLIE CHAPLIN GOING STRONG AT STAR KINEMA. To choose which is the more attractive side of this week's strong Kinema programmes would be a, hard task. "What's-His-Name?" a lengthy and engrossing domestic drama—to which was assigned during the former part of the week one of the chief places in the pro- gramme—was a very well-staged and pathetic story of love-triumphant. On the other hand, one was provided with extremely funny antics by the wonderful Charlie Chaplin, "the uni- versal rib-tickler." Certainly we have seen him in better films, yet "Charlie's Musical Career" left little to be desired. "The Chil- dren of Tulip Land" was a pretty coloured film taken in Holland; whilst "A Soldier's Mother" gave an intense and gruesome de- scription of a deplorable Hun episode at the Front. "Pathe's Animated Gazette" was this time devoted to the lighter side of British Army training. To-day's bills-of-fare once again bear the name of "Charlie" in capital letters; whilst the "drama principe " is entitled "The Men from Mexico." For Next Week. Two specially, attractive films have been secured to top the bill at next week's shows. The big thing for the first three nights will be "The Brute!" and for the second three nights Behind the Scenes." A Girl and Her Looks. Tell a girl she has a pretty nose and she will become cross-eyed from constantly looking at it. A girl can look at a portrait pof her curly- haired grandmother for hours, wondering how she did it.
